Why are you blaming me then, if I actually know something? What can I tell this slave? If I stay quiet, he'll explode. So I have to say this: "Forgive me, like you'd forgive someone in love. I'm not in control of myself. I'm mad."

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-with-c.originalText: It is circumstances (difficulties) which show what men are. Therefore when a difficulty falls upon you, remember that God, like a trainer of wrestlers, has matched you with a rough young man. For what purpose? you may say. Why, that you may become an Olympic conqueror; but it is not accomplished without sweat. In my opinion no man has had a more profitable difficulty than you have had, if you choose to make use of it as an athlete would deal with a young antagonist.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-with-c.plainEnglish: Difficult situations reveal who you really are. So when trouble hits you, remember that God is like a wrestling coach who pairs you with a tough opponent. Why? So you can become a champion. But you can't win without sweating for it. I think no one has ever gotten a better opportunity than the one you have right now — if you choose to use it like an athlete uses a sparring partner.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-with-c.originalText: We are now sending a scout to Rome; but no man sends a cowardly scout, who, if he only hears a noise and sees a shadow anywhere, comes running back in terror and reports that the enemy is close at hand. So now if you should come and tell us: "Fearful is the state of affairs at Rome; terrible is death; terrible is exile; terrible is calumny; terrible is poverty; fly, my friends, the enemy is near," we shall answer: "Begone, prophesy for yourself; we have committed only one fault, that we sent such a scout."
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-with-c.plainEnglish: Say we're sending a scout to Rome. You don't send a coward who hears one noise or sees a shadow and comes running back in terror, yelling that the enemy is coming. So if you come to us and say: 'Things are terrible in Rome! Death is awful! Exile is awful! Public shame is awful! Poverty is awful! Run, friends, the enemy is coming!' — we'll tell you: 'Get lost. Go prophesy somewhere else. Our only mistake was sending a scout like you.'

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-with-c.originalText: Diogenes, who was sent as a scout before you, made a different report to us. He says that death is no evil, for neither is it base; he says that fame (reputation) is the noise of madmen. And what has this spy said about pain, about pleasure, and about poverty? He says that to be naked is better than any purple robe, and to sleep on the bare ground is the softest bed; and he gives as a proof of each thing that he affirms his own courage, his tranquillity, his freedom, and the healthy appearance and compactness of his body. There is no enemy near, he says; all is peace. How so, Diogenes? "See," he replies, "if I am struck, if I have been wounded, if I have fled from any man." This is what a scout ought to be. But you come to us and tell us one thing after another. Will you not go back, and you will see clearer when you have laid aside fear?
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-with-c.plainEnglish: Diogenes went ahead of us as a scout and brought back a different report. He says death is no evil — it's not shameful. He says fame is just noise made by crazy people. And what did this scout say about pain, pleasure, and poverty? He says being naked is better than wearing royal robes. Sleeping on the bare ground is the softest bed. He proves each claim through his own courage, calmness, freedom, and healthy, strong body. "There's no enemy nearby," he says. "All is peaceful." How can that be, Diogenes? "Look," he replies, "have I been struck? Have I been wounded? Have I run away from anyone?" This is what a scout should be. But you come to us telling us one frightening thing after another. Go back out there. You'll see more clearly once you've gotten rid of your fear.

discourses_on-the-same.originalText: If these things are true, and if we are not silly, and are not acting hypocritically when we say that the good of man is in the will, and the evil too, and that everything else does not concern us, why are we still disturbed, why are we still afraid? The things about which we have been busied are in no man's power; and the things which are in the power of others, we care not for. What kind of trouble have we still?
discourses_on-the-same.plainEnglish: If all this is true, and we're not being foolish or fake when we say that good and evil come from our choices — and everything else doesn't matter to us — then why are we still upset? Why are we still afraid? The things we've been worrying about are outside everyone's control. The things that are in other people's control don't concern us. So what's left to trouble us?

discourses_on-the-same.originalText: But give me directions. Why should I give you directions? Has not Zeus given you directions? Has he not given to you what is your own free from hindrance and free from impediment, and what is not your own subject to hindrance and impediment? What directions then, what kind of orders did you bring when you came from him? Keep by every means what is your own; do not desire what belongs to others. Fidelity (integrity) is your own, virtuous shame is your own; who then can take these things from you? who else than yourself will hinder you from using them? But how do you act?
discourses_on-the-same.plainEnglish: But give me directions. Why should I give you directions? Hasn't Zeus already given you directions? Hasn't he given you what's truly yours — free from any obstacles? And what's not truly yours — subject to obstacles? So what directions did you bring when you came from him? Keep what's yours by any means necessary. Don't desire what belongs to others. Your integrity is yours. Your sense of honor is yours. Who can take these things from you? Who else but you will stop yourself from using them? But how do you actually act?

discourses_on-the-same.originalText: When you seek what is not your own, you lose that which is your own. Having such promptings and commands from Zeus, what kind do you still ask from me? Am I more powerful than he, am I more worthy of confidence? But if you observe these, do you want any others besides? "Well, but he has not given these orders," you will say. Produce your præcognitions ([Greek: prolaepseis]), produce these proofs of philosophers, produce what you have often heard, and produce what you have said yourself, produce what you have read, produce what you have meditated on; and you will then see that all these things are from God.
discourses_on-the-same.plainEnglish: When you chase after things that aren't yours, you lose what actually belongs to you. If Zeus himself gives you these rules and commands, what more do you need from me? Am I more powerful than he is? Am I more trustworthy? If you follow these commands, do you really need any others? "But he never gave me these orders," you'll say. Then bring out your basic ideas. Bring out your philosophical proofs. Bring out what you've heard so many times, what you've said yourself, what you've read, what you've thought about. You'll see that all these things come from God.

discourses_on-the-same.originalText: If I have set my admiration on the poor body, I have given myself up to be a slave; if on my poor possessions, I also make myself a slave. For I immediately make it plain with what I may be caught; as if the snake draws in his head, I tell you to strike that part of him which he guards; and do you be assured that whatever part you choose to guard, that part your master will attack. Remembering this, whom will you still flatter or fear?
discourses_on-the-same.plainEnglish: If you place too much value on your body, you become a slave to it. If you place too much value on your possessions, you become a slave to them too. You immediately show others your weak spot — your vulnerability. It's like a snake pulling its head back to protect it. That just tells you exactly where to strike. Be sure of this: whatever you desperately try to protect is exactly what someone else will use to control you. Remember this truth. Who will you still try to please or fear?

discourses_on-the-same.originalText: But I should like to sit where the Senators sit. Do you see that you are putting yourself in straits, you are squeezing yourself? How then shall I see well in any other way in the amphitheatre? Man, do not be a spectator at all, and you will not be squeezed. Why do you give yourself trouble? Or wait a little, and when the spectacle is over, seat yourself in the place reserved for the Senators and sun yourself. For remember this general truth, that it is we who squeeze ourselves, who put ourselves in straits; that is, our opinions squeeze us and put us in straits. For what is it to be reviled? Stand by a stone and revile it, and what will you gain? If then a man listens like a stone, what profit is there to the reviler? But if the reviler has as a stepping-stone (or ladder) the weakness of him who is reviled, then he accomplishes something. Strip him. What do you mean by him? Lay hold of his garment, strip it off. I have insulted you. Much good may it do you.
discourses_on-the-same.plainEnglish: But I want to sit where the Senators sit. Do you see what you're doing to yourself? You're putting yourself in a tight spot. You're squeezing yourself. How else can I get a good view at the amphitheater? Listen — don't go to the show at all, and you won't get squeezed. Why are you making trouble for yourself? Or just wait a little. When the show is over, go sit in the Senators' seats and enjoy the sun. Remember this basic truth: we squeeze ourselves. We put ourselves in tight spots. Our opinions do this to us. What does it mean to be insulted? Go stand by a rock and insult it. What do you accomplish? Nothing. If a person listens like a rock, what good does it do the insulter? But if the insulter can use the weakness of the insulted person as a stepping stone, then he gets somewhere. Strip him naked. What do you mean, strip him? Grab his clothes and pull them off. "I have insulted you." Good for you.

discourses_on-the-same.originalText: This was the practice of Socrates; this was the reason why he always had one face. But we choose to practise and study anything rather than the means by which we shall be unimpeded and free. You say: "Philosophers talk paradoxes." But are there no paradoxes in the other arts? And what is more paradoxical than to puncture a man's eye in order that he may see? If any one said this to a man ignorant of the surgical art, would he not ridicule the speaker? Where is the wonder, then, if in philosophy also many things which are true appear paradoxical to the inexperienced?
discourses_on-the-same.plainEnglish: This is how Socrates lived. This is why he always had the same calm expression on his face. But we choose to practice and study everything except the one thing that would make us truly free and unimpeded. You complain: "Philosophers say things that don't make sense." But don't other fields have things that sound crazy too? What sounds more insane than cutting into someone's eye so they can see better? If you said that to someone who knew nothing about surgery, wouldn't they laugh at you? So why are you surprised that in philosophy, many true things sound strange to beginners?

discourses_in-how-many-ways-appearances-.originalText: Appearances are to us in four ways. For either things appear as they are; or they are not, and do not even appear to be; or they are, and do not appear to be; or they are not, and yet appear to be. Further, in all these cases to form a right judgment (to hit the mark) is the office of an educated man. But whatever it is that annoys (troubles) us, to that we ought to apply a remedy. If the sophisms of Pyrrho and of the Academics are what annoys (troubles), we must apply the remedy to them. If it is the persuasion of appearances, by which some things appear to be good, when they are not good, let us seek a remedy for this.
discourses_in-how-many-ways-appearances-.plainEnglish: Things can appear to us in four ways. Sometimes things appear exactly as they are. Sometimes they don't exist and don't appear to exist either. Sometimes they do exist but don't appear to exist. And sometimes they don't exist but appear to exist anyway. In all these cases, making the right judgment is what an educated person does. But whatever is bothering you — that's where you need to focus your remedy. If the clever arguments of Pyrrho and the Academics are troubling you, then apply your remedy there. If it's the deceptive power of appearances — making some things look good when they're actually not good — then seek a remedy for that.

discourses_in-how-many-ways-appearances-.originalText: If it is habit which annoys us, we must try to seek aid against habit. What aid, then, can we find against habit? The contrary habit. You hear the ignorant say: "That unfortunate person is dead; his father and mother are overpowered with sorrow; he was cut off by an untimely death and in a foreign land." Hear the contrary way of speaking. Tear yourself from these expressions; oppose to one habit the contrary habit; to sophistry oppose reason, and the exercise and discipline of reason; against persuasive (deceitful) appearances we ought to have manifest præcognitions ([Greek: prolaepseis]), cleared of all impurities and ready to hand.
discourses_in-how-many-ways-appearances-.plainEnglish: If bad habits are bothering you, you need to fight them. How do you fight a habit? With the opposite habit. You hear ignorant people say: "That poor person is dead. His parents are crushed with grief. He died too young and far from home." Listen to the opposite way of talking. Pull yourself away from these words. Fight one habit with its opposite. Fight bad reasoning with good reasoning. Train your mind to think clearly. When things seem scary or sad, you need clear thoughts ready to use — thoughts that aren't clouded by emotion.

discourses_in-how-many-ways-appearances-.originalText: When death appears an evil, we ought to have this rule in readiness, that it is fit to avoid evil things, and that death is a necessary thing. For what shall I do, and where shall I escape it? Suppose that I am not Sarpedon, the son of Zeus, nor able to speak in this noble way. I will go and I am resolved either to behave bravely myself or to give to another the opportunity of doing so; if I cannot succeed in doing anything myself, I will not grudge another the doing of something noble. Suppose that it is above our power to act thus; is it not in our power to reason thus? Tell me where I can escape death; discover for me the country, show me the men to whom I must go, whom death does not visit. Discover to me a charm against death. If I have not one, what do you wish me to do? I cannot escape from death. Shall I not escape from the fear of death, but shall I die lamenting and trembling?
discourses_in-how-many-ways-appearances-.plainEnglish: When death seems like something terrible, remember this rule: we should avoid evil things, but death is unavoidable. So what am I supposed to do? Where can I run from it? Let's say I'm not some hero like Sarpedon who can speak nobly about death. Even so, I'll go forward. I'm determined to either act bravely myself or give someone else the chance to do something brave. If I can't accomplish anything great myself, I won't begrudge someone else doing something noble. But suppose even that is beyond us — can't we at least think clearly about this? Tell me where I can escape death. Show me the country where death doesn't exist. Show me the people death never visits. Find me a magic spell against death. If there isn't one, what do you want me to do? I can't escape death. So should I at least escape the fear of death? Or should I die crying and shaking?

discourses_in-how-many-ways-appearances-.originalText: For the origin of perturbation is this, to wish for something, and that this should not happen. Therefore if I am able to change externals according to my wish, I change them; but if I cannot, I am ready to tear out the eyes of him who hinders me. For the nature of man is not to endure to be deprived of the good, and not to endure the falling into the evil. Then at last, when I am neither able to change circumstances nor to tear out the eyes of him who hinders me, I sit down and groan, and abuse whom I can, Zeus and the rest of the gods. For if they do not care for me, what are they to me? Yes, but you will be an impious man. In what respect, then, will it be worse for me than it is now? To sum up, remember that unless piety and your interest be in the same thing, piety cannot be maintained in any man. Do not these things seem necessary (true)?
discourses_in-how-many-ways-appearances-.plainEnglish: Here's how upset feelings start: you want something, and then it doesn't happen. So if I can change external things to match what I want, I'll change them. But if I can't, I'm ready to attack whoever is stopping me. It's human nature — we can't stand being deprived of good things, and we can't stand bad things happening to us. Finally, when I can neither change my circumstances nor attack the person blocking me, I sit and complain and curse whoever I can reach — Zeus and the other gods. If they don't care about me, what good are they to me? "But then you'll be impious." How will that make things worse for me than they already are? Here's the point: remember that unless being pious actually serves your interests, no one can stay pious. Don't these things seem obviously true?

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.originalText: What is the cause of assenting to anything? The fact that it appears to be true. It is not possible then to assent to that which appears not to be true. Why? Because this is the nature of the understanding, to incline to the true, to be dissatisfied with the false, and in matters uncertain to withhold assent. What is the proof of this? Imagine (persuade yourself), if you can, that it is now night. It is not possible. Take away your persuasion that it is day. It is not possible. Persuade yourself or take away your persuasion that the stars are even in number. It is impossible.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.plainEnglish: Why do you agree with something? Because it seems true to you. You can't agree with something that seems false. Why not? Because that's how your mind works. It naturally goes toward what's true. It rejects what's false. When things are unclear, it holds back. Want proof? Try to convince yourself it's nighttime right now. You can't do it. Try to stop believing it's daytime. You can't. Try to convince yourself the stars are an even number, or try to stop believing it. Impossible.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.originalText: When then any man assents to that which is false, be assured that he did not intend to assent to it as false, for every soul is unwillingly deprived of the truth, as Plato says; but the falsity seemed to him to be true. Well, in acts what have we of the like kind as we have here truth or falsehood? We have the fit and the not fit (duty and not duty), the profitable and the unprofitable, that which is suitable to a person and that which is not, and whatever is like these. Can then a man think that a thing is useful to him and not choose it? He cannot.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.plainEnglish: When someone believes something false, don't think they chose to believe a lie. Nobody wants to be wrong, as Plato said. The false thing just looked true to them. Now, when it comes to actions, what do we have that's like truth and falsehood? We have what's right and what's wrong. What helps us and what hurts us. What fits our character and what doesn't. Can someone think something is good for them and then not want it? No way.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.originalText: How says Medea? "'Tis true I know what evil I shall do, But passion overpowers the better counsel." She thought that to indulge her passion and take vengeance on her husband was more profitable than to spare her children. It was so; but she was deceived. Show her plainly that she is deceived, and she will not do it; but so long as you do not show it, what can she follow except that which appears to herself (her opinion)? Nothing else. Why then are you angry with the unhappy woman that she has been bewildered about the most important things, and is become a viper instead of a human creature? And why not, if it is possible, rather pity, as we pity the blind and the lame, so those who are blinded and maimed in the faculties which are supreme?
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.plainEnglish: Look at what Medea says: "I know what I'm about to do is wrong, but my anger is stronger than my better judgment." She thought getting revenge on her husband was worth more than sparing her children. That's how it seemed to her — but she was wrong. Show her clearly that she's wrong, and she won't do it. But as long as you don't show her, what else can she follow except what seems right to her? Nothing else. So why are you angry with this poor woman for being confused about the most important things? Why hate her for becoming a monster instead of staying human? Why not pity her instead, the way we pity the blind and the lame? She's just as disabled — except her damage is in the most important part of all.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.originalText: Whoever then clearly remembers this, that to man the measure of every act is the appearance (the opinion), whether the thing appears good or bad. If good, he is free from blame; if bad, himself suffers the penalty, for it is impossible that he who is deceived can be one person, and he who suffers another person—whoever remembers this will not be angry with any man, will not be vexed at any man, will not revile or blame any man, nor hate, nor quarrel with any man.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.plainEnglish: Remember this clearly: every person acts based on how things appear to them. If something seems good to them, you can't blame them for acting on it. If something seems bad to them, they suffer for their mistake. The person who is deceived and the person who suffers are the same person. When you remember this, you won't get angry at anyone. You won't be annoyed with anyone. You won't insult or blame anyone. You won't hate anyone or pick fights with anyone.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.originalText: So then all these great and dreadful deeds have this origin, in the appearance (opinion)? Yes, this origin and no other. The Iliad is nothing else than appearance and the use of appearances. It appeared to Alexander to carry off the wife of Menelaus. It appeared to Helene to follow him. If then it had appeared to Menelaus to feel that it was a gain to be deprived of such a wife, what would have happened? Not only would the Iliad have been lost, but the Odyssey also. On so small a matter then did such great things depend?
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.plainEnglish: So all these great and terrible events come from one thing: how we see things? Yes, that's the only source. The Iliad is nothing but opinions and what people do with their opinions. Alexander thought it was right to steal Menelaus's wife. Helen thought it was right to go with him. But what if Menelaus had thought, 'Good riddance to that wife'? What would have happened then? We wouldn't have the Iliad or the Odyssey. Such huge consequences from such a small thing — how we choose to see events?

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.originalText: But what do you mean by such great things? Wars and civil commotions, and the destruction of many men and cities. And what great matter is this? Is it nothing? But what great matter is the death of many oxen, and many sheep, and many nests of swallows or storks being burnt or destroyed? Are these things then like those? Very like. Bodies of men are destroyed, and the bodies of oxen and sheep; the dwellings of men are burnt, and the nests of storks. What is there in this great or dreadful? Or show me what is the difference between a man's house and a stork's nest, as far as each is a dwelling; except that man builds his little houses of beams and tiles and bricks, and the stork builds them of sticks and mud. Are a stork and a man then like things? What say you? In body they are very much alike.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.plainEnglish: But what do you mean by "such great things"? Wars and civil unrest, and the destruction of many people and cities. What's so important about this? Is it nothing? Well, what's so important about many oxen dying, or many sheep, or many nests of swallows or storks being burned or destroyed? Are these things similar? Very similar. Human bodies are destroyed, and so are the bodies of oxen and sheep. Human homes are burned, and so are storks' nests. What's so great or terrible about this? Or show me the difference between a human house and a stork's nest, since both are homes. The only difference is that humans build their little houses from wood beams, tiles, and bricks, while storks build theirs from sticks and mud. Are a stork and a human similar things then? What do you say? In terms of their bodies, they're very much alike.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.originalText: Does a man then differ in no respect from a stork? Don't suppose that I say so; but there is no difference in these matters (which I have mentioned). In what then is the difference? Seek and you will find that there is a difference in another matter. See whether it is not in a man the understanding of what he does, see if it is not in social community, in fidelity, in modesty, in steadfastness, in intelligence. Where then is the great good and evil in men? It is where the difference is. If the difference is preserved and remains fenced round, and neither modesty is destroyed, nor fidelity, nor intelligence, then the man also is preserved; but if any of these things is destroyed and stormed like a city, then the man too perishes: and in this consist the great things.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.plainEnglish: So does a man differ from a stork in any way? Don't think I'm saying no. But there's no difference when it comes to the things I just mentioned. So where is the difference? Look for it and you'll find the difference lies somewhere else. Notice that humans understand what they're doing. Notice they live in communities. They show loyalty, modesty, courage, and intelligence. So where do you find great good and evil in people? Right where the difference lies. If you preserve and protect these qualities — if you don't destroy your modesty, loyalty, or intelligence — then you preserve yourself as a human being. But if any of these gets destroyed and overrun like a conquered city, then you as a person are destroyed too. This is what the truly important things are.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.originalText: Alexander, you say, sustained great damage then when the Hellenes invaded and when they ravaged Troy, and when his brothers perished. By no means; for no man is damaged by an action which is not his own; but what happened at that time was only the destruction of stork's nests. Now the ruin of Alexander was when he lost the character of modesty, fidelity, regard to hospitality, and to decency. When was Achilles ruined? Was it when Patroclus died? Not so. But it happened when he began to be angry, when he wept for a girl, when he forgot that he was at Troy not to get mistresses, but to fight. These things are the ruin of men, this is being besieged, this is the destruction of cities, when right opinions are destroyed, when they are corrupted.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-angry.plainEnglish: You say Alexander suffered great damage when the Greeks invaded Troy and his brothers died. Not at all. No one is damaged by actions that aren't their own. What happened then was just the destruction of stork's nests. Alexander's real ruin came when he lost his sense of decency, loyalty, hospitality, and honor. When was Achilles ruined? When Patroclus died? No. It happened when he gave in to anger, when he cried over a girl, when he forgot he was at Troy to fight, not to chase women. These things ruin men. This is what it means to be under siege. This is how cities fall — when right thinking is destroyed and corrupted.

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: The being (nature) of the good is a certain will; the being of the bad is a certain kind of will. What, then, are externals? Materials for the will, about which the will being conversant shall obtain its own good or evil. How shall it obtain the good? If it does not admire (over-value) the materials; for the opinions about the materials, if the opinions are right, make the will good: but perverse and distorted opinions make the will bad. God has fixed this law, and says, "If you would have anything good, receive it from yourself." You say, No, but I will have it from another. Do not so: but receive it from yourself.
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: Good comes from having the right kind of will. Bad comes from having the wrong kind of will. So what about external things? They're just raw material for your will to work with. Your will becomes good or bad based on how it handles this material. How does it become good? By not overvaluing the material itself. If you have the right opinions about external things, your will becomes good. If you have twisted, wrong opinions about them, your will becomes bad. God has set up this rule: "If you want anything good, get it from yourself." You say, "No, I want to get it from someone else." Don't do that. Get it from yourself.

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: Therefore when the tyrant threatens and calls me, I say, Whom do you threaten? If he says, I will put you in chains, I say, You threaten my hands and my feet. If he says, I will cut off your head, I reply, You threaten my head. If he says, I will throw you into prison, I say, You threaten the whole of this poor body. If he threatens me with banishment, I say the same. Does he then not threaten you at all? If I feel that all these things do not concern me, he does not threaten me at all; but if I fear any of them, it is I whom he threatens. Whom then do I fear? the master of what? The master of things which are in my own power? There is no such master. Do I fear the master of things which are not in my power? And what are these things to me?
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: So when a tyrant threatens me and summons me, I ask: Who are you threatening? If he says, "I'll put you in chains," I say, "You're threatening my hands and feet." If he says, "I'll cut off your head," I reply, "You're threatening my head." If he says, "I'll throw you in prison," I say, "You're threatening this poor body." If he threatens banishment, I say the same thing. So does he threaten me at all? If I realize these things don't really concern me, then he's not threatening me at all. But if I'm afraid of any of them, then yes — he is threatening me. So who should I fear? The master of what? The master of things that are in my control? No such master exists. Should I fear the master of things outside my control? But what do those things have to do with me?

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: Do you philosophers then teach us to despise kings? I hope not. Who among us teaches to claim against them the power over things which they possess? Take my poor body, take my property, take my reputation, take those who are about me. If I advise any persons to claim these things, they may truly accuse me. Yes, but I intend to command your opinions also. And who has given you this power? How can you conquer the opinion of another man? By applying terror to it, he replies, I will conquer it. Do you not know that opinion conquers itself, and is not conquered by another? But nothing else can conquer will except the will itself.
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: Do we philosophers teach you to despise kings? I hope not. Who among us tells you to fight them for the power they have? Take my body, take my property, take my reputation, take the people around me. If I told anyone to fight for these things, you could rightly accuse me. But you say, 'I want to control your thoughts too.' Who gave you that power? How can you conquer another person's mind? 'By scaring them,' you say, 'I'll conquer it.' Don't you know that the mind conquers itself? It's not conquered by others. Nothing else can conquer the will except the will itself.

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: For this reason too the law of God is most powerful and most just, which is this: Let the stronger always be superior to the weaker. Ten are stronger than one. For what? For putting in chains, for killing, for dragging whither they choose, for taking away what a man has. The ten therefore conquer the one in this in which they are stronger. In what then are the ten weaker? If the one possesses right opinions and the others do not. Well then, can the ten conquer in this matter? How is it possible? If we were placed in the scales, must not the heavier draw down the scale in which it is.
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: Here's why God's law is so powerful and fair: the stronger always beats the weaker. Ten people are stronger than one person. Stronger at what? At putting someone in chains, killing them, dragging them wherever they want, taking their stuff. So yes, ten people beat one person in these ways because they're stronger. But where are the ten people weaker? When the one person has the right ideas and the ten don't. Can the ten people win in that area? How could they? If you put us on a scale, wouldn't the heavier side pull the scale down?

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: How strange then that Socrates should have been so treated by the Athenians. Slave, why do you say Socrates? Speak of the thing as it is: how strange that the poor body of Socrates should have been carried off and dragged to prison by stronger men, and that anyone should have given hemlock to the poor body of Socrates, and that it should breathe out the life. Do these things seem strange, do they seem unjust, do you on account of these things blame God? Had Socrates then no equivalent for these things? Where then for him was the nature of good? Whom shall we listen to, you or him? And what does Socrates say? "Anytus and Melitus can kill me, but they cannot hurt me." And further, he says, "If it so pleases God, so let it be."
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: How strange that the Athenians treated Socrates so badly! Wait — stop calling him Socrates. Let's be precise here. How strange that some stronger men dragged Socrates's poor body off to prison. How strange that someone gave hemlock poison to Socrates's poor body and made it stop breathing. Do these things seem strange to you? Do they seem unfair? Do you blame God for them? Did Socrates get nothing good in return? Where was his sense of what's truly good? Who should we listen to — you or him? What does Socrates say? "Anytus and Melitus can kill me, but they cannot hurt me." And he also says, "If this is what God wants, so be it."

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: But show me that he who has the inferior principles overpowers him who is superior in principles. You will never show this, nor come near showing it; for this is the law of nature and of God that the superior shall always overpower the inferior. In what? In that in which it is superior. One body is stronger than another: many are stronger than one: the thief is stronger than he who is not a thief. This is the reason why I also lost my lamp, because in wakefulness the thief was superior to me. But the man bought the lamp at this price: for a lamp he became a thief, a faithless fellow, and like a wild beast. This seemed to him a good bargain. Be it so.
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: But show me someone with weaker principles who defeats someone with stronger principles. You never will. You can't even come close. This is a law of nature and God: the superior always beats the inferior. In what way? In whatever makes it superior. One body is stronger than another. Many people are stronger than one person. A thief is stronger than someone who isn't a thief. That's why I lost my lamp too — the thief was better than me at staying awake. But look at what the man paid for that lamp. For one lamp, he became a thief, a liar, and a savage. He thought it was a good deal. Fine. Let him think that.

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: But a man has seized me by the cloak, and is drawing me to the public place: then others bawl out, Philosopher, what has been the use of your opinions? see, you are dragged to prison, you are going to be beheaded. And what system of philosophy could I have made so that, if a stronger man should have laid hold of my cloak, I should not be dragged off; that if ten men should have laid hold of me and cast me into prison, I should not be cast in? Have I learned nothing else then? I have learned to see that everything which happens, if it be independent of my will, is nothing to me. I may ask, if you have not gained by this. Why then do you seek advantage in anything else than in that in which you have learned that advantage is?
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: But someone grabs me by my cloak and drags me to the town square. Then others shout, "Philosopher, what good are your beliefs now? Look, you're being dragged to prison. You're about to be executed." What philosophy could I have developed that would stop a stronger man from grabbing my cloak and dragging me away? What system would prevent ten men from throwing me in prison? Have I learned nothing then? I have learned to see that everything that happens — if it's beyond my control — means nothing to me. Haven't you gained something from this? Then why do you look for benefit anywhere else except in what you've learned has real value?

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: Will you not leave the small arguments about these matters to others, to lazy fellows, that they may sit in a corner and receive their sorry pay, or grumble that no one gives them anything; and will you not come forward and make use of what you have learned? For it is not these small arguments that are wanted now; the writings of the Stoics are full of them. What then is the thing which is wanted? A man who shall apply them, one who by his acts shall bear testimony to his words. Assume, I intreat you, this character, that we may no longer use in the schools the examples of the ancients, but may have some example of our own.
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: Will you leave the little debates about these ideas to other people? Let the lazy ones sit around getting their small paychecks or complaining that no one pays them anything. You should step forward and actually use what you've learned. We don't need more small arguments right now. The Stoic writings are already full of them. What do we need instead? Someone who will actually apply these ideas. Someone whose actions back up their words. Please, take on this role. Then we won't have to keep using examples from ancient times in our schools. We'll have an example from our own time.

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: To whom then does the contemplation of these matters (philosophical inquiries) belong? To him who has leisure, for man is an animal that loves contemplation. But it is shameful to contemplate these things as runaway slaves do; we should sit, as in a theatre, free from distraction, and listen at one time to the tragic actor, at another time to the lute-player; and not do as slaves do. As soon as the slave has taken his station he praises the actor and at the same time looks round; then if any one calls out his master's name, the slave is immediately frightened and disturbed. It is shameful for philosophers thus to contemplate the works of nature.
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: Who should explore these philosophical questions? Anyone who has time to think, because humans naturally love to contemplate things. But it's shameful to contemplate like runaway slaves do. You should sit like you're in a theater, free from distractions. Listen to the tragic actor one moment, the musician the next. Don't act like slaves. As soon as a slave takes his seat, he starts praising the actor but keeps looking around. If someone calls his master's name, the slave panics and gets disturbed. It's shameful for philosophers to contemplate nature's works this way.

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: For what is a master? Man is not the master of man; but death is, and life and pleasure and pain; for if he comes without these things, bring Cæsar to me and you will see how firm I am. But when he shall come with these things, thundering and lightning, and when I am afraid of them, what do I do then except to recognize my master like the runaway slave? But so long as I have any respite from these terrors, as a runaway slave stands in the theatre, so do I. I bathe, I drink, I sing; but all this I do with terror and uneasiness. But if I shall release myself from my masters, that is from those things by means of which masters are formidable, what further trouble have I, what master have I still?
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: What makes someone a master over you? One person can't truly master another. But death can master you. So can life, pleasure, and pain. If someone comes to threaten me without using these things, bring Caesar himself — you'll see how steady I am. But when he comes with these weapons, thundering and flashing like lightning, and I'm afraid? Then I'm just recognizing my real master, like a runaway slave who finally gets caught. As long as I get a break from these terrors, I'm like that runaway slave hiding in a theater crowd. I bathe, I drink, I sing — but I do it all with fear and anxiety. But if I free myself from these masters — from the things that make masters scary in the first place — what trouble do I have left? What master do I still have?

discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.originalText: What then, ought we to publish these things to all men? No, but we ought to accommodate ourselves to the ignorant and to say: "This man recommends to me that which he thinks good for himself. I excuse him." For Socrates also excused the jailer who had the charge of him in prison and was weeping when Socrates was going to drink the poison, and said, "How generously he laments over us." Does he then say to the jailer that for this reason we have sent away the women? No, but he says it to his friends who were able to hear (understand) it; and he treats the jailer as a child.
discourses_on-constancy-or-firmness.plainEnglish: So should we go around telling everyone these ideas? No. We should adapt to people who don't understand and say: "This person is recommending what he thinks is good for himself. I forgive him." Socrates did this too. When his jailer was crying because Socrates was about to drink the poison, Socrates excused him and said, "How kindly he grieves for us." Did Socrates tell the jailer that this is why we sent the women away? No. He said that to his friends who could understand it. He treated the jailer like a child.

discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.originalText: The opinion of the philosophers perhaps seem to some to be a paradox; but still let us examine as well as we can, if it is true that it is possible to do everything both with caution and with confidence. For caution seems to be in a manner contrary to confidence, and contraries are in no way consistent. That which seems to many to be a paradox in the matter under consideration in my opinion is of this kind; if we asserted that we ought to employ caution and confidence in the same things, men might justly accuse us of bringing together things which cannot be united. But now where is the difficulty in what is said?
discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.plainEnglish: What philosophers say might sound impossible to some people. But let's look at whether it's really true that you can do everything with both caution and confidence. Caution seems like the opposite of confidence. And opposites can't work together. What seems impossible to many people is this: if we said you should use caution and confidence on the same things, people would rightly say we're trying to combine things that don't go together. But what's actually difficult about what we're saying?

discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.originalText: for if these things are true, which have been often said and often proved, that the nature of good is in the use of appearances, and the nature of evil likewise, and that things independent of our will do not admit either the nature of evil or of good, what paradox do the philosophers assert if they say that where things are not dependent on the will, there you should employ confidence, but where they are dependent on the will, there you should employ caution? For if the bad consists in the bad exercise of the will, caution ought only to be used where things are dependent on the will. But if things independent of the will and not in our power are nothing to us, with respect to these we must employ confidence; and thus we shall both be cautious and confident, and indeed confident because of our caution. For by employing caution towards things which are really bad, it will result that we shall have confidence with respect to things which are not so.
discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.plainEnglish: If what philosophers keep saying is true — that good and evil come from how we handle our thoughts, not from external things — then their advice makes perfect sense. They tell us to be confident about things we can't control, but careful about things we can control. What's so strange about that? If evil only comes from misusing our will, then we should only be cautious with things that involve our will. External things that we can't control don't matter to us. So we can be confident about them. This way, we're both cautious and confident at the same time. We're confident precisely because we're being cautious in the right places. When you're careful about what's actually bad — the misuse of your will — you can be confident about everything else.

discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.originalText: We are then in the condition of deer; when they flee from the huntsmen's feathers in fright, whither do they turn and in what do they seek refuge as safe? They turn to the nets, and thus they perish by confounding things which are objects of fear with things that they ought not to fear. Thus we also act: in what cases do we fear? In things which are independent of the will. In what cases on the contrary do we behave with confidence, as if there were no danger? In things dependent on the will. To be deceived then, or to act rashly, or shamelessly, or with base desire to seek something, does not concern us at all, if we only hit the mark in things which are independent of our will. But where there is death or exile or pain or infamy, there we attempt to run away, there we are struck with terror.
discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.plainEnglish: We're like deer running from hunters. When deer see the feathers on arrows, they panic and run straight into the nets. They die because they confused what they should fear with what they shouldn't fear. We do the same thing. What do we fear? Things we can't control. What do we act confident about, like there's no danger? Things we can control. We don't worry at all about being foolish, reckless, shameless, or chasing the wrong things — as long as we succeed with things outside our control. But when we face death, exile, pain, or disgrace, we try to run away. We're terrified.

discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.originalText: Therefore, as we may expect it to happen with those who err in the greatest matters, we convert natural confidence (that is, according to nature) into audacity, desperation, rashness, shamelessness; and we convert natural caution and modesty into cowardice and meanness, which are full of fear and confusion. For if a man should transfer caution to those things in which the will may be exercised and the acts of the will, he will immediately by willing to be cautious have also the power of avoiding what he chooses; but if he transfer it to the things which are not in his power and will, and attempt to avoid the things which are in the power of others, he will of necessity fear, he will be unstable, he will be disturbed; for death or pain is not formidable, but the fear of pain or death. For this reason we commend the poet, who said: "Not death is evil, but a shameful death."
discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.plainEnglish: When we mess up on the biggest things in life, here's what happens: We turn our natural confidence into recklessness, desperation, and shamelessness. We turn our natural caution into cowardice and weakness, both full of fear and confusion. If you apply caution to things you can control — your choices and actions — you'll actually be able to avoid what you want to avoid. But if you try to be cautious about things outside your control, things other people control, you'll inevitably become fearful, unstable, and disturbed. Death and pain aren't scary by themselves. What's scary is the fear of death and pain. That's why we praise the poet who said: "Death isn't evil — only a shameful death is evil."

discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.originalText: Confidence (courage) then ought to be employed against death, and caution against the fear of death. But now we do the contrary, and employ against death the attempt to escape; and to our opinion about it we employ carelessness, rashness, and indifference. These things Socrates properly used to call tragic masks; for as to children masks appear terrible and fearful from inexperience, we also are affected in like manner by events (the things which happen in life) for no other reason than children are by masks. For what is a child? Ignorance. What is a child? Want of knowledge. For when a child knows these things, he is in no way inferior to us. What is death?
discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.plainEnglish: You should use courage when facing death, and caution when dealing with your fear of death. But we do the opposite. We try to run away from death, while we're careless and reckless with our thoughts about it. Socrates called this wearing tragic masks. Kids get scared of masks because they don't know any better. We react the same way to life events for the same reason kids fear masks. What is a child? Someone who doesn't know things. Someone who lacks knowledge. When a child learns these things, they're just as capable as we are. So what is death?

discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.originalText: A tragic mask. Turn it and examine it. See, it does not bite. The poor body must be separated from the spirit either now or later as it was separated from it before. Why then are you troubled if it be separated now? for if it is not separated now, it will be separated afterwards. Why? That the period of the universe may be completed, for it has need of the present, and of the future, and of the past. What is pain? A mask. Turn it and examine it. The poor flesh is moved roughly, then on the contrary smoothly. If this does not satisfy (please) you, the door is open; if it does, bear (with things). For the door ought to be open for all occasions; and so we have no trouble.
discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.plainEnglish: A tragic mask. Turn it around and look at it. See? It doesn't bite. Your poor body must separate from your spirit either now or later — just like it was separated before you were born. So why are you upset if it separates now? If not now, then later. Why does this happen? So the universe can complete its cycle. It needs the present, the future, and the past. What is pain? A mask. Turn it around and examine it. Your flesh gets roughed up, then it gets smooth again. If this doesn't satisfy you, the door is open. If it does satisfy you, then endure things. The door should always be open for every situation. That way we have no trouble.

discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.originalText: What then is the fruit of these opinions? It is that which ought to be the most noble and the most becoming to those who are really educated, release from perturbation, release from fear. Freedom. For in these matters we must not believe the many, who say that free persons only ought to be educated, but we should rather believe the philosophers who say that the educated only are free. How is this? In this manner: Is freedom anything else than the power of living as we choose? Nothing else. Tell me then, ye men, do you wish to live in error? We do not. No one then who lives in error is free. Do you wish to live in fear? Do you wish to live in sorrow? Do you wish to live in perturbation? By no means. No one then who is in a state of fear or sorrow or perturbation is free; but whoever is delivered from sorrows and fears and perturbations, he is at the same time also delivered from servitude. How then can we continue to believe you, most dear legislators, when you say, We only allow free persons to be educated?
discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.plainEnglish: So what's the point of all this philosophy? The best thing it can give you is what truly educated people should have: freedom from anxiety and fear. Real freedom. Don't listen to most people who say only free citizens deserve education. Listen to the philosophers instead. They say only the educated are truly free. How does that work? Simple: What is freedom? The ability to live how you choose. Nothing more. So tell me — do you want to live in ignorance? No. Then anyone living in ignorance isn't free. Do you want to live in fear? Do you want to live in sadness? Do you want to live in constant worry? Of course not. Then no one who feels fear, sadness, or worry is free. But whoever breaks free from these troubles also breaks free from slavery. So how can we keep believing lawmakers who say 'Only free citizens get to be educated'?

discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.originalText: For philosophers say we allow none to be free except the educated; that is, God does not allow it. When then a man has turned round before the prætor his own slave, has he done nothing? He has done something. What? He has turned round his own slave before the prætor. Has he done nothing more? Yes: he is also bound to pay for him the tax called the twentieth. Well then, is not the man who has gone through this ceremony become free? No more than he is become free from perturbations. Have you who are able to turn round (free) others no master? is not money your master, or a girl or a boy, or some tyrant or some friend of the tyrant? Why do you trouble then when you are going off to any trial (danger) of this kind? It is for this reason that I often say, study and hold in readiness these principles by which you may determine what those things are with reference to which you ought to be cautious, courageous in that which does not depend on your will, cautious in that which does depend on it.
discourses_that-confidence-courage-is-no.plainEnglish: Philosophers say only the educated are truly free — that God only allows it for them. So when a man goes before the magistrate and officially frees his own slave, has he accomplished nothing? He's done something. What exactly? He's freed his slave in front of the magistrate. Nothing more? Well yes — he also has to pay the freedom tax. So then, has the man who went through this ceremony become free himself? No more than he's become free from his own anxieties. You who can free others — don't you have a master? Isn't money your master? Or some girl or boy? Or some tyrant or friend of a tyrant? Then why do you get worked up when you face any test like this? This is why I keep saying: study these principles and keep them ready. Use them to figure out what deserves your attention. Be bold with things outside your control. Be careful with things that are up to you.

discourses_of-tranquillity-freedom-from-.originalText: Consider, you who are going into court, what you wish to maintain and what you wish to succeed in. For if you wish to maintain a will conformable to nature, you have every security, every facility, you have no troubles. For if you wish to maintain what is in your own power and is naturally free, and if you are content with these, what else do you care for? For who is the master of such things? Who can take them away? If you choose to be modest and faithful, who shall not allow you to be so? If you choose not to be restrained or compelled, who shall compel you to desire what you think that you ought not to desire?
discourses_of-tranquillity-freedom-from-.plainEnglish: Think about this: you're heading to court. What do you want to defend? What do you want to win? If you want to defend a life that follows nature, you have complete security. You have every advantage. You have no problems. If you want to defend what's actually in your power — what's naturally free — and if you're satisfied with those things, what else matters? Who controls things like that? Who can take them away? If you choose to be humble and honest, who can stop you? If you choose not to be held back or forced into anything, who can make you want something you think you shouldn't want?

discourses_of-tranquillity-freedom-from-.originalText: who shall compel you to avoid what you do not think fit to avoid? But what do you say? The judge will determine against you something that appears formidable; but that you should also suffer in trying to avoid it, how can he do that? When then the pursuit of objects and the avoiding of them are in your power, what else do you care for? Let this be your preface, this your narrative, this your confirmation, this your victory, this your peroration, this your applause (or the approbation which you will receive).
discourses_of-tranquillity-freedom-from-.plainEnglish: Who can force you to avoid something you don't think you should avoid? But what do you say? The judge might rule against you with something that seems scary. But can he also make you suffer while you're trying to avoid it? How could he do that? When going after things and avoiding things are in your power, what else matters? Let this be your opening. Let this be your story. Let this be your proof. Let this be your victory. Let this be your closing argument. Let this be your applause.

discourses_of-tranquillity-freedom-from-.originalText: Therefore Socrates said to one who was reminding him to prepare for his trial, Do you not think then that I have been preparing for it all my life? By what kind of preparation? I have maintained that which was in my own power. How then? I have never done anything unjust either in my private or in my public life.
discourses_of-tranquillity-freedom-from-.plainEnglish: That's why Socrates said to someone who told him to prepare for his trial, "Don't you think I've been preparing for this my whole life?" The person asked, "What kind of preparation?" Socrates answered, "I've focused on what was in my control. I've never done anything unjust in my private life or my public life."

discourses_of-tranquillity-freedom-from-.originalText: But if you wish to maintain externals also, your poor body, your little property, and your little estimation, I advise you to make from this moment all possible preparation, and then consider both the nature of your judge and your adversary. If it is necessary to embrace his knees, embrace his knees; if to weep, weep; if to groan, groan. For when you have subjected to externals what is your own, then be a slave and do not resist, and do not sometimes choose to be a slave, and sometimes not choose, but with all your mind be one or the other, either free or a slave, either instructed or uninstructed, either a well-bred cock or a mean one, either endure to be beaten until you die or yield at once; and let it not happen to you to receive many stripes and then to yield. But if these things are base, determine immediately. Where is the nature of evil and good? It is where truth is: where truth is and where nature is, there is caution: where truth is, there is courage where nature is.
discourses_of-tranquillity-freedom-from-.plainEnglish: But if you want to hold onto externals too — your fragile body, your small possessions, your little reputation — then I advise you to prepare as much as possible right now. Consider both the nature of your judge and your opponent. If you need to beg on your knees, beg on your knees. If you need to cry, cry. If you need to groan, groan. Once you've made what's truly yours subject to external things, then be a slave and don't resist. Don't sometimes choose to be a slave and sometimes not. With your whole mind, be one or the other — either free or enslaved, either educated or ignorant, either a noble fighting cock or a cowardly one. Either endure being beaten until you die, or give up immediately. Don't let yourself take many blows and then surrender anyway. But if these things are shameful, decide right now. Where is the nature of good and evil? It's where truth is. Where truth and nature are, there is wisdom. Where truth is, there is courage where nature is.

discourses_of-tranquillity-freedom-from-.originalText: For this reason also it is ridiculous to say, Suggest something to me (tell me what to do). What should I suggest to you? Well, form my mind so as to accommodate itself to any event. Why that is just the same as if a man who is ignorant of letters should say, Tell me what to write when any name is proposed to me. For if I should tell him to write Dion, and then another should come and propose to him not the name of Dion but that of Theon, what will be done? what will he write? But if you have practised writing, you are also prepared to write (or to do) anything that is required. If you are not, what can I now suggest? For if circumstances require something else, what will you say, or what will you do? Remember then this general precept and you will need no suggestion. But if you gape after externals, you must of necessity ramble up and down in obedience to the will of your master. And who is the master? He who has the power over the things which you seek to gain or try to avoid.
discourses_of-tranquillity-freedom-from-.plainEnglish: This is why it's ridiculous when someone says, "Give me advice. Tell me what to do." What should I tell you? "Train your mind to handle whatever happens." But that's like someone who can't read saying, "Tell me what to write when someone gives me a name." If I tell him to write "Dion," and then someone else comes and asks him to write "Theon" instead, what happens? What will he write? But if you've practiced writing, you're ready to write anything that's needed. If you haven't practiced, what can I possibly suggest? If circumstances demand something different, what will you say or do? Remember this basic rule and you won't need suggestions. But if you chase after external things, you'll inevitably run around following your master's orders. And who is your master? Whoever controls the things you're trying to get or avoid.

discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.originalText: Things themselves (materials) are indifferent; but the use of them is not indifferent. How then shall a man preserve firmness and tranquillity, and at the same time be careful and neither rash nor negligent? If he imitates those who play at dice. The counters are indifferent; the dice are indifferent. How do I know what the cast will be? But to use carefully and dexterously the cast of the dice, this is my business. Thus then in life also the chief business is this: distinguish and separate things, and say: Externals are not in my power: will is in my power. Where shall I seek the good and the bad? Within, in the things which are my own. But in what does not belong to you call nothing either good or bad, or profit or damage or anything of the kind.
discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.plainEnglish: Things themselves don't matter — but how you use them does. So how do you stay calm and steady while still being careful? Not careless, but not stressed out either? Think of people playing dice. The dice don't matter. The counters don't matter. You can't control what numbers come up. But using whatever you roll well and skillfully — that's your job. Life works the same way. Your main task is this: separate things clearly. Say to yourself: 'External things are not up to me. My choices are up to me.' Where should you look for good and bad? Inside yourself, in the things that actually belong to you. But for everything that doesn't belong to you, don't call it good or bad, helpful or harmful, or anything like that.

discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.originalText: What then? Should we use such things carelessly? In no way: for this on the other hand is bad for the faculty of the will, and consequently against nature; but we should act carefully because the use is not indifferent, and we should also act with firmness and freedom from perturbations because the material is indifferent. For where the material is not indifferent, there no man can hinder me or compel me. Where I can be hindered and compelled, the obtaining of those things is not in my power, nor is it good or bad; but the use is either bad or good, and the use is in my power. But it is difficult to mingle and to bring together these two things—the carefulness of him who is affected by the matter (or things about him), and the firmness of him who has no regard for it; but it is not impossible: and if it is, happiness is impossible.
discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.plainEnglish: So what then? Should we be careless with external things? Absolutely not. Being careless damages your will and goes against your nature. You should act carefully because how you use things matters. But you should also act firmly and calmly because the things themselves don't matter. Here's the key: when something truly doesn't matter, no one can stop you or force you. When someone can stop you or force you, getting that thing isn't up to you — so it's neither good nor bad. But how you use it? That's either good or bad. And that use is up to you. It's hard to combine these two attitudes: being careful like someone who cares about things, while staying firm like someone who doesn't care about them. But it's not impossible. And if it were impossible, happiness would be impossible too.

discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.originalText: But we should act as we do in the case of a voyage. What can I do? I can choose the master of the ship, the sailors, the day, the opportunity. Then comes a storm. What more have I to care for? for my part is done. The business belongs to another, the master. But the ship is sinking—what then have I to do? I do the only thing that I can, not to be drowned full of fear, nor screaming nor blaming God, but knowing that what has been produced must also perish: for I am not an immortal being, but a man, a part of the whole, as an hour is a part of the day: I must be present like the hour, and past like the hour. What difference then does it make to me how I pass away, whether by being suffocated or by a fever, for I must pass through some such means.
discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.plainEnglish: Think of it like taking a sea voyage. What can you do? You can pick the ship's captain, the crew, when to leave, the right moment to go. Then a storm hits. What else should you worry about? Your part is done. The rest belongs to someone else — the captain. But what if the ship is sinking? What then? You do the only thing you can. You don't drown full of fear. You don't scream or blame God. You know that everything born must die. You're not immortal. You're human, part of the whole — like an hour is part of the day. You show up like the hour does, then pass like the hour does. So what difference does it make how you die? Suffocation or fever — you have to go somehow.

discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.originalText: How then is it said that some external things are according to nature and others contrary to nature? It is said as it might be said if we were separated from union (or society): for to the foot I shall say that it is according to nature for it to be clean; but if you take it as a foot and as a thing not detached (independent), it will befit it both to step into the mud and tread on thorns, and sometimes to be cut off for the good of the whole body; otherwise it is no longer a foot. We should think in some such way about ourselves also. What are you? A man. If you consider yourself as detached from other men, it is according to nature to live to old age, to be rich, to be healthy.
discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.plainEnglish: How can we say some external things are natural and others unnatural? Think of it this way: imagine we were separated from society. I could tell a foot that it's natural for it to stay clean. But if you think of the foot as part of the whole body, then it makes sense for it to step in mud, walk on thorns, and sometimes even be cut off for the good of the entire body. Otherwise, it's no longer really a foot. We should think about ourselves the same way. What are you? A human being. If you think of yourself as separate from other people, then it seems natural to live to old age, be rich, and stay healthy.

discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.originalText: But if you consider yourself as a man and a part of a certain whole, it is for the sake of that whole that at one time you should be sick, at another time take a voyage and run into danger, and at another time be in want, and in some cases die prematurely. Why then are you troubled? Do you not know, that as a foot is no longer a foot if it is detached from the body, so you are no longer a man if you are separated from other men. For what is a man? A part of a state, of that first which consists of gods and of men; then of that which is called next to it, which is a small image of the universal state.
discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.plainEnglish: But if you see yourself as a human being and part of something bigger, then sometimes you need to get sick for the sake of that bigger whole. Sometimes you need to travel and face danger. Sometimes you need to go without. Sometimes you even need to die young. So why does this bother you? Don't you know that a foot is no longer a foot once it's cut off from the body? In the same way, you're no longer human if you're separated from other humans. What is a human being? A part of a community. First, the great community of gods and humans. Then the smaller community right around you, which is like a mini version of that universal community.

discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.originalText: What then must I be brought to trial; must another have a fever, another sail on the sea, another die, and another be condemned? Yes, for it is impossible in such a universe of things, among so many living together, that such things should not happen, some to one and others to others. It is your duty then since you are come here, to say what you ought, to arrange these things as it is fit. Then some one says, "I shall charge you with doing me wrong." Much good may it do you: I have done my part; but whether you also have done yours, you must look to that; for there is some danger of this too, that it may escape your notice.
discourses_how-magnanimity-is-consistent.plainEnglish: So what if I have to go to court? What if someone else gets sick, or sails across the ocean, or dies, or gets convicted? Yes, these things will happen. In a world this big, with so many people living together, such things are bound to happen to some people and not others. Your job, since you're here, is to say what you should say and handle these situations properly. Then someone says, "I'm going to accuse you of wronging me." Go ahead — good luck with that. I've done my part. Whether you've done yours is something you need to figure out. There's a real risk you might not even notice if you haven't.

discourses_of-indifference.originalText: The hypothetical proposition is indifferent: the judgment about it is not indifferent, but it is either knowledge or opinion or error. Thus life is indifferent: the use is not indifferent. When any man then tells you that these things also are indifferent, do not become negligent; and when a man invites you to be careful (about such things), do not become abject and struck with admiration of material things. And it is good for you to know your own preparation and power, that in those matters where you have not been prepared, you may keep quiet, and not be vexed, if others have the advantage over you. For you too in syllogisms will claim to have the advantage over them; and if others should be vexed at this, you will console them by saying, "I have learned them, and you have not." Thus also where there is need of any practice, seek not that which is acquired from the need (of such practice), but yield in that matter to those who have had practice, and be yourself content with firmness of mind.
discourses_of-indifference.plainEnglish: A logical statement might be neutral. But your judgment about it isn't neutral — it's either knowledge, opinion, or error. Life itself is neutral. How you use it isn't neutral. When someone tells you that everything is neutral, don't get lazy. And when someone urges you to worry about external things, don't become pathetic and amazed by material stuff. It's good to know your own skills and abilities. In areas where you're not prepared, stay quiet. Don't get upset if others are better than you there. You'll have the advantage over them in logic. If they get upset about that, comfort them by saying, "I learned this stuff. You didn't." Same thing when you need practice at something. Don't demand respect just because you need the practice. Let the experienced people handle it. Be content with having a strong mind.

discourses_of-indifference.originalText: Go and salute a certain person. How? Not meanly. But I have been shut out, for I have not learned to make my way through the window; and when I have found the door shut, I must either come back or enter through the window. But still speak to him. In what way? Not meanly. But suppose that you have not got what you wanted. Was this your business, and not his? Why then do you claim that which belongs to another? Always remember what is your own, and what belongs to another; and you will not be disturbed.
discourses_of-indifference.plainEnglish: Go greet someone. How? Don't grovel. But what if they shut me out? That's because I never learned to sneak through the window. When I find the door closed, I either go back or climb through the window. But still talk to him. How? Don't grovel. But what if you don't get what you wanted? Was that your job or his? Why are you demanding something that belongs to someone else? Always remember what's yours and what belongs to others. Then you won't be upset.

discourses_of-indifference.originalText: Chrysippus therefore said well, So long as future things are uncertain, I always cling to those which are more adapted to the conservation of that which is according to nature; for God himself has given me the faculty of such choice. But if I knew that it was fated (in the order of things) for me to be sick, I would even move towards it; for the foot also, if it had intelligence, would move to go into the mud. For why are ears of corn produced? Is it not that they may become dry? And do they not become dry that they may be reaped? for they are not separated from communion with other things. If then they had perception, ought they to wish never to be reaped? But this is a curse upon ears of corn to be never reaped. So we must know that in the case of men too it is a curse not to die, just the same as not to be ripened and not to be reaped.
discourses_of-indifference.plainEnglish: Chrysippus put it well: As long as the future is uncertain, I stick with what helps preserve my natural self. God gave me the ability to choose this way. But if I knew for certain I was destined to get sick, I would actually move toward sickness. Even a foot, if it could think, would step into mud when that's where it needs to go. Why do ears of corn grow? So they can dry out. And why do they dry out? So they can be harvested. They're not cut off from everything else. If corn could feel and think, should it wish never to be harvested? That would be a curse — corn that's never reaped. We need to understand that for humans too, it's a curse not to die. Just like it would be a curse for corn never to ripen and never to be harvested.

discourses_of-indifference.originalText: But since we must be reaped, and we also know that we are reaped, we are vexed at it; for we neither know what we are nor have we studied what belongs to man, as those who have studied horses know what belongs to horses. But Chrysantas when he was going to strike the enemy checked himself when he heard the trumpet sounding a retreat: so it seemed better to him to obey the general's command than to follow his own inclination. But not one of us chooses, even when necessity summons, readily to obey it, but weeping and groaning we suffer what we do suffer, and we call them "circumstances." What kind of circumstances, man?
discourses_of-indifference.plainEnglish: We all must die, and we know we must die. But we get upset about it. Why? Because we don't know what we really are. We haven't studied what it means to be human the way horse trainers study what it means to be a horse. Chrysantas was about to strike his enemy when he heard the trumpet call for retreat. He stopped. It seemed better to obey his general's command than follow his own desire to fight. But none of us does this. Even when necessity calls, we don't obey willingly. We cry and complain as we suffer what we must suffer. And we call these things "circumstances." What kind of circumstances, man?

discourses_of-indifference.originalText: If you give the name of circumstances to the things which are around you, all things are circumstances; but if you call hardships by this name, what hardship is there in the dying of that which has been produced? But that which destroys is either a sword, or a wheel, or the sea, or a tile, or a tyrant. Why do you care about the way of going down to Hades? All ways are equal. But if you will listen to the truth, the way which the tyrant sends you is shorter. A tyrant never killed a man in six months: but a fever is often a year about it. All these things are only sound and the noise of empty names.
discourses_of-indifference.plainEnglish: If you call everything around you "circumstances," then everything is a circumstance.
