But if you call them "hardships," what's really hard about something that was created eventually dying? The thing that destroys might be a sword, a wheel, the sea, a falling tile, or a tyrant. Why do you care how you die? All ways of dying are the same. But if you want the truth, the way a tyrant kills you is actually faster. A tyrant never takes six months to kill someone. But a fever often drags it out for a year. All these distinctions are just noise — empty words that mean nothing.

discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.originalText: Through an unreasonable regard to divination many of us omit many duties. For what more can the diviner see than death or danger or disease, or generally things of that kind? If then I must expose myself to danger for a friend, and if it is my duty even to die for him, what need have I then for divination? Have I not within me a diviner who has told me the nature of good and of evil, and has explained to me the signs (or marks) of both? What need have I then to consult the viscera of victims or the flight of birds, and why do I submit when he says, It is for your interest?
discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.plainEnglish: Too many of us skip our duties because we worry too much about fortune telling and omens. What can a fortune teller really see? Death, danger, sickness — things like that. But say I need to risk my life for a friend. Say it's my duty to die for him if necessary. What do I need fortune telling for then? I already have a fortune teller inside me. It's told me what's good and what's evil. It's shown me the signs of both. So why do I need to examine animal guts or watch how birds fly? Why do I listen when the fortune teller says, 'This is good for you'?

discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.originalText: For does he know what is for my interest, does he know what is good; and as he has learned the signs of the viscera, has he also learned the signs of good and evil? For if he knows the signs of these, he knows the signs both of the beautiful and of the ugly, and of the just and of the unjust. Do you tell me, man, what is the thing which is signified for me: is it life or death, poverty or wealth? But whether these things are for my interest or whether they are not, I do not intend to ask you. Why don't you give your opinion on matters of grammar, and why do you give it here about things on which we are all in error and disputing with one another?
discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.plainEnglish: Does this fortune-teller really know what's good for me? Does he know what's actually good? Sure, he learned to read animal guts. But did he also learn to read the signs of good and evil? If he knows those signs, then he knows the signs of what's beautiful and ugly, just and unjust. Tell me — what are you predicting for me? Life or death? Poverty or wealth? But whether these things are actually good for me or not — I'm not going to ask you that. Why don't you stick to giving opinions about grammar? Why are you weighing in on questions that we're all confused about and arguing over?

discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.originalText: What then leads us to frequent use of divination? Cowardice, the dread of what will happen. This is the reason why we flatter the diviners. Pray, master, shall I succeed to the property of my father? Let us see: let us sacrifice on the occasion. Yes, master, as fortune chooses. When he has said, You shall succeed to the inheritance, we thank him as if we received the inheritance from him. The consequence is that they play upon us.
discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.plainEnglish: So why do we keep asking fortune-tellers what will happen? Cowardice. Fear of the future. That's why we suck up to them. "Please, master, will I inherit my father's money?" Let's see — let's make a sacrifice and find out. "Yes, master, fortune says so." When he tells us we'll get the inheritance, we thank him like he's the one giving it to us. The result? They play us for fools.

discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.originalText: Will you not then seek the nature of good in the rational animal? for if it is not there, you will not choose to say that it exists in any other thing (plant or animal). What then? are not plants and animals also the works of God? They are; but they are not superior things, nor yet parts of the gods. But you are a superior thing; you are a portion separated from the Deity; you have in yourself a certain portion of him. Why then are you ignorant of your own noble descent? Why do you not know whence you came? will you not remember when you are eating who you are who eat and whom you feed? When you are in social intercourse, when you are exercising yourself, when you are engaged in discussion, know you not that you are nourishing a god, that you are exercising a god? Wretch, you are carrying about a god with you, and you know it not. Do you think that I mean some god of silver or of gold, and external? You carry him within yourself, and you perceive not that you are polluting him by impure thoughts and dirty deeds.
discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.plainEnglish: Look for what's truly good in rational beings — in humans. If you can't find it there, don't bother claiming it exists anywhere else. What about plants and animals? Sure, they're God's work too. But they're not superior beings. They're not pieces of the divine. You are superior. You are a piece separated from God. You carry part of him inside you. So why don't you know how noble your origins are? Why don't you know where you came from? When you eat, remember who you are and who you're feeding. When you're with others, when you're working out, when you're having discussions — know that you're nourishing a god and exercising a god. You fool! You're walking around with a god inside you and you don't even realize it. Do you think I mean some statue made of silver or gold? Something outside yourself? You carry him within you. And you don't even notice that you're polluting him with dirty thoughts and shameful actions.

discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.originalText: And if an image of God were present, you would not dare to do any of the things which you are doing; but when God himself is present within and sees all and hears all, you are not ashamed of thinking such things and doing such things, ignorant as you are of your own nature and subject to the anger of God. Then why do we fear when we are sending a young man from the school into active life, lest he should do anything improperly, eat improperly, have improper intercourse with women; and lest the rags in which he is wrapped should debase him, lest fine garments should make him proud. This youth (if he acts thus) does not know his own God; he knows not with whom he sets out (into the world). But can we endure when he says, "I wish I had you (God) with me." Have you not God with you? and do you seek for any other when you have him? or will God tell you anything else than this?
discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.plainEnglish: If a statue of God were in front of you, you wouldn't dare do the things you're doing now. But when God himself is present inside you, seeing and hearing everything, you're not ashamed of your thoughts and actions. You don't understand your own nature. You've made God angry. So why do we worry when we send a young person out into the world? We fear he'll act badly, eat the wrong things, sleep with the wrong people. We worry that his poor clothes will shame him or that fine clothes will make him proud. This young man doesn't know his own God. He doesn't know who goes with him into the world. But can we stand it when he says, "I wish I had you with me, God"? Don't you have God with you already? Why look for someone else when you have him? What else could God possibly tell you?

discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.originalText: If you were a statue of Phidias, either Athena or Zeus, you would think both of yourself and of the artist, and if you had any understanding (power of perception) you would try to do nothing unworthy of him who made you or of yourself, and try not to appear in an unbecoming dress (attitude) to those who look upon you. But now because Zeus has made you, for this reason do you care not how you shall appear? And yet is the artist (in the one case) like the artist in the other? or the work in the one case like the other? And what work of an artist, for instance, has in itself the faculties, which the artist shows in making it? Is it not marble or bronze, or gold or ivory? and the Athena of Phidias, when she has once extended the hand and received in it the figure of Victory, stands in that attitude for ever. But the works of God have power of motion, they breathe, they have the faculty of using the appearances of things and the power of examining them.
discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.plainEnglish: If you were a statue made by Phidias — either Athena or Zeus — you would be mindful of both yourself and your creator. If you had any awareness, you would try to do nothing unworthy of the artist who made you or of yourself. You wouldn't want to appear poorly to those who look at you. But now Zeus has made you. Don't you care how you appear? Is the human artist really like the divine artist? Is the statue really like you? What work of art has within itself the same abilities that the artist shows in making it? A statue is just marble or bronze or gold or ivory. Phidias's statue of Athena extends her hand and holds the figure of Victory — and stays that way forever. But God's works can move. They breathe. They can perceive things and examine them.

discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.originalText: Being the work of such an artist do you dishonor him? And what shall I say, not only that he made you, but also entrusted you to yourself and made you a deposit to yourself? Will you not think of this too, but do you also dishonor your guardianship? But if God had entrusted an orphan to you, would you thus neglect him? He has delivered yourself to your own care, and says: "I had no one fitter to entrust him to than yourself; keep him for me such as he is by nature, modest, faithful, erect, unterrified, free from passion and perturbation." And then you do not keep him such.
discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.plainEnglish: You are the work of such a skilled artist — and you dishonor him? And what can I say? He didn't just make you. He also put you in charge of yourself. He made you responsible for yourself. Won't you think about this too? Are you really going to dishonor this trust? If God had put an orphan in your care, would you neglect the child like this? He has given you yourself to take care of. He says: "I had no one better to trust with this job than you. Keep him as he naturally is — modest, faithful, upright, fearless, free from strong emotions and anxiety." And then you don't keep him that way.

discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.originalText: But some will say, Whence has this fellow got the arrogance which he displays and these supercilious looks? I have not yet so much gravity as befits a philosopher; for I do not yet feel confidence in what I have learned and in what I have assented to. I still fear my own weakness. Let me get confidence and then you shall see a countenance such as I ought to have and an attitude such as I ought to have; then I will show to you the statue, when it is perfected, when it is polished. What do you expect? a supercilious countenance? Does the Zeus at Olympia lift up his brow? No, his look is fixed as becomes him who is ready to say: Irrevocable is my word and shall not fail.—Iliad, i., 526. Such will I show myself to you, faithful, modest, noble, free from perturbation.
discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.plainEnglish: But some people will say, "Where does this guy get his arrogance and that superior look?" I haven't developed the proper dignity of a philosopher yet. I don't feel confident in what I've learned and accepted. I still fear my own weakness. Let me gain confidence first. Then you'll see the face I should have and the attitude I should have. Then I'll show you the statue when it's finished and polished. What do you expect — a superior look? Does the statue of Zeus at Olympia raise his eyebrows in arrogance? No. His expression is steady, like someone ready to say: "My word cannot be changed and will not fail." That's how I will show myself to you: faithful, humble, noble, and undisturbed.

discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.originalText: What, and immortal, too, except from old age, and from sickness? No, but dying as becomes a god, sickening as becomes a god. This power I possess; this I can do. But the rest I do not possess, nor can I do. I will show the nerves (strength) of a philosopher. What nerves are these? A desire never disappointed, an aversion which never falls on that which it would avoid, a proper pursuit ([Greek: hormaen]), a diligent purpose, an assent which is not rash. These you shall see.
discourses_how-we-ought-to-use-divinatio.plainEnglish: What, immortal too, except for old age and sickness? No — but dying like a god should die, getting sick like a god should get sick. This power I have. This I can do. But the rest? I don't have it, and I can't do it. I'll show you what real strength looks like in a philosopher. What kind of strength? Never wanting something you can't get. Never trying to avoid something that will happen anyway. Acting with purpose. Staying focused on what matters. Not jumping to conclusions. This is what you'll see from me.

discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.originalText: It is no common (easy) thing to do this only, to fulfil the promise of a man's nature. For what is a man? The answer is, A rational and mortal being. Then by the rational faculty from whom are we separated? From wild beasts. And from what others? From sheep and like animals. Take care then to do nothing like a wild beast; but if you do, you have lost the character of a man; you have not fulfilled your promise. See that you do nothing like a sheep; but if you do, in this case also the man is lost. What then do we do as sheep? When we act gluttonously, when we act lewdly, when we act rashly, filthily, inconsiderately, to what have we declined? To sheep. What have we lost? The rational faculty. When we act contentiously and harmfully and passionately and violently, to what have we declined? To wild beasts. Consequently some of us are great wild beasts, and others little beasts, of a bad disposition and small, whence we may say, Let me be eaten by a lion. But in all these ways the promise of a man acting as a man is destroyed.
discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.plainEnglish: It's not easy to fulfill your nature as a human being. What is a human being? A rational, mortal creature. Our rational mind is what separates us from wild beasts. It also separates us from sheep and similar animals. So be careful not to act like a wild beast. If you do, you've lost your humanity. You haven't kept your promise. Make sure you don't act like a sheep either. If you do, you've also lost what makes you human. What do we do when we act like sheep? We overeat. We're sexually reckless. We're impulsive, dirty, and thoughtless. When we do these things, we've sunk to the level of sheep. We've lost our rational mind. What about when we're argumentative, harmful, emotional, and violent? Then we've sunk to the level of wild beasts. Some of us become big wild beasts. Others become small, nasty little beasts. At that point, we might as well say, "Let a lion eat me." Either way, we've destroyed what it means to act like a human being.

discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.originalText: For when is a conjunctive (complex) proposition maintained? When it fulfils what its nature promises; so that the preservation of a complex proposition is when it is a conjunction of truths. When is a disjunctive maintained? When it fulfils what it promises. When are flutes, a lyre, a horse, a dog, preserved? (When they severally keep their promise.) What is the wonder then if man also in like manner is preserved, and in like manner is lost? Each man is improved and preserved by corresponding acts, the carpenter by acts of carpentry, the grammarian by acts of grammar. But if a man accustoms himself to write ungrammatically, of necessity his art will be corrupted and destroyed. Thus modest actions preserve the modest man, and immodest actions destroy him; and actions of fidelity preserve the faithful man, and the contrary actions destroy him. And on the other hand contrary actions strengthen contrary characters: shamelessness strengthens the shameless man, faithlessness the faithless man, abusive words the abusive man, anger the man of an angry temper, and unequal receiving and giving make the avaricious man more avaricious.
discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.plainEnglish: When does a complex statement work? When it does what it's supposed to do. A complex statement survives when all its parts are true. When does an either-or statement work? When it does what it promises. When do flutes, lyres, horses, and dogs stay in good condition? When they do what they're meant to do. So why be surprised that people work the same way? Each person improves and survives by doing the right actions. A carpenter gets better by doing carpentry. A grammarian gets better by doing grammar. But if someone gets used to writing bad grammar, his skill will definitely get worse and fall apart. Good actions preserve good people. Bad actions destroy them. Faithful actions preserve faithful people. The opposite actions destroy them. And the flip side is also true — opposite actions strengthen opposite traits. Shameless acts make shameless people stronger. Faithless acts make faithless people stronger. Harsh words make harsh people stronger. Anger makes angry people angrier. Taking more than you give makes greedy people greedier.

discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.originalText: For this reason philosophers admonish us not to be satisfied with learning only, but also to add study, and then practice. For we have long been accustomed to do contrary things, and we put in practice opinions which are contrary to true opinions. If then we shall not also put in practice right opinions, we shall be nothing more than the expositors of the opinions of others. For now who among us is not able to discourse according to the rules of art about good and evil things (in this fashion)?
discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.plainEnglish: This is why philosophers tell us not to stop at just learning. We also need to study deeply, then practice what we've learned. We've spent years doing the wrong things. We've lived by bad ideas instead of true ones. If we don't start practicing the right ideas, we'll be nothing more than people who repeat what others have said. Right now, who among us can't give a proper speech about good and evil?

discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.originalText: That of things some are good, and some are bad, and some are indifferent: the good then are virtues, and the things which participate in virtues; and the bad are the contrary; and the indifferent are wealth, health, reputation. Then, if in the midst of our talk there should happen some greater noise than usual, or some of those who are present should laugh at us, we are disturbed. Philosopher, where are the things which you were talking about? Whence did you produce and utter them? From the lips, and thence only. Why then do you corrupt the aids provided by others? Why do you treat the weightiest matters as if you were playing a game of dice?
discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.plainEnglish: Some things are good, some are bad, and some don't matter either way. The good things are virtues and anything that helps you be virtuous. The bad things are the opposite. The things that don't matter are wealth, health, and reputation. But then, if there's a loud noise while we're talking, or someone in the room laughs at us, we get upset. So where's your philosophy now? Where are all those ideas you were just discussing? They came from your mouth — just words. Why are you letting other people's reactions ruin what you've learned? Why are you treating the most important matters like you're rolling dice in a game?

discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.originalText: For it is one thing to lay up bread and wine as in a storehouse, and another thing to eat. That which has been eaten, is digested, distributed, and is become sinews, flesh, bones, blood, healthy color, healthy breath. Whatever is stored up, when you choose you can readily take and show it; but you have no other advantage from it except so far as to appear to possess it. For what is the difference between explaining these doctrines and those of men who have different opinions?
discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.plainEnglish: There's a big difference between storing bread and wine in a warehouse and actually eating them. When you eat food, it gets digested and becomes part of you — your muscles, flesh, bones, blood, healthy skin, and healthy breathing. But stored food? Sure, you can grab it and show it off whenever you want. The only benefit you get is looking like you own something. So what's the difference between repeating these teachings and repeating the teachings of people who think completely differently?

discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.originalText: Sit down now and explain according to the rules of art the opinions of Epicurus, and perhaps you will explain his opinions in a more useful manner than Epicurus himself. Why then do you call yourself a Stoic? Why do you deceive the many? Why do you act the part of a Jew, when you are a Greek? Do you not see how (why) each is called a Jew, or a Syrian, or an Egyptian? and when we see a man inclining to two sides, we are accustomed to say, This man is not a Jew, but he acts as one. But when he has assumed the affects of one who has been imbued with Jewish doctrine and has adopted that sect, then he is in fact and he is named a Jew.
discourses_that-when-we-cannot-fulfil-th.plainEnglish: Go ahead and explain Epicurus's teachings by the proper methods. You might even explain them better than Epicurus did. So why call yourself a Stoic? Why lie to people? Why act like a Jew when you're really Greek? Don't you see what makes someone a Jew, a Syrian, or an Egyptian? When we see someone torn between two sides, we say, "This person isn't really a Jew — he's just pretending." But when someone truly takes on the feelings and beliefs of Jewish teaching and joins that way of life, then he really is a Jew. That's when we call him one.

discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.originalText: Consider who you are. In the first place, you are a man; and this is one who has nothing superior to the faculty of the will, but all other things subjected to it; and the faculty itself he possesses unenslaved and free from subjection. Consider then from what things you have been separated by reason. You have been separated from wild beasts; you have been separated from domestic animals ([Greek: probaton]). Further, you are a citizen of the world, and a part of it, not one of the subservient (serving), but one of the principal (ruling) parts, for you are capable of comprehending the divine administration and of considering the connection of things.
discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.plainEnglish:
Think about who you are. First, you're a human being. And humans have something special — the power to choose. This power of choice is superior to everything else. All other things serve it. And this power itself is free. No one can enslave it.

Think about what sets you apart because of your ability to reason. You're different from wild animals. You're different from farm animals. Beyond that, you're a citizen of the entire world. You're part of it — not as a servant, but as one of the ruling parts. You can understand how the universe works. You can see how everything connects.

discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.originalText: What then does the character of a citizen promise (profess)? To hold nothing as profitable to himself; to deliberate about nothing as if he were detached from the community, but to act as the hand or foot would do, if they had reason and understood the constitution of nature, for they would never put themselves in motion nor desire anything otherwise than with reference to the whole. Therefore, the philosophers say well, that if the good man had foreknowledge of what would happen, he would co-operate towards his own sickness and death and mutilation, since he knows that these things are assigned to him according to the universal arrangement, and that the whole is superior to the part, and the state to the citizen. But now because we do not know the future, it is our duty to stick to the things which are in their nature more suitable for our choice, for we were made among other things for this.
discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.plainEnglish: What does being a good citizen require? It means you don't think only about what benefits you personally. You don't make decisions as if you're separate from your community. Instead, you act like a hand or foot would act if it could think and understood how the body works — it would never move or want anything except what's good for the whole body. This is why philosophers say that if a good person knew the future, he would willingly accept his own illness, death, and injury. He would know these things are assigned to him by the universal order. The whole is more important than the part. The state is more important than the citizen. But since we can't know the future, we should stick to choosing things that are naturally better for us to choose. After all, we were made for this purpose among others.

discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.originalText: After this, remember that you are a son. What does this character promise? To consider that everything which is the son's belongs to the father, to obey him in all things, never to blame him to another, nor to say or do anything which does him injury, to yield to him in all things and give way, co-operating with him as far as you can. After this know that you are a brother also, and that to this character it is due to make concessions; to be easily persuaded, to speak good of your brother, never to claim in opposition to him any of the things which are independent of the will, but readily to give them up, that you may have the larger share in what is dependent on the will. For see what a thing it is, in place of a lettuce, if it should so happen, or a seat, to gain for yourself goodness of disposition. How great is the advantage.
discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.plainEnglish: Remember that you are a son. What does being a son require? Think of everything you have as belonging to your father. Obey him in everything. Never badmouth him to others or say or do anything that hurts him. Give way to him in all things and cooperate with him as much as you can. Remember too that you are a brother. What does being a brother require? Make compromises. Be easy to convince. Speak well of your brother. Never fight him over things that aren't up to you anyway — just let him have them. Focus instead on what is up to you. Think about it: you might give up a head of lettuce or a chair, but you gain good character in return. What a bargain that is.

discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.originalText: Next to this, if you are a senator of any state, remember that you are a senator; if a youth, that you are a youth; if an old man, that you are an old man; for each of such names, if it comes to be examined, marks out the proper duties. But if you go and blame your brother, I say to you, You have forgotten who you are and what is your name. In the next place, if you were a smith and made a wrong use of the hammer, you would have forgotten the smith; and if you have forgotten the brother and instead of a brother have become an enemy, would you appear not to have changed one thing for another in that case? And if instead of a man, who is a tame animal and social, you are become a mischievous wild beast, treacherous, and biting, have you lost nothing?
discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.plainEnglish: Remember your role. If you're a senator in any government, remember you're a senator. If you're young, remember you're young. If you're old, remember you're old. Each title comes with specific duties that you need to examine and understand. But if you go around criticizing your brother, I'm telling you: you've forgotten who you are and what you're supposed to be. Think about it this way. If you were a blacksmith and you used your hammer wrong, you'd have forgotten how to be a blacksmith. If you've forgotten how to be a brother and become an enemy instead, haven't you clearly traded one thing for another? And if instead of being a human — a civilized, social creature — you've become a harmful wild animal, sneaky and vicious, haven't you lost something important?

discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.originalText: But (I suppose) you must lose a bit of money that you may suffer damage? And does the loss of nothing else do a man damage? If you had lost the art of grammar or music, would you think the loss of it a damage? and if you shall lose modesty, moderation ([Greek: chtastolaen]) and gentleness, do you think the loss nothing? And yet the things first mentioned are lost by some cause external and independent of the will, and the second by our own fault; and as to the first neither to have them nor to lose them is shameful; but as to the second, not to have them and to lose them is shameful and matter of reproach and a misfortune.
discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.plainEnglish: But you think you must lose some money and suffer damage? Does losing anything else damage a person? If you lost your knowledge of grammar or music, would you call that damage? And if you lose your sense of shame, self-control, and gentleness — do you think losing those things is nothing? Here's the difference: you lose the first things (money, knowledge) because of outside forces beyond your control. You lose the second things (character traits) through your own fault. With the first group, having them or losing them isn't shameful. But with the second group — not having them and losing them is shameful, disgraceful, and truly unfortunate.

discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.originalText: What then? shall I not hurt him who has hurt me? In the first place consider what hurt ([Greek: blabae]) is, and remember what you have heard from the philosophers. For if the good consists in the will (purpose, intention, [Greek: proaireeis]), and the evil also in the will, see if what you say is not this: What then, since that man has hurt himself by doing an unjust act to me, shall I not hurt myself by doing some unjust act to him? Why do we not imagine to ourselves (mentally think of) something of this kind?
discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.plainEnglish: What then? Should I hurt someone who hurt me? First, think about what "hurt" really means. Remember what the philosophers taught you. If good comes from your choices and evil comes from your choices too, then listen to what you're actually saying: "Since that person hurt himself by being unfair to me, should I hurt myself by being unfair back to him?" Why don't we think about it this way?

discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.originalText: But where there is any detriment to the body or to our possession, there is harm there; and where the same thing happens to the faculty of the will, there is (you suppose) no harm; for he who has been deceived or he who has done an unjust act neither suffers in the head nor in the eye nor in the hip, nor does he lose his estate; and we wish for nothing else than (security to) these things. But whether we shall have the will modest and faithful or shameless and faithless, we care not the least, except only in the school so far as a few words are concerned. Therefore our proficiency is limited to these few words; but beyond them it does not exist even in the slightest degree.
discourses_how-we-may-discover-the-dutie.plainEnglish: When your body gets hurt or you lose your possessions, you call that harm. But when your will gets corrupted — when you're deceived or do something unjust — you think that's no harm at all. The person who lies or acts unfairly doesn't get a headache or lose their house. And those are the only things we care about protecting. We don't care whether our will becomes decent and trustworthy, or shameless and unreliable. We only worry about that in school, and only with a few fancy words. So our progress stops at those few words. Beyond that, we make no real progress at all.

discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.originalText: The beginning of philosophy, to him at least who enters on it in the right way and by the door is a consciousness of his own weakness and inability about necessary things; for we come into the world with no natural notion of a right-angled triangle, or of a diesis (a quarter tone), or of a half-tone; but we learn each of these things by a certain transmission according to art; and for this reason those who do not know them do not think that they know them. But as to good and evil, and beautiful and ugly, and becoming and unbecoming, and happiness and misfortune, and proper and improper, and what we ought to do and what we ought not to do, who ever came into the world without having an innate idea of them?
discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.plainEnglish: Philosophy starts with recognizing how little you actually know about what matters most. You weren't born knowing geometry or musical theory. You had to learn these through careful instruction. People who don't know these subjects admit they don't know them. But when it comes to good and evil, beautiful and ugly, right and wrong, happiness and misery, proper behavior — who doesn't think they already know all about these things? Everyone acts like they were born with perfect understanding of what matters most in life.

discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.originalText: Wherefore we all use these names, and we endeavor to fit the preconceptions to the several cases (things) thus: he has done well; he has not done well; he has done as he ought, not as he ought; he has been unfortunate, he has been fortunate; he is unjust, he is just; who does not use these names? who among us defers the use of them till he has learned them, as he defers the use of the words about lines (geometrical figures) or sounds? And the cause of this is that we come into the world already taught as it were by nature some things on this matter ([Greek: topon]), and proceeding from these we have added to them self-conceit ([Greek: oiaesin]).
discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.plainEnglish: That's why we all use these words. We try to match our basic ideas to specific situations: "He did well." "He did badly." "He did the right thing." "He didn't do what he should have." "He got unlucky." "He got lucky." "He's unfair." "He's fair." Who doesn't use these words? Who waits to learn them first, like we do with geometry or music? Nobody. The reason is simple: we come into the world already knowing some things about right and wrong — like nature taught us. Then we build on that foundation and add our own opinions.

discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.originalText: For why, a man says, do I not know the beautiful and the ugly? Have I not the notion of it? You have. Do I not adapt it to particulars? You do. Do I not then adapt it properly? In that lies the whole question; and conceit is added here; for beginning from these things which are admitted men proceed to that which is matter of dispute by means of unsuitable adaptation; for if they possessed this power of adaptation in addition to those things, what would hinder them from being perfect? But now since you think that you properly adapt the preconceptions to the particulars, tell me whence you derive this (assume that you do so).
discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.plainEnglish: A person says, "Why don't I know what's beautiful and what's ugly? Don't I have some idea about it?" Yes, you do. "Don't I apply this idea to specific things?" Yes, you do. "Don't I apply it correctly?" That's the whole question right there. And this is where arrogance creeps in. People start with things everyone agrees on, then jump to disputed topics using bad logic. If they actually knew how to apply their ideas correctly, what would stop them from being perfect? But since you think you're applying your basic concepts correctly to specific cases, tell me — where do you get this confidence that you're doing it right?

discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.originalText: Because I think so. But it does not seem so to another, and he thinks that he also makes a proper adaptation; or does he not think so? He does think so. Is it possible then that both of you can properly apply the preconceptions to things about which you have contrary opinions? It is not possible. Can you then show us anything better towards adapting the preconceptions beyond your thinking that you do? Does the madman do any other things than the things which seem to him right? Is then this criterion sufficient for him also? It is not sufficient. Come then to something which is superior to seeming ([Greek: tou dochein]). What is this?
discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.plainEnglish: Because I think so. But someone else disagrees, and he thinks his view is right too. Doesn't he think so? Yes, he does. So can both of you be right when you have opposite opinions about the same thing? No, you can't. Can you show me anything better for getting the right view than just "because I think so"? A crazy person also does what seems right to him. Is "it seems right to me" good enough for him too? No, it's not. So we need something better than just what seems right. What is that?

discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.originalText: Observe, this is the beginning of philosophy, a perception of the disagreement of men with one another, and an inquiry into the cause of the disagreement, and a condemnation and distrust of that which only "seems," and a certain investigation of that which "seems" whether it "seems" rightly, and a discovery of some rule ([Greek: chanonos]), as we have discovered a balance in the determination of weights, and a carpenter's rule (or square) in the case of straight and crooked things.—This is the beginning of philosophy. Must we say that all things are right which seem so to all? And how is it possible that contradictions can be right?—Not all then, but all which seem to us to be right.—How more to you than those which seem right to the Syrians? why more than what seem right to the Egyptians? why more than what seems right to me or to any other man? Not at all more.
discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.plainEnglish:
Here's where philosophy begins. You notice that people disagree with each other. You ask why they disagree. You become suspicious of what only "appears" to be true. You investigate whether these appearances are actually right. You try to find some standard to measure by — like we use scales for weight and rulers for straight lines.

This is how philosophy starts. Should we say that everything is right just because it seems right to everyone? But how can contradictory things both be right? Well then, maybe only the things that seem right to us are actually right. But why should what seems right to you matter more than what seems right to Syrians? Why more than what seems right to Egyptians? Why more than what seems right to me or anyone else? It doesn't matter more at all.

discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.originalText: What then "seems" to every man is not sufficient for determining what "is"; for neither in the case of weights nor measures are we satisfied with the bare appearance, but in each case we have discovered a certain rule. In this matter then is there no rule superior to what "seems"? And how is it possible that the most necessary things among men should have no sign (mark), and be incapable of being discovered? There is then some rule. And why then do we not seek the rule and discover it, and afterwards use it without varying from it, not even stretching out the finger without it? For this, I think, is that which when it is discovered cures of their madness those who use mere "seeming" as a measure, and misuse it; so that for the future proceeding from certain things (principles) known and made clear we may use in the case of particular things the preconceptions which are distinctly fixed.
discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.plainEnglish: What something "seems" like to each person isn't enough to determine what it actually "is." We don't trust appearances when we're weighing or measuring things — we use reliable standards instead. So why would there be no reliable standard for more important matters? How could the most essential questions in human life have no clear signs and be impossible to figure out? There must be some standard. So why don't we look for this standard and find it? Why don't we use it consistently afterwards, not even lifting a finger without it? I think this standard, once we find it, will cure the madness of people who rely only on how things "seem" and use that badly. Then we can start from clear, known principles and apply our well-defined concepts to specific situations.

discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.originalText: What is the matter presented to us about which we are inquiring? Pleasure (for example). Subject it to the rule, throw it into the balance. Ought the good to be such a thing that it is fit that we have confidence in it? Yes. And in which we ought to confide? It ought to be. Is it fit to trust to anything which is insecure? No. Is then pleasure anything secure? No. Take it then and throw it out of the scale, and drive it far away from the place of good things. But if you are not sharp-sighted, and one balance is not enough for you, bring another. Is it fit to be elated over what is good? Yes. Is it proper then to be elated over present pleasure? See that you do not say that it is proper; but if you do, I shall then not think you worthy even of the balance. Thus things are tested and weighed when the rules are ready. And to philosophize is this, to examine and confirm the rules; and then to use them when they are known is the act of a wise and good man.
discourses_what-the-beginning-of-philoso.plainEnglish: What are we examining here? Let's say pleasure. Put it to the test. Weigh it carefully. Should something good be trustworthy? Yes. Should we be able to rely on it? Absolutely. Can you trust something that's unreliable? No. Is pleasure reliable? No. Then throw it out. Kick it far away from the list of good things. If you're still not seeing clearly and one test isn't enough, try another. Should good things make you feel proud? Yes. So should present pleasure make you feel proud? Think carefully before you answer. If you say yes, you're not even worth giving a scale to. This is how you test and weigh things when you have solid rules. Philosophy means examining and proving these rules. Then using them once you know them — that's what a wise and good person does.

discourses_of-disputation-or-discussion.originalText: What things a man must learn in order to be able to apply the art of disputation, has been accurately shown by our philosophers (the Stoics); but with respect to the proper use of the things, we are entirely without practice. Only give to any of us, whom you please, an illiterate man to discuss with, and he cannot discover how to deal with the man. But when he has moved the man a little, if he answers beside the purpose, he does not know how to treat him, but he then either abuses or ridicules him, and says, He is an illiterate man; it is not possible to do anything with him. Now a guide, when he has found a man out of the road, leads him into the right way; he does not ridicule or abuse him and then leave him. Do you also show the illiterate man the truth, and you will see that he follows. But so long as you do not show him the truth, do not ridicule him, but rather feel your own incapacity.
discourses_of-disputation-or-discussion.plainEnglish: Our philosophers have figured out exactly what you need to learn to argue well. But when it comes to actually using these skills? We're terrible at it. Give any of us an uneducated person to debate, and we don't know what to do with them. As soon as they say something off-topic or confusing, we're lost. We end up insulting them or making fun of them. We say, "This person is ignorant — there's no point trying." But think about a guide who finds someone lost on the road. Does he mock them and walk away? No. He leads them back to the right path. You should do the same thing. Show the uneducated person what's true, and you'll see they can follow along. But if you're not showing them the truth, don't ridicule them. Recognize your own failure instead.

discourses_of-disputation-or-discussion.originalText:
Now this was the first and chief peculiarity of Socrates, never to be irritated in argument, never to utter anything abusive, anything insulting, but to bear with abusive persons and to put an end to the quarrel. If you would know what great power he had in this way, read the Symposium of Xenophon, and you will see how many quarrels he put an end to. Hence with good reason in the poets also this power is most highly praised:

Quickly with skill he settles great disputes.
Hesiod, Theogony, v. 87.
discourses_of-disputation-or-discussion.plainEnglish:
Here was Socrates' greatest and most important trait: he never got angry in arguments. He never said anything mean or insulting. Instead, he put up with people who were being nasty to him and found ways to end the fights. If you want to see how powerful this ability was, read Xenophon's Symposium. You'll see how many arguments he stopped. The poets had good reason to praise this skill so highly:

"Quickly with skill he settles great disputes."
Hesiod, Theogony, v. 87.

discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.originalText: When I see a man anxious, I say, What does this man want? If he did not want something which is not in his power, how could he be anxious? For this reason a lute player when he is singing by himself has no anxiety, but when he enters the theatre, he is anxious, even if he has a good voice and plays well on the lute; for he not only wishes to sing well, but also to obtain applause: but this is not in his power. Accordingly, where he has skill, there he has confidence. Bring any single person who knows nothing of music, and the musician does not care for him. But in the matter where a man knows nothing and has not been practised, there he is anxious. What matter is this? He knows not what a crowd is or what the praise of a crowd is. However, he has learned to strike the lowest chord and the highest; but what the praise of the many is, and what power it has in life, he neither knows nor has he thought about it. Hence he must of necessity tremble and grow pale.
discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.plainEnglish: When I see someone anxious, I ask: What does this person want? If they didn't want something outside their control, how could they be anxious? Think about a lute player. When he's alone practicing, he's not anxious. But when he steps on stage, he gets nervous — even if he has a good voice and plays well. Why? Because he doesn't just want to perform well. He also wants the audience to applaud him. But applause isn't up to him. So where he has skill, he feels confident. Bring him someone who knows nothing about music, and he doesn't worry about impressing them. But in areas where he's ignorant and unpracticed, he gets anxious. What area is that? He doesn't understand what a crowd is or what crowd approval means. He's learned to play the lowest and highest notes on his lute. But he's never learned what public praise really is or what power it has in life. He's never even thought about it. So of course he has to tremble and turn pale.

discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.originalText: Is any man then afraid about things which are not evils? No. Is he afraid about things which are evils, but still so far within his power that they may not happen? Certainly he is not. If then the things which are independent of the will are neither good nor bad, and all things which do depend on the will are within our power, and no man can either take them from us or give them to us, if we do not choose, where is room left for anxiety? But we are anxious about our poor body, our little property, about the will of Cæsar; but not anxious about things internal.
discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.plainEnglish: Is anyone afraid of things that aren't actually bad? No. Is anyone afraid of things that are bad but still under their control so they can prevent them? Of course not. So here's the thing: everything outside your will isn't good or bad. Everything that depends on your will is under your control. No one can take these things from you or give them to you unless you let them. So where's the room for worry? But we do worry — about our weak bodies, our few possessions, what Caesar might do. We just don't worry about what's inside us.

discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.originalText: Are we anxious about not forming a false opinion? No, for this is in my power. About not exerting our movements contrary to nature? No, not even about this. When then you see a man pale, as the physician says, judging from the complexion, this man's spleen is disordered, that man's liver; so also say, this man's desire and aversion are disordered, he is not in the right way, he is in a fever. For nothing else changes the color, or causes trembling or chattering of the teeth, or causes a man to
discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.plainEnglish: Are we worried about forming false beliefs? No, because that's under our control. Are we worried about acting against our nature? No, not even that. When you see someone go pale, a doctor looks at their color and says, "This person's spleen is sick, that person's liver is sick." You should do the same thing. Say, "This person's desires are sick. Their fears are sick. They're off track. They have a fever." Nothing else makes you change color, or shake, or makes your teeth chatter, or makes you

discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.originalText:
Sink in his knees and shift from foot to foot.
Iliad, xiii., 281.
discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.plainEnglish: Sink to his knees and shift from foot to foot.

meaningCheck.verification_notes: This appears to be a fragment or citation from Homer's Iliad without sufficient context to provide meaningful philosophical translation.

discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.originalText: For this reason, when Zeno was going to meet Antigonus, he was not anxious, for Antigonus had no power over any of the things which Zeno admired; and Zeno did not care for those things over which Antigonus had power. But Antigonus was anxious when he was going to meet Zeno, for he wished to please Zeno; but this was a thing external (out of his power). But Zeno did not want to please Antigonus; for no man who is skilled in any art wishes to please one who has no such skill.
discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.plainEnglish: This explains why Zeno felt no anxiety when he went to meet King Antigonus. The king had no power over anything that Zeno valued. And Zeno didn't care about the things the king controlled. But Antigonus was anxious about meeting Zeno. He wanted Zeno to like him — but that was out of his control. Zeno didn't care whether the king liked him or not. After all, no skilled person tries to impress someone who lacks that same skill.

discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.originalText: Should I try to please you? Why? I suppose, you know the measure by which one man is estimated by another. Have you taken pains to learn what is a good man and what is a bad man, and how a man becomes one or the other? Why then are you not good yourself? How, he replies, am I not good? Because no good man laments or groans or weeps, no good man is pale and trembles, or says, How will he receive me, how will he listen to me? Slave, just as it pleases him. Why do you care about what belongs to others? Is it now his fault if he receives badly what proceeds from you? Certainly. And is it possible that a fault should be one man's, and the evil in another? No. Why then are you anxious about that which belongs to others?
discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.plainEnglish: Should I try to please you? Why? I assume you know how people judge each other. Have you bothered to learn what makes a person good or bad? And how someone becomes one way or the other? Then why aren't you good yourself? "How am I not good?" he asks. Because good people don't complain or moan or cry. Good people don't go pale and shake. They don't say "How will he receive me? How will he listen to me?" Listen, he'll react however he wants to react. Why do you care about things that belong to other people? Is it his fault if he responds badly to what you say or do? Of course it is. Can one person be at fault while another person suffers the consequences? No. So why are you worried about things that belong to other people?

discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.originalText: Your question is reasonable; but I am anxious how I shall speak to him. Cannot you then speak to him as you choose? But I fear that I may be disconcerted? If you are going to write the name of Dion, are you afraid that you would be disconcerted? By no means. Why? is it not because you have practised writing the name? Certainly. Well, if you were going to read the name, would you not feel the same? and why? Because every art has a certain strength and confidence in the things which belong to it. Have you then not practised speaking? and what else did you learn in the school? Syllogisms and sophistical propositions? For what purpose? was it not for the purpose of discoursing skilfully? and is not discoursing skilfully the same as discoursing seasonably and cautiously and with intelligence, and also without making mistakes and without hindrance, and besides all this with confidence? Yes.
discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.plainEnglish: Your question makes sense. But I'm worried about how I'll talk to him. Can't you just speak to him however you want? But I'm afraid I might get flustered. If you were going to write Dion's name, would you be afraid of getting flustered? Of course not. Why not? Because you've practiced writing that name, right? Exactly. Well, if you were going to read the name out loud, wouldn't you feel just as confident? And why? Because every skill gives you strength and confidence in the things it covers. Haven't you practiced speaking? What else did you learn in school? Logic puzzles and tricky arguments? What was the point of all that? Wasn't it to learn how to speak well? And doesn't speaking well mean speaking at the right time, carefully, intelligently, without mistakes, without stumbling — and yes, with confidence? Absolutely.

discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.originalText: When then you are mounted on a horse and go into a plain, are you anxious at being matched against a man who is on foot, and anxious in a matter in which you are practised, and he is not? Yes, but that person (to whom I am going to speak) has power to kill me. Speak the truth, then, unhappy man, and do not brag, nor claim to be a philosopher, nor refuse to acknowledge your masters, but so long as you present this handle in your body, follow every man who is stronger than yourself. Socrates used to practice speaking, he who talked as he did to the tyrants, to the dicasts (judges), he who talked in his prison. Diogenes had practised speaking, he who spoke as he did to Alexander, to the pirates, to the person who bought him. These men were confident in the things which they practised. But do you walk off to your own affairs and never leave them: go and sit in a corner, and weave syllogisms, and propose them to another. There is not in you the man who can rule a state.
discourses_on-anxiety-solicitude.plainEnglish: When you're on horseback riding into an open field, are you worried about facing someone on foot? Are you anxious about something you're skilled at while he's not? 'Yes, but that person I'm going to confront has the power to kill me.' Then tell the truth, you miserable fool. Don't boast or call yourself a philosopher or refuse to admit who your real masters are. As long as your body gives others this handle to grab, you'll follow anyone stronger than you. Socrates practiced speaking — the same man who spoke boldly to tyrants, to judges, and even in prison. Diogenes practiced speaking too — he who spoke fearlessly to Alexander, to pirates, and to the man who bought him as a slave. These men were confident because they had trained for what they faced. But you? Go back to your own little corner. Sit there and weave together logical arguments and present them to other students. You're not the kind of person who can lead a state.

discourses_to-naso.originalText: When a certain Roman entered with his son and listened to one reading, Epictetus said, This is the method of instruction; and he stopped. When the Roman asked him to go on, Epictetus said, Every art when it is taught causes labor to him who is unacquainted with it and is unskilled in it, and indeed the things which proceed from the arts immediately show their use in the purpose for which they were made; and most of them contain something attractive and pleasing. For indeed to be present and to observe how a shoemaker learns is not a pleasant thing; but the shoe is useful and also not disagreeable to look at. And the discipline of a smith when he is learning is very disagreeable to one who chances to be present and is a stranger to the art: but the work shows the use of the art. But you will see this much more in music; for if you are present while a person is learning, the discipline will appear most disagreeable; and yet the results of music are pleasing and delightful to those who know nothing of music.
discourses_to-naso.plainEnglish: A Roman man came in with his son to hear a lesson. Epictetus began teaching, then stopped. When the Roman asked him to continue, Epictetus said: This is how teaching works. Every skill causes struggle for someone who doesn't know it yet. But the things that come from these skills quickly show their purpose. Most skills have something attractive and pleasing about them. Watch someone learn to make shoes — it's not pleasant to see. But the finished shoe is useful and looks good. Watch a blacksmith learning his trade — it's painful to watch if you don't know the craft. But the final work shows the value of the skill. You'll see this most clearly with music. If you watch someone learning to play, it sounds terrible. But the results of music are beautiful and delightful, even to people who know nothing about music.

discourses_to-naso.originalText: And here we conceive the work of a philosopher to be something of this kind: he must adapt his wish ([Greek: boulaesin]) to what is going on, so that neither any of the things which are taking place shall take place contrary to our wish, nor any of the things which do not take place shall not take place when we wish that they should. From this the result is to those who have so arranged the work of philosophy, not to fail in the desire, nor to fall in with that which they would avoid; without uneasiness, without fear, without perturbation to pass through life themselves, together with their associates maintaining the relations both natural and acquired, as the relation of son, of father, of brother, of citizen, of man, of wife, of neighbor, of fellow-traveller, of ruler, of ruled. The work of a philosopher we conceive to be something like this. It remains next to inquire how this must be accomplished.
discourses_to-naso.plainEnglish: Here's what we think a philosopher's job looks like: you must align your wishes with what's actually happening. That way, nothing that happens goes against what you want. And nothing that doesn't happen leaves you wishing it had. When you arrange your philosophy this way, you won't fail to get what you desire. You won't run into what you're trying to avoid. You'll live without anxiety, fear, or inner turmoil. And you'll maintain all your relationships properly — as a son, father, brother, citizen, human being, spouse, neighbor, fellow traveler, leader, or follower. This is what we think a philosopher's work looks like. The next question is: how do you actually do this?

discourses_to-naso.originalText: We see then that the carpenter ([Greek: techton]) when he has learned certain things becomes a carpenter; the pilot by learning certain things becomes a pilot. May it not then in philosophy also not be sufficient to wish to be wise and good, and that there is also a necessity to learn certain things? We inquire then what these things are. The philosophers say that we ought first to learn that there is a God and that he provides for all things; also that it is not possible to conceal from him our acts, or even our intentions and thoughts. The next thing is to learn what is the nature of the gods; for such as they are discovered to be, he, who would please and obey them, must try with all his power to be like them. If the divine is faithful, man also must be faithful; if it is free, man also must be free; if beneficent, man also must be beneficent; if magnanimous, man also must be magnanimous; as being then an imitator of God he must do and say everything consistently with this fact.
discourses_to-naso.plainEnglish: Look at how this works. A carpenter learns certain skills and becomes a carpenter. A ship pilot learns certain skills and becomes a pilot. So in philosophy, it's not enough to just want to be wise and good. You also need to learn certain things. What things? The philosophers say you should first learn that God exists and takes care of everything. You can't hide your actions from him. You can't even hide your intentions and thoughts. Next, you need to learn what the gods are like. Once you understand their nature, you must try with all your strength to be like them if you want to please and obey them. If the divine is faithful, you must be faithful. If it's free, you must be free. If it's generous, you must be generous. If it's noble, you must be noble. Since you're copying God, everything you do and say must match this fact.

discourses_to-or-against-those-who-obsti.originalText: When some persons have heard these words, that a man ought to be constant (firm), and that the will is naturally free and not subject to compulsion, but that all other things are subject to hindrance, to slavery, and are in the power of others, they suppose that they ought without deviation to abide by everything which they have determined. But in the first place that which has been determined ought to be sound (true). I require tone (sinews) in the body, but such as exists in a healthy body, in an athletic body; but if it is plain to me that you have the tone of a frenzied man and you boast of it, I shall say to you, Man, seek the physician; this is not tone, but atony (deficiency in right tone).
discourses_to-or-against-those-who-obsti.plainEnglish: Some people hear that you should be firm and that your will is naturally free and can't be forced — while everything else can be blocked, enslaved, or controlled by others. So they think they should stick to every decision they make without ever changing course. But first, what you've decided needs to be sound. I want strength in the body, but the kind that exists in a healthy body, an athletic body. If I can see that you have the strength of a madman and you're proud of it, I'll tell you: Friend, go see a doctor. That's not strength — that's weakness.

discourses_to-or-against-those-who-obsti.originalText: In a different way something of the same kind is felt by those who listen to these discourses in a wrong manner; which was the case with one of my companions, who for no reason resolved to starve himself to death. I heard of it when it was the third day of his abstinence from food, and I went to inquire what had happened. "I have resolved," he said. "But still tell me what it was which induced you to resolve; for if you have resolved rightly, we shall sit with you and assist you to depart, but if you have made an unreasonable resolution, change your mind." "We ought to keep to our determinations." "What are you doing, man? We ought to keep not to all our determinations, but to those which are right; for if you are now persuaded that it is right, do not change your mind, if you think fit, but persist and say, We ought to abide by our determinations.
discourses_to-or-against-those-who-obsti.plainEnglish: Something similar happens to people who misunderstand these teachings. This happened to one of my friends, who decided for no good reason to starve himself to death. When I heard about it on his third day without food, I went to find out what was going on. "I've made up my mind," he said. "But tell me what made you decide this," I replied. "If you've made a good decision, we'll sit with you and help you die. But if this is a bad decision, change your mind." "We should stick to our decisions," he said. "What are you doing, man? We should stick to our right decisions, not all of them. If you're convinced this is right, then don't change your mind. Stick with it and say, 'We should follow through on our decisions.'

discourses_to-or-against-those-who-obsti.originalText: Will you not make the beginning and lay the foundation in an inquiry whether the determination is sound or not sound, and so then build on it firmness and security? But if you lay a rotten and ruinous foundation, will not your miserable little building fall down the sooner, the more and the stronger are the materials which you shall lay on it? Without any reason would you withdraw from us out of life a man who is a friend and a companion, a citizen of the same city, both the great and the small city? Then while you are committing murder and destroying a man who has done no wrong, do you say that you ought to abide by your determinations? And if it ever in any way came into your head to kill me, ought you to abide by your determinations?"
discourses_to-or-against-those-who-obsti.plainEnglish: Won't you start by examining whether your decision is sound or not? Won't you build on that foundation to create something firm and secure? But if you lay a rotten foundation, won't your pathetic little building collapse faster when you pile more weight on top? For no good reason, you want to remove from life a man who is your friend and companion. He's a fellow citizen — both of the great city and the small one. So while you're committing murder and destroying an innocent man, you say you should stick to your decisions? If it ever crossed your mind to kill me, should you stick to that decision too?

discourses_to-or-against-those-who-obsti.originalText: for what is greater and more useful than for you to be persuaded that it is not sufficient to have made your determination and not to change it. This is the tone (energy) of madness, not of health.—I will die, if you compel me to this.—Why, man? What has happened?—I have determined—I have had a lucky escape that you have not determined to kill me—I take no money. Why?—I have determined—Be assured that with the very tone (energy) which you now use in refusing to take, there is nothing to hinder you at some time from inclining without reason to take money, and then saying, I have determined. As in a distempered body, subject to defluxions, the humor inclines sometimes to these parts, and then to those, so too a sickly soul knows not which way to incline; but if to this inclination and movement there is added a tone (obstinate resolution), then the evil becomes past help and cure.
discourses_to-or-against-those-who-obsti.plainEnglish: What could be more important than understanding this: just making a decision and refusing to change it isn't enough. This stubborn energy is madness, not health. "I'll die before I do this!" Why? What happened? "I've made up my mind." Lucky for me you didn't decide to kill me instead. "I won't take money." Why not? "I've decided." Here's the thing — that same stubborn energy you're using to refuse money? Nothing stops you from flip-flopping later and taking it, then saying "I've decided" again. It's like a sick body where fluid moves around randomly — first here, then there. A sick soul doesn't know which way to lean either. But when you add this stubborn tone to the confusion, the problem becomes impossible to fix.

discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.originalText: Where is the good? In the will. Where is the evil? In the will. Where is neither of them? In those things which are independent of the will. Well then? Does any one among us think of these lessons out of the schools? Does any one meditate (strive) by himself to give an answer to things as in the case of questions?—Is it day?—Yes.—Is it night?—No.—Well, is the number of stars even?—I cannot say.—When money is shown (offered) to you, have you studied to make the proper answer, that money is not a good thing? Have you practised yourself in these answers, or only against sophisms? Why do you wonder then if in the cases which you have studied, in those you have improved; but in those which you have not studied, in those you remain the same?
discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.plainEnglish: Where is good found? In your will. Where is evil found? In your will. Where is neither good nor evil? In things that have nothing to do with your will. So here's my question: does anyone actually think about these lessons outside of class? Does anyone practice giving answers to real situations the way they do with test questions? Like: Is it day? Yes. Is it night? No. Is the number of stars even? I don't know. But when someone offers you money, have you practiced giving the right answer — that money isn't actually good? Have you drilled yourself on these real answers, or only on clever arguments? So why are you surprised that you've gotten better at the things you've practiced, but stayed the same at the things you haven't?

discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.originalText: When the rhetorician knows that he has written well, that he has committed to memory what he has written, and brings an agreeable voice, why is he still anxious? Because he is not satisfied with having studied. What then does he want? To be praised by the audience? For the purpose then of being able to practise declamation he has been disciplined; but with respect to praise and blame he has not been disciplined. For when did he hear from any one what praise is, what blame is, what the nature of each is, what kind of praise should be sought, or what kind of blame should be shunned? And when did he practise this discipline which follows these words (things)? Why then do you still wonder, if in the matters which a man has learned, there he surpasses others, and in those in which he has not been disciplined, there he is the same with the many.
discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.plainEnglish: A public speaker knows he's written a good speech. He's memorized it. He has a pleasant voice. So why is he still nervous? Because he's not satisfied with just having studied. What does he really want? He wants the audience to praise him. Here's the thing: he's been trained to give speeches, but he's never been trained to handle praise and criticism. When did anyone ever teach him what praise really is? What criticism really is? What kind of praise is worth seeking? What kind of criticism should he ignore? When did he ever practice dealing with these things? So why are you surprised that he excels at what he's learned but struggles with what he's never been taught, just like everyone else?

discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.originalText: So the lute player knows how to play, sings well, and has a fine dress, and yet he trembles when he enters on the stage; for these matters he understands, but he does not know what a crowd is, nor the shouts of a crowd, nor what ridicule is. Neither does he know what anxiety is, whether it is our work or the work of another, whether it is possible to stop it or not. For this reason if he has been praised, he leaves the theatre puffed up, but if he has been ridiculed, the swollen bladder has been punctured and subsides.
discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.plainEnglish: Take a musician who knows how to play, sings beautifully, and dresses well. But he still shakes with fear when he walks on stage. He understands music, but he doesn't understand what a crowd really is. He doesn't know what shouting means, or what mockery actually is. He doesn't know what anxiety is — whether it comes from him or from outside forces, whether he can control it or not. So when people praise him, he leaves the theater feeling blown up with pride. But when they mock him, his ego gets punctured like a balloon and deflates completely.

discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.originalText: This is the case also with ourselves. What do we admire? Externals. About what things are we busy? Externals. And have we any doubt then why we fear or why we are anxious? What then happens when we think the things, which are coming on us, to be evils? It is not in our power not to be afraid, it is not in our power not to be anxious. Then we say, Lord God, how shall I not be anxious? Fool, have you not hands, did not God make them for you? Sit down now and pray that your nose may not run. Wipe yourself rather and do not blame him. Well then, has he given to you nothing in the present case? Has he not given to you endurance? Has he not given to you magnanimity? Has he not given to you manliness? When you have such hands do you still look for one who shall wipe your nose?
discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.plainEnglish: We do the same thing ourselves. What do we admire? External things. What keeps us busy? External things. So why are we surprised that we feel fear and anxiety? What happens when we think the things coming at us are bad? We can't help but be afraid. We can't help but be anxious. Then we say, "God, how can I not be anxious?" You fool, don't you have hands? Didn't God give them to you? Don't sit there praying that your nose won't run. Wipe it yourself and stop blaming him. So has he given you nothing to deal with your current situation? Hasn't he given you endurance? Hasn't he given you courage? Hasn't he given you strength? When you have such hands, do you still look for someone else to wipe your nose?

discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.originalText: But we neither study these things nor care for them. Give me a man who cares how he shall do anything, not for the obtaining of a thing, but who cares about his own energy. What man, when he is walking about, cares for his own energy? Who, when he is deliberating, cares about his own deliberation, and not about obtaining that about which he deliberates? And if he succeeds, he is elated and says, How well we have deliberated; did I not tell you, brother, that it is impossible, when we have thought about anything, that it should not turn out thus? But if the thing should turn out otherwise, the wretched man is humbled; he knows not even what to say about what has taken place. Who among us for the sake of this matter has consulted a seer? Who among us as to his actions has not slept in indifference? Who? Give (name) to me one that I may see the man whom I have long been looking for, who is truly noble and ingenuous, whether young or old; name him.
discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.plainEnglish: But we don't study these things or care about them. Show me someone who cares about how he does something — not about getting what he wants, but about his own effort and character. When someone is walking around, does he care about his own energy? When he's making a decision, does he care about how well he thinks it through? Or does he only care about getting what he's deciding about? If he succeeds, he gets excited and says, "Look how well we planned this! Didn't I tell you, friend, that when we think something through, it has to work out?" But if things go wrong, the poor guy is crushed. He doesn't even know what to say about what happened. Who among us has ever consulted a fortune-teller about this kind of thing? Who hasn't been careless about his own actions? Who? Give me one name so I can see the person I've been looking for so long — someone who is truly noble and honest, whether young or old. Name him.

discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.originalText: What then are the things which are heavy on us and disturb us? What else than opinions? What else than opinions lies heavy upon him who goes away and leaves his companions and friends and places and habits of life? Now little children, for instance, when they cry on the nurse leaving them for a short time, forget their sorrow if they receive a small cake. Do you choose then that we should compare you to little children? No, by Zeus, for I do not wish to be pacified by a small cake, but by right opinions. And what are these? Such as a man ought to study all day, and not to be affected by anything that is not his own, neither by companion nor place nor gymnasia, and not even by his own body, but to remember the law and to have it before his eyes.
discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.plainEnglish: What weighs on us and upsets us? What else but our opinions? What else but opinions burden someone who has to leave their friends and familiar places and old habits? Look at little children. When their nurse leaves for a bit, they cry. But give them a cookie and they forget all about it. Do you want us to compare you to little children? No way. I don't want you pacified by a cookie, but by correct thinking. And what does that mean? It means you should spend all day learning what belongs to you and what doesn't. Don't let yourself get rattled by things that aren't yours — not your friends, not your location, not the gym, not even your own body. Remember the law of nature and keep it in front of you.

discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.originalText: And what is the divine law? To keep a man's own, not to claim that which belongs to others, but to use what is given, and when it is not given, not to desire it; and when a thing is taken away, to give it up readily and immediately, and to be thankful for the time that a man has had the use of it, if you would not cry for your nurse and mamma. For what matter does it make by what thing a man is subdued, and on what he depends? In what respect are you better than he who cries for a girl, if you grieve for a little gymnasium, and little porticos, and young men, and such places of amusement?
discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.plainEnglish: What is the divine law? Keep what's truly yours. Don't claim what belongs to others. Use what you're given. When you're not given something, don't crave it. When something is taken away, let it go quickly and willingly.
