Be grateful for the time you had it — if you don't want to be like a child crying for his nurse and mama. What difference does it make what controls you or what you depend on? How are you any better than someone who cries over losing a girlfriend, if you're grieving over losing access to a little gym, some porticos, young people, and other fun places?

discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.originalText: Another comes and laments that he shall no longer drink the water of Dirce. Is the Marcian water worse than that of Dirce? But I was used to the water of Dirce. And you in turn will be used to the other. Then if you become attached to this also, cry for this too, and try to make a verse like the verse of Euripides, The hot baths of Nero and the Marcian water. See how tragedy is made when common things happen to silly men.
discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.plainEnglish: Another person complains that he won't be able to drink from his favorite spring anymore. Is the new water source really worse than the old one? "But I was used to my old water," he says. Well, you'll get used to the new water too. Then if you get attached to that water, you'll cry about losing it as well. You'll make up dramatic poetry like Euripides: "Oh, the hot baths of Nero and the pure spring water!" See how people turn ordinary things into tragedies when they're being foolish.

discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.originalText: When then shall I see Athens again and the Acropolis? Wretch, are you not content with what you see daily? Have you anything better or greater to see than the sun, the moon, the stars, the whole earth, the sea? But if indeed you comprehend Him who administers the whole, and carry him about in yourself, do you still desire small stones and a beautiful rock?
discourses_that-we-do-not-strive-to-use-.plainEnglish: "When will I see Athens again? When will I see the Acropolis?" You fool, aren't you satisfied with what you see every day? Do you have anything better or greater to see than the sun, the moon, the stars, the whole earth, the sea? But if you truly understand the one who runs everything, and you carry him inside yourself, do you still crave little stones and a pretty rock?

discourses_how-we-must-adapt-preconcepti.originalText: What is the first business of him who philosophizes? To throw away self-conceit ([Greek: oiaesis]). For it is impossible for a man to begin to learn that which he thinks that he knows. As to things then which ought to be done and ought not to be done, and good and bad, and beautiful and ugly, all of us talking of them at random go to the philosophers; and on these matters we praise, we censure, we accuse, we blame, we judge and determine about principles honorable and dishonorable. But why do we go to the philosophers? Because we wish to learn what we do not think that we know. And what is this? Theorems. For we wish to learn what philosophers say as being something elegant and acute; and some wish to learn that they may get profit from what they learn. It is ridiculous then to think that a person wishes to learn one thing, and will learn another; or further, that a man will make proficiency in that which he does not learn.
discourses_how-we-must-adapt-preconcepti.plainEnglish:
What's the first thing someone who wants to study philosophy must do? Give up thinking they already know everything. You can't start learning something you think you already understand.

We all talk randomly about what we should and shouldn't do. We debate good and bad, beautiful and ugly. We praise and blame. We judge what's honorable and what isn't. Then we go to philosophers for guidance.

But why do we go to them? Because we want to learn what we don't think we know. What's that? Their theories and ideas. We want to hear what philosophers say because it sounds clever and sharp. Some people want to learn so they can profit from it.

But here's the problem: it's ridiculous to think you'll learn one thing when you actually want to learn something else. And you can't make progress in something you're not really learning.

discourses_how-we-must-adapt-preconcepti.originalText: But the many are deceived by this which deceived also the rhetorician Theopompus, when he blames even Plato for wishing everything to be defined. For what does he say? Did none of us before you use the words good or just, or do we utter the sounds in an unmeaning and empty way without understanding what they severally signify? Now who tells you, Theopompus, that we had not natural notions of each of these things and preconceptions ([Greek: prolaepseis])? But it is not possible to adapt preconceptions to their correspondent objects if we have not distinguished (analyzed) them, and inquired what object must be subjected to each preconception. You may make the same charge against physicians also. For who among us did not use the words healthy and unhealthy before Hippocrates lived, or did we utter these words as empty sounds? For we have also a certain preconception of health, but we are not able to adapt it. For this reason one says, Abstain from food; another says, Give food; another says, Bleed; and another says, Use cupping. What is the reason? is it any other than that a man cannot properly adapt the preconceptions of health to particulars?
discourses_how-we-must-adapt-preconcepti.plainEnglish: Most people get fooled by the same thing that fooled the speaker Theopompus when he criticized Plato for wanting to define everything. What does Theopompus say? "Did none of us use words like 'good' or 'just' before you came along? Were we just making empty sounds without knowing what they meant?" But Theopompus, who says we didn't have natural ideas about these things already built into us? The problem isn't that we lack basic concepts. The problem is that we can't match those concepts to real situations unless we've carefully thought through what each concept actually covers. You could make the same criticism of doctors. Who among us didn't use words like 'healthy' and 'sick' before Hippocrates was born? Were we just making empty sounds? We do have a basic idea of what health means. But we can't apply it properly. That's why one doctor says "Stop eating," another says "Eat more," another says "Let some blood," and another says "Use suction cups." Why does this happen? It's because people can't properly connect their basic ideas about health to specific cases.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running. If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write. But when you shall not have read for thirty days in succession, but have done something else, you will know the consequence. In the same way, if you shall have lain down ten days, get up and attempt to make a long walk, and you will see how your legs are weakened. Generally then if you would make anything a habit, do it; if you would not make it a habit, do not do it, but accustom yourself to do something else in place of it.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: Every habit and skill gets stronger when you practice it. Walking gets easier by walking. Running gets easier by running. Want to be a good reader? Read. Want to be a writer? Write. But if you don't read for thirty days straight and do other things instead, you'll see what happens. Same thing if you lie in bed for ten days, then get up and try to take a long walk. Your legs will be weak. So here's the rule: if you want to build a habit, do it. If you don't want a habit, don't do it. Train yourself to do something else instead.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: In this manner certainly, as philosophers say, also diseases of the mind grow up. For when you have once desired money, if reason be applied to lead to a perception of the evil, the desire is stopped, and the ruling faculty of our mind is restored to the original authority. But if you apply no means of cure, it no longer returns to the same state, but being again excited by the corresponding appearance, it is inflamed to desire quicker than before: and when this takes place continually, it is henceforth hardened (made callous), and the disease of the mind confirms the love of money. For he who has had a fever, and has been relieved from it, is not in the same state that he was before, unless he has been completely cured. Something of the kind happens also in diseases of the soul. Certain traces and blisters are left in it, and unless a man shall completely efface them, when he is again lashed on the same places, the lash will produce not blisters (weals) but sores.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: This is how mental diseases grow, according to philosophers. Say you want money. If you use reason to see that this desire is harmful, you can stop it. Your mind returns to its natural, healthy state. But if you don't treat the problem, things get worse. The next time something triggers that desire, it flares up faster and stronger than before. Keep letting this happen, and the desire hardens into a permanent condition. The mental disease takes hold completely. It's like physical fever. Someone who recovers from fever isn't the same as someone who was never sick — unless they're completely cured. Mental diseases work the same way. They leave traces and tender spots in your soul. If you don't heal them completely, the next time you get hit in those same spots, you won't just get blisters. You'll get open wounds.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: If then you wish not to be of an angry temper, do not feed the habit: throw nothing on it which will increase it: at first keep quiet, and count the days on which you have not been angry. I used to be in passion every day; now every second day; then every third, then every fourth. But if you have intermitted thirty days, make a sacrifice to God. For the habit at first begins to be weakened, and then is completely destroyed. "I have not been vexed to-day, nor the day after, nor yet on any succeeding day during two or three months; but I took care when some exciting things happened." Be assured that you are in a good way.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: If you don't want to be an angry person, don't feed the habit. Don't give it anything that will make it stronger. Start by staying quiet and counting the days you didn't get angry. I used to get mad every day. Then it was every other day. Then every third day, then every fourth. If you go thirty days without anger, make an offering to God. The habit gets weaker at first, then it's completely destroyed. "I haven't been upset today, or yesterday, or for two or three months now. But I was careful when things happened that could set me off." Trust me — you're on the right track.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: How then shall this be done? Be willing at length to be approved by yourself, be willing to appear beautiful to God, desire to be in purity with your own pure self and with God. Then when any such appearance visits you, Plato says, Have recourse to expiations, go a suppliant to the temples of the averting deities. It is even sufficient if you resort to the society of noble and just men, and compare yourself with them, whether you find one who is living or dead.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: How do you do this? Start wanting to approve of yourself. Want to appear beautiful to God. Desire to be pure with your own pure self and with God. Then when any such temptation visits you, Plato says: Go through purification rituals. Go as a beggar to the temples of the gods who turn away evil. It's even enough if you spend time with noble and just people. Compare yourself with them, whether you find someone living or dead.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: But in the first place, be not hurried away by the rapidity of the appearance, but say, Appearances, wait for me a little; let me see who you are, and what you are about; let me put you to the test. And then do not allow the appearance to lead you on and draw lively pictures of the things which will follow; for if you do, it will carry you off wherever it pleases. But rather bring in to oppose it some other beautiful and noble appearance, and cast out this base appearance. And if you are accustomed to be exercised in this way, you will see what shoulders, what sinews, what strength you have. But now it is only trifling words, and nothing more.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: First, don't let your immediate reactions sweep you away. When something appears in your mind, say, "Wait a minute. Let me see what you really are. Let me test you." Don't let that first impression take over and paint vivid pictures of what might happen next. If you do, it will drag you wherever it wants. Instead, bring in a better, nobler thought to fight against it. Push out the ugly thought. If you practice this regularly, you'll see what real strength and power you have. But right now, you're just talking about it and nothing more.

discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.originalText: This is the true athlete, the man who exercises himself against such appearances. Stay, wretch, do not be carried away. Great is the combat, divine is the work; it is for kingship, for freedom, for happiness, for freedom from perturbation. Remember God; call on him as a helper and protector, as men at sea call on the Dioscuri in a storm. For what is a greater storm than that which comes from appearances which are violent and drive away the reason? For the storm itself, what else is it but an appearance? For take away the fear of death, and suppose as many thunders and lightnings as you please, and you will know what calm and serenity there is in the ruling faculty. But if you have once been defeated and say that you will conquer hereafter, and then say the same again, be assured that you will at last be in so wretched a condition and so weak that you will not even know afterwards that you are doing wrong, but you will even begin to make apologies (defences) for your wrong-doing, and then you will confirm the saying of Hesiod to be true, With constant ills the dilatory strives.
discourses_how-we-should-struggle-agains.plainEnglish: This is what a true athlete looks like — someone who trains against these mental impressions. Stop right there, you fool. Don't let yourself get swept away. This is a huge fight. The work is sacred. You're fighting for control, for freedom, for happiness, for peace of mind. Remember God. Call on him to help and protect you, like sailors call on their gods during a storm. What storm is worse than the one that comes from violent impressions that drive away your reason? The storm itself — what is it but an impression? Take away your fear of death. Let there be as much thunder and lightning as you want. You'll see how calm and peaceful your mind can be. But if you lose once and say "I'll win next time," then say the same thing again, you can be sure you'll end up so miserable and weak that you won't even know you're doing wrong anymore. You'll start making excuses for your bad behavior. Then you'll prove Hesiod right: "The person who keeps putting things off struggles with constant troubles."

discourses_of-inconsistency.originalText: Some things men readily confess, and other things they do not. No one then will confess that he is a fool or without understanding; but quite the contrary you will hear all men saying, I wish that I had fortune equal to my understanding. But men readily confess that they are timid, and they say: I am rather timid, I confess; but as to other respects you will not find me to be foolish. A man will not readily confess that he is intemperate; and that he is unjust, he will not confess at all. He will by no means confess that he is envious or a busybody. Most men will confess that they are compassionate. What then is the reason?
discourses_of-inconsistency.plainEnglish: People admit some things about themselves easily. Other things they don't. No one will admit they're stupid or lack understanding. You'll hear everyone say the opposite: "I wish my luck matched my intelligence." But people do admit they're fearful. They say: "I'm pretty timid, I'll give you that. But don't think I'm foolish in other ways." A person won't easily admit they lack self-control. They definitely won't admit they're unfair. They absolutely won't confess to being jealous or a meddler. Most people will admit they're compassionate. So what's going on here?

discourses_of-inconsistency.originalText: The chief thing (the ruling thing) is inconsistency and confusion in the things which relate to good and evil. But different men have different reasons; and generally what they imagine to be base, they do not confess at all. But they suppose timidity to be a characteristic of a good disposition, and compassion also; but silliness to be the absolute characteristic of a slave. And they do not at all admit (confess) the things which are offences against society. But in the case of most errors for this reason chiefly they are induced to confess them, because they imagine that there is something involuntary in them as in timidity and compassion; and if a man confess that he is in any respect intemperate, he alleges love (or passion) as an excuse for what is involuntary. But men do not imagine injustice to be at all involuntary. There is also in jealousy, as they suppose, something involuntary; and for this reason they confess to jealousy also.
discourses_of-inconsistency.plainEnglish: The main problem is that people are confused and inconsistent about what's good and what's bad. Different people have different excuses. Generally, they won't admit to the things they think are truly shameful. They think being timid shows good character. They think compassion does too. But they think being foolish is what slaves do. They won't admit to crimes against society at all. But they'll confess to most other mistakes. Why? Because they imagine these mistakes are involuntary — like being timid or compassionate. If someone admits to being undisciplined, they blame it on love or passion. They say it was involuntary. But people never think injustice is involuntary. They also think jealousy has something involuntary about it. That's why they'll confess to jealousy too.

discourses_of-inconsistency.originalText: Living then among such men, who are so confused, so ignorant of what they say, and of the evils which they have or have not, and why they have them, or how they shall be relieved of them, I think it is worth the trouble for a man to watch constantly (and to ask) whether I also am one of them, what imagination I have about myself, how I conduct myself, whether I conduct myself as a prudent man, whether I conduct myself as a temperate man, whether I ever say this, that I have been taught to be prepared for everything that may happen. Have I the consciousness, which a man who knows nothing ought to have, that I know nothing? Do I go to my teacher as men go to oracles, prepared to obey? or do I like a snivelling boy go to my school to learn history and understand the books which I did not understand before, and, if it should happen so, to explain them also to others?
discourses_of-inconsistency.plainEnglish: You live among people who are confused and ignorant. They don't know what they're saying. They don't understand their problems or why they have them or how to fix them. So it's worth the effort to constantly watch yourself and ask: Am I one of them too? What do I think about myself? How do I act? Do I act like a wise person? Do I act with self-control? Do I ever claim that I've been taught to handle whatever happens? Do I have the awareness that someone who knows nothing should have — that I know nothing? When I go to my teacher, do I go like people go to oracles, ready to obey? Or do I go like a whining kid going to school just to learn facts and understand books I didn't get before, and maybe show off by explaining them to others?

discourses_of-inconsistency.originalText: Man, you have had a fight in the house with a poor slave, you have turned the family upside down, you have frightened the neighbors, and you come to me as if you were a wise man, and you take your seat and judge how I have explained some word, and how I have babbled whatever came into my head. You come full of envy, and humbled, because you bring nothing from home; and you sit during the discussion thinking of nothing else than how your father is disposed towards you and your brother. What are they saying about me there? now they think that I am improving, and are saying, He will return with all knowledge. I wish I could learn everything before I return; but much labor is necessary, and no one sends me anything, and the baths at Nicopolis are dirty; everything is bad at home, and bad here.
discourses_of-inconsistency.plainEnglish: Look at you. You had a fight at home with some poor slave. You turned your whole household upside down. You scared the neighbors. Then you come to me acting like you're some wise man. You sit down and judge how I explained some word, or how I rambled about whatever popped into my head. You show up full of jealousy and feeling small because you've got nothing to show from home. During our discussions, you're not even listening. You're just thinking about how your father feels about you compared to your brother. 'What are they saying about me back there? They probably think I'm getting better at this. They're expecting me to come back knowing everything.' You wish you could learn it all before going home. But real learning takes hard work. No one sends you money. The baths here in Nicopolis are filthy. Everything sucks at home, and everything sucks here too.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: What a man applies himself to earnestly, that he naturally loves. Do men then apply themselves earnestly to the things which are bad? By no means. Well, do they apply themselves to things which in no way concern themselves? Not to these either. It remains then that they employ themselves earnestly only about things which are good; and if they are earnestly employed about things, they love such things also. Whoever then understands what is good can also know how to love; but he who cannot distinguish good from bad, and things which are neither good nor bad from both, how can he possess the power of loving? To love, then, is only in the power of the wise.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: Whatever you put serious effort into, you naturally come to love. So do people put serious effort into bad things? No. Do they put effort into things that don't matter to them at all? No, not those either. That leaves only one option: people put serious effort into things they think are good. And if you work hard at something, you love it. So whoever truly understands what's good can also know how to love properly. But someone who can't tell good from bad, or neutral things from either — how could they know how to love? Real love only belongs to the wise.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: For universally, be not deceived, every animal is attached to nothing so much as to its own interests. Whatever then appears to it an impediment to this interest, whether this be a brother, or a father, or a child, or beloved, or lover, it hates, spurns, curses; for its nature is to love nothing so much as its own interests: this is father, and brother, and kinsman, and country, and God. When then the gods appear to us to be an impediment to this, we abuse them and throw down their statues and burn their temples, as Alexander ordered the temples of Aesculapius to be burned when his dear friend died.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: Don't fool yourself about this universal truth: every living creature cares about nothing more than its own interests. Whatever seems to block those interests — whether it's a brother, father, child, beloved, or lover — it will hate, reject, and curse. By nature, we love nothing more than our own interests. Our interests become our father, brother, family, country, and God. So when the gods seem to stand in our way, we curse them. We tear down their statues and burn their temples. Just like Alexander ordered the temples of Aesculapius burned when his dear friend died.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: For this reason, if a man put in the same place his interest, sanctity, goodness, and country, and parents, and friends, all these are secured: but if he puts in one place his interest, in another his friends, and his country and his kinsmen and justice itself, all these give way, being borne down by the weight of interest. For where the I and the Mine are placed, to that place of necessity the animal inclines; if in the flesh, there is the ruling power; if in the will, it is there; and if it is in externals, it is there. If then I am there where my will is, then only shall I be a friend such as I ought to be, and son, and father; for this will be my interest, to maintain the character of fidelity, of modesty, of patience, of abstinence, of active co-operation, of observing my relations (towards all). But if I put myself in one place, and honesty in another, then the doctrine of Epicurus becomes strong, which asserts either that there is no honesty or it is that which opinion holds to be honest (virtuous).
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: Here's the point: if you put your self-interest in the same place as your values — your sense of what's sacred, good, and right, along with your duties to country, parents, and friends — then all of these are protected. But if you put your self-interest in one place and your friends, country, family, and justice in another place, all the good things get crushed under the weight of self-interest. Whatever you consider most important — that's where your attention goes. If you think your body matters most, that's where your focus goes. If you think your choices matter most, that's where it goes. If you think external things matter most, that's where it goes. Only when I place myself where my will is — only then will I be the kind of friend I should be, the kind of son and father I should be. Because then it will be in my interest to stay faithful, modest, patient, self-controlled, and helpful. It will be in my interest to do right by everyone in my life. But if I put myself in one place and honesty in another, then Epicurus wins. His teaching says either there is no such thing as real virtue, or virtue is just whatever people happen to think is virtuous.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: It was through this ignorance that the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians quarrelled, and the Thebans with both; and the great king quarrelled with Hellas, and the Macedonians with both: and the Romans with the Getae. And still earlier the Trojan war happened for these reasons. Alexander was the guest of Menelaus, and if any man had seen their friendly disposition, he would not have believed any one who said that they were not friends. But there was cast between them (as between dogs) a bit of meat, a handsome woman, and about her war arose. And now when you see brothers to be friends appearing to have one mind, do not conclude from this anything about their friendship, not even if they swear it and say that it is impossible for them to be separated from one another. For the ruling principle of a bad man cannot be trusted; it is insecure, has no certain rule by which it is directed, and is overpowered at different times by different appearances.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: All these wars happened because of ignorance. The Athenians fought the Spartans. The Thebans fought both of them. The Persian king fought the Greeks. The Macedonians fought everyone. The Romans fought the Getae. And long before that, the Trojan War happened for the same reasons. Alexander was Menelaus's guest. If you had seen how friendly they were, you would never have believed anyone who said they weren't friends. But then someone threw a piece of meat between them — like you'd do with dogs. That meat was a beautiful woman. And over her, war broke out. Now when you see brothers acting friendly and seeming to agree on everything, don't assume anything about their friendship. Don't trust them even if they swear oaths and say nothing could ever separate them. You can't trust the mind of a bad person. It's unstable. It has no reliable principles to guide it. Different things overpower it at different times.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: But examine, not what other men examine, if they are born of the same parents and brought up together, and under the same pedagogue; but examine this only, wherein they place their interest, whether in externals or in the will. If in externals, do not name them friends, no more than name them trustworthy or constant, or brave or free; do not name them even men, if you have any judgment. For that is not a principle of human nature which makes them bite one another, and abuse one another, and occupy deserted places or public places, as if they were mountains, and in the courts of justice display the acts of robbers; nor yet that which makes them intemperate and adulterers and corrupters, nor that which makes them do whatever else men do against one another through this one opinion only, that of placing themselves and their interests in the things which are not within the power of their will.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: Don't judge people by whether they share the same parents or grew up together or had the same teacher. Judge them by this alone: where do they put their focus? Do they care about external things or about their own will and choices? If they focus on externals, don't call them friends. Don't call them trustworthy, steady, brave, or free. Don't even call them human beings if you have any sense. It's not human nature that makes people attack each other, abuse each other, and fight over empty land or public spaces like wild animals. It's not human nature that makes them rob each other in courtrooms. It's not human nature that makes them lustful, unfaithful, and corrupt. It's not human nature that drives all the terrible things people do to each other. There's only one thing behind all this bad behavior: they put themselves and their interests in things they can't actually control.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: But if you hear that in truth these men think the good to be only there, where will is, and where there is a right use of appearances, no longer trouble yourself whether they are father or son, or brothers, or have associated a long time and are companions, but when you have ascertained this only, confidently declare that they are friends, as you declare that they are faithful, that they are just. For where else is friendship than where there is fidelity, and modesty, where there is a communion of honest things and of nothing else.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: But if you discover that these people truly believe good exists only where there is proper intention and right judgment, then don't worry about whether they're your father, son, brothers, or long-time companions. Once you've confirmed this one thing about them, you can confidently call them friends. You can say they're trustworthy and just. Where else does friendship exist except where you find loyalty, decency, and shared commitment to honest things — and nothing else?

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: But you may say, Such a one treated me with regard so long; and did he not love me? How do you know, slave, if he did not regard you in the same way as he wipes his shoes with a sponge, or as he takes care of his beast? How do you know, when you have ceased to be useful as a vessel, he will not throw you away like a broken platter? But this woman is my wife, and we have lived together so long. And how long did Eriphyle live with Amphiaraus, and was the mother of children and of many? But a necklace came between them: and what is a necklace? It is the opinion about such things. That was the bestial principle, that was the thing which broke asunder the friendship between husband and wife, that which did not allow the woman to be a wife nor the mother to be a mother.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: But you might say, "He treated me well for so long — didn't he love me?" How do you know, you fool, that he didn't regard you the same way he uses a sponge to clean his shoes? Or the way he takes care of his livestock? How do you know that once you stop being useful to him, he won't toss you aside like a broken dish? "But this woman is my wife, and we've been together so long." And how long did Eriphyle live with Amphiaraus? She was his wife and the mother of his children. But a necklace came between them. And what is a necklace? It's just our opinion about such things. That was the animal instinct at work. That's what destroyed the friendship between husband and wife. That's what stopped the woman from being a wife and the mother from being a mother.

discourses_on-friendship.originalText: And let every man among you who has seriously resolved either to be a friend himself or to have another for his friend, cut out these opinions, hate them, drive them from his soul. And thus first of all he will not reproach himself, he will not be at variance with himself, he will not change his mind, he will not torture himself. In the next place, to another also, who is like himself, he will be altogether and completely a friend. But he will bear with the man who is unlike himself, he will be kind to him, gentle, ready to pardon on account of his ignorance, on account of his being mistaken in things of the greatest importance; but he will be harsh to no man, being well convinced of Plato's doctrine that every mind is deprived of truth unwillingly. If you cannot do this, yet you can do in all other respects as friends do, drink together, and lodge together, and sail together, and you may be born of the same parents, for snakes also are: but neither will they be friends, nor you, so long as you retain these bestial and cursed opinions.
discourses_on-friendship.plainEnglish: If you want to be a true friend or have true friends, you need to tear out certain poisonous opinions. Hate them. Drive them out of your soul. When you do this, first you'll stop beating yourself up. You won't fight with yourself anymore. You won't keep changing your mind. You won't torture yourself. Second, you'll be a complete and genuine friend to others who think like you. You'll also be patient with people who think differently. You'll be kind to them, gentle, ready to forgive them because they're ignorant and confused about what really matters. You won't be harsh with anyone, because you know Plato was right: no one chooses to be wrong. If you can't manage this, sure, you can still hang out like friends do. You can drink together, live together, travel together. You might even be born from the same parents, just like snakes are. But you won't actually be friends — neither will they — as long as you hold onto these savage and damaging beliefs.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: Every man will read a book with more pleasure or even with more ease, if it is written in fairer characters. Therefore every man will also listen more readily to what is spoken, if it is signified by appropriate and becoming words. We must not say then that there is no faculty of expression: for this affirmation is the characteristic of an impious and also of a timid man. Of an impious man, because he undervalues the gifts which come from God, just as if he would take away the commodity of the power of vision, or hearing, or of seeing. Has then God given you eyes to no purpose? and to no purpose has he infused into them a spirit so strong and of such skilful contrivance as to reach a long way and to fashion the forms of things which are seen? What messenger is so swift and vigilant? And to no purpose has he made the interjacent atmosphere so efficacious and elastic that the vision penetrates through the atmosphere which is in a manner moved? And to no purpose has he made light, without the presence of which there would be no use in any other thing?
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: Everyone enjoys reading a book more when it's written clearly. Everyone listens more willingly when ideas are expressed with the right words. So don't claim there's no such thing as skill in communication. That's what impious and cowardly people say. Impious, because they dismiss gifts that come from God — like they'd deny the value of sight or hearing. Did God give you eyes for no reason? Did he put such a strong and skillful spirit in them for nothing — one that can see far and make sense of what you're looking at? What messenger moves as fast and stays as alert as your vision? Did he make the air between you and objects work so well for no reason — air that your sight cuts through like it's moving? Did he create light for no purpose, when without it nothing else would matter?

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: Man, be neither ungrateful for these gifts nor yet forget the things which are superior to them. But indeed for the power of seeing and hearing, and indeed for life itself, and for the things which contribute to support it, for the fruits which are dry, and for wine and oil give thanks to God: but remember that he has given you something else better than all these, I mean the power of using them, proving them, and estimating the value of each. For what is that which gives information about each of these powers, what each of them is worth? Is it each faculty itself? Did you ever hear the faculty of vision saying anything about itself? or the faculty of hearing? or wheat, or barley, or a horse, or a dog? No; but they are appointed as ministers and slaves to serve the faculty which has the power of making use of the appearances of things.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: Be grateful for what you have, but don't forget the better things. Yes, thank God for your sight and hearing. Thank him for your life and everything that keeps you alive — your food, wine, and oil. But remember: he gave you something better than all of these. He gave you the power to use them, test them, and judge what each one is worth. What tells you about each of these abilities? What tells you what each one is worth? Does each ability speak for itself? Have you ever heard your eyesight comment on itself? Or your hearing? Have wheat, barley, a horse, or a dog ever told you their value? No. They exist to serve the one ability that can actually judge appearances and make sense of them.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: And if you inquire what is the value of each thing, of whom do you inquire? who answers you? How then can any other faculty be more powerful than this, which uses the rest as ministers and itself proves each and pronounces about them? for which of them knows what itself is, and what is its own value? which of them knows when it ought to employ itself and when not? what faculty is it which opens and closes the eyes, and turns them away from objects to which it ought not to apply them and does apply them to other objects? Is it the faculty of vision? No, but it is the faculty of the will. What is that faculty which closes and opens the ears? what is that by which they are curious and inquisitive, or on the contrary unmoved by what is said? is it the faculty of hearing? It is no other than the faculty of the will.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: When you ask what something is worth, who do you ask? Who gives you the answer? How can any other ability be more powerful than this one — the one that uses all the others like servants and tests each one and makes judgments about them? Which of your abilities knows what it really is and what it's worth? Which one knows when to work and when to stay quiet? What ability opens and closes your eyes? What turns them away from things they shouldn't look at and toward things they should? Is it your eyesight? No. It's your will. What closes and opens your ears? What makes them curious and eager to listen, or completely uninterested in what's being said? Is it your hearing? No. It's nothing other than your will.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: Will this faculty then, seeing that it is amidst all the other faculties which are blind and dumb and unable to see anything else except the very acts for which they are appointed in order to minister to this (faculty) and serve it, but this faculty alone sees sharp and sees what is the value of each of the rest; will this faculty declare to us that anything else is the best, or that itself is? And what else does the eye do when it is opened than see? But whether we ought to look on the wife of a certain person, and in what manner, who tells us? The faculty of the will. And whether we ought to believe what is said or not to believe it, and if we do believe, whether we ought to be moved by it or not, who tells us? Is it not the faculty of the will?
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: So this one faculty can see clearly while all the other faculties are blind and mute. They can only do their specific jobs — serving this main faculty. But this faculty alone sees sharply and judges the value of all the rest. Will this faculty tell us that something else is most important? Or will it say that it itself is most important? What does the eye do when it opens? It sees. But should you look at another man's wife? And how should you look? Who decides that? Your will does. Should you believe what someone tells you? And if you do believe it, should you let it affect you? Who decides? Your faculty of will.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: But if you ask me what then is the most excellent of all things, what must I say? I cannot say the power of speaking, but the power of the will, when it is right ([Greek: orthae]). For it is this which uses the other (the power of speaking), and all the other faculties both small and great. For when this faculty of the will is set right, a man who is not good becomes good: but when it fails, a man becomes bad. It is through this that we are unfortunate, that we are fortunate, that we blame one another, are pleased with one another. In a word, it is this which if we neglect it makes unhappiness, and if we carefully look after it, makes happiness.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: But if you ask me what the most excellent thing is, what should I say? I can't say it's the power of speaking. It's the power of the will — when it's right. This is what controls everything else, including speech and all your other abilities, big and small. When your will is set right, a bad person becomes good. When it fails, a person becomes bad. This is why we're unlucky or lucky. This is why we blame each other or are pleased with each other. In short, if we neglect our will, we become unhappy. If we take care of it, we become happy.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: What then is usually done? Men generally act as a traveller would do on his way to his own country, when he enters a good inn, and being pleased with it should remain there. Man, you have forgotten your purpose: you were not travelling to this inn, but you were passing through it. But this is a pleasant inn. And how many other inns are pleasant? and how many meadows are pleasant? yet only for passing through. But your purpose is this, to return to your country, to relieve your kinsmen of anxiety, to discharge the duties of a citizen, to marry, to beget children, to fill the usual magistracies. For you are not come to select more pleasant places, but to live in these where you were born and of which you were made a citizen.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: What do people usually do? They act like a traveler who finds a nice inn on his way home and decides to stay there forever. Man, you've forgotten why you're traveling. You weren't going to this inn to live there. You were just passing through. But this is such a pleasant inn! Sure, and how many other inns are pleasant? How many meadows are beautiful? They're all just for passing through. Your real purpose is to get back home, to ease your family's worries, to do your duties as a citizen, to marry, to have children, to serve in public office. You didn't come here to hunt for the most pleasant places. You came to live in the place where you were born and where you belong as a citizen.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: Something of the kind takes place in the matter which we are considering. Since by the aid of speech and such communication as you receive here you must advance to perfection, and purge your will and correct the faculty which makes use of the appearances of things; and since it is necessary also for the teaching (delivery) of theorems to be effected by a certain mode of expression and with a certain variety and sharpness, some persons captivated by these very things abide in them, one captivated by the expression, another by syllogisms, another again by sophisms, and still another by some other inn ([Greek: paudocheiou]) of the kind; and there they stay and waste away as they were among sirens.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: Something similar happens in what we're discussing here. You come here to learn through speech and instruction. You're supposed to use this to reach perfection — to purge your will and fix how you handle impressions. The teaching has to use a certain style of speaking with variety and sharpness. But some people get captivated by these very tools. One person falls in love with fancy expressions. Another gets obsessed with logical arguments. Another gets hooked on clever tricks of reasoning. And another gets trapped by some other roadside inn of this kind. They stay there and waste away, like sailors who stopped to listen to the sirens.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: Man, your purpose (business) was to make yourself capable of using conformably to nature the appearances presented to you, in your desires not to be frustrated, in your aversion from things not to fall into that which you would avoid, never to have no luck (as one may say), nor ever to have bad luck, to be free, not hindered, not compelled, conforming yourself to the administration of Zeus, obeying it, well satisfied with this, blaming no one, charging no one with fault, able from your whole soul to utter these verses: Lead me, O Zeus, and thou too Destiny.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: Your job was to learn how to handle whatever life throws at you in line with nature. You wanted to get what you desire without being crushed when you don't. You wanted to avoid what you hate without falling into it anyway. You wanted to never have bad luck or good luck — just to be free, unblocked, and not forced into anything. You wanted to align yourself with how Zeus runs the world, to obey willingly, to be completely satisfied with this arrangement. You wanted to blame no one, find fault with no one, and be able to say with your whole heart: 'Lead me, Zeus, and you too, Destiny.'

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: TO (OR AGAINST) A PERSON WHO WAS ONE OF THOSE WHO WERE NOT VALUED (ESTEEMED) BY HIM.—A certain person said to him (Epictetus): Frequently I desired to hear you and came to you, and you never gave me any answer; and now, if it is possible, I entreat you to say something to me. Do you think, said Epictetus, that as there is an art in anything else, so there is also an art in speaking, and that he who has the art, will speak skilfully, and he who has not, will speak unskilfully?—I do think so.—He then who by speaking receives benefit himself, and is able to benefit others, will speak skilfully; but he who is rather damaged by speaking and does damage to others, will he be unskilled in this art of speaking? And you may find that some are damaged and others benefited by speaking. And are all who hear benefited by what they hear? Or will you find that among them also some are benefited and some damaged? There are both among these also, he said.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: A man came to Epictetus and said: "I've wanted to hear you speak many times. I came to you, but you never answered me. Now please, if you can, say something to me." Epictetus replied: "Do you think there's skill involved in speaking, just like there's skill in anything else? Someone with skill speaks well, and someone without skill speaks poorly?" "Yes, I think so," the man said. "Then someone who benefits himself and others when he speaks — he speaks skillfully. But someone who harms himself and others when he speaks — isn't he unskilled at speaking? You'll find that some people are harmed by speaking and others are helped by it. And do all listeners benefit from what they hear? Or do you find that some listeners are helped and some are harmed?" "Both," the man said.

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: In this case also then those who hear skilfully are benefited, and those who hear unskilfully are damaged? He admitted this. Is there then a skill in hearing also, as there is in speaking? It seems so. If you choose, consider the matter in this way also. The practice of music, to whom does it belong? To a musician. And the proper making of a statue, to whom do you think that it belongs? To a statuary. And the looking at a statue skilfully, does this appear to you to require the aid of no art? This also requires the aid of art. Then if speaking properly is the business of the skilful man, do you see that to hear also with benefit is the business of the skilful man? Now as to speaking and hearing perfectly, and usefully, let us for the present, if you please, say no more, for both of us are a long way from everything of the kind. But I think that every man will allow this, that he who is going to hear philosophers requires some amount of practice in hearing. Is it not so?
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: So the people who listen well get something good out of it. And the people who listen badly get hurt by it? He agreed. So there's a skill to listening, just like there's a skill to speaking? It seems like it. Think about it this way if you want. Who does music belong to? A musician. Who should make a statue properly? A sculptor. And looking at a statue the right way — doesn't that take some skill too? Yes, that takes skill too. So if speaking well is the job of a skilled person, can you see that listening well is also the job of a skilled person? Now, about speaking and listening perfectly and usefully — let's not talk about that right now if you don't mind. We're both far from being good at either one. But I think everyone will agree on this: if you're going to listen to philosophers, you need some practice at listening. Right?

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: Why then do you say nothing to me? I can only say this to you, that he who knows not who he is, and for what purpose he exists, and what is this world, and with whom he is associated, and what things are the good and the bad, and the beautiful and the ugly, and who neither understands discourse nor demonstration, nor what is true nor what is false, and who is not able to distinguish them, will neither desire according to nature nor turn away nor move towards, nor intend (to act), nor assent, nor dissent, nor suspend his judgment: to say all in a few words, he will go about dumb and blind, thinking that he is somebody, but being nobody. Is this so now for the first time? Is it not the fact that ever since the human race existed, all errors and misfortunes have arisen through this ignorance?
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: Why don't you say anything to me? Here's what I can tell you: If you don't know who you are, why you exist, what this world is, who you're connected to, what's good and bad, what's beautiful and ugly — if you don't understand reasoning or proof, can't tell truth from lies, can't distinguish between them — then you won't desire the right things. You won't avoid the right things. You won't move toward what you should or intend to act properly. You won't agree or disagree with the right things. You won't hold back judgment when you should. In short, you'll stumble around deaf and blind, thinking you're somebody important when you're actually nobody. Is this happening for the first time? Haven't all human errors and disasters always come from exactly this kind of ignorance?

discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.originalText: This is all that I have to say to you; and I say even this not willingly. Why? Because you have not roused me. For what must I look to in order to be roused, as men who are expert in riding are roused by generous horses? Must I look to your body? You treat it disgracefully. To your dress? That is luxurious. To your behavior, to your look? That is the same as nothing. When you would listen to a philosopher, do not say to him, You tell me nothing; but only show yourself worthy of hearing or fit for hearing; and you will see how you will move the speaker.
discourses_on-the-power-of-speaking.plainEnglish: That's all I have to say to you. And honestly, I don't even want to say this much. Why? Because you haven't inspired me to speak. What should inspire me to teach, the way skilled horsemen get excited by good horses? Should I be inspired by your body? You abuse it. Your clothes? They're fancy and overdone. Your behavior and appearance? They're worth nothing. When you want to hear a philosopher speak, don't tell him "You're not teaching me anything." Instead, show that you're worth teaching — that you're ready to listen. Then you'll see how much the teacher wants to share with you.

discourses_that-logic-is-necessary.originalText:
When one of those who were present said,
Persuade me that logic is necessary, he replied, Do you wish me to
prove this to you? The answer was, Yes. Then I must use a demonstrative
form of speech. This was granted. How then will you know if I am
cheating you by my argument? The man was silent. Do you see, said
Epictetus, that you yourself are admitting that logic is necessary, if
without it you cannot know so much as this, whether logic is necessary
or not necessary?
discourses_that-logic-is-necessary.plainEnglish: Someone in the audience said, "Convince me that logic is necessary." Epictetus replied, "Do you want me to prove this to you?" The person said yes. "Then I'll have to use logical reasoning," Epictetus said. The person agreed. "But then how will you know if I'm tricking you with my argument?" The person had no answer. "You see," said Epictetus, "you're already admitting that logic is necessary. Without it, you can't even tell whether logic itself is necessary or not."

discourses_of-finery-in-dress.originalText: A certain young man, a rhetorician, came to see Epictetus, with his hair dressed more carefully than was usual and his attire in an ornamental style; whereupon Epictetus said, Tell me if you do not think that some dogs are beautiful and some horses, and so of all other animals. I do think so, the youth replied. Are not then some men also beautiful and others ugly? Certainly. Do we then for the same reason call each of them in the same kind beautiful, or each beautiful for something peculiar? And you will judge of this matter thus. Since we see a dog naturally formed for one thing, and a horse for another, and for another still, as an example, a nightingale, we may generally and not improperly declare each of them to be beautiful then when it is most excellent according to its nature; but since the nature of each is different, each of them seems to me to be beautiful in a different way. Is it not so? He admitted that it was.
discourses_of-finery-in-dress.plainEnglish: A young speech teacher came to see Epictetus. His hair was perfectly styled and his clothes were fancy. Epictetus said, "Tell me — don't you think some dogs are beautiful and some horses are beautiful? Same with all other animals?" The young man said, "Yes, I do." "Well then, aren't some people beautiful and others ugly?" "Definitely." "But do we call them beautiful for the same reasons, or does each thing have its own kind of beauty?" Epictetus continued: "Think about it this way. Dogs are naturally made for one purpose, horses for another, and nightingales for yet another. We can say each one is beautiful when it's excellent according to its own nature. But since each has a different nature, each is beautiful in a different way. Don't you think?" The young man agreed.

discourses_of-finery-in-dress.originalText: That then which makes a dog beautiful, makes a horse ugly; and that which makes a horse beautiful, makes a dog ugly, if it is true that their natures are different. It seems to be so. For I think that what makes a Pancratiast beautiful, makes a wrestler to be not good, and a runner to be most ridiculous; and he who is beautiful for the Pentathlon, is very ugly for wrestling. It is so, said he. What then makes a man beautiful? Is it that which in its kind makes both a dog and a horse beautiful? It is, he said. What then makes a dog beautiful? The possession of the excellence of a dog. And what makes a horse beautiful? The possession of the excellence of a horse.
discourses_of-finery-in-dress.plainEnglish: What makes a dog beautiful makes a horse ugly. What makes a horse beautiful makes a dog ugly. This happens because they have different natures. Think about it this way: What makes a fighter good at pankration makes a wrestler weak and a runner look ridiculous. Someone who's built perfectly for the pentathlon looks terrible as a wrestler. "True," he said. So what makes a human beautiful? The same thing that makes a dog or horse beautiful in their own way. "Yes," he said. What makes a dog beautiful? Having the qualities that make a dog excellent. What makes a horse beautiful? Having the qualities that make a horse excellent.

discourses_of-finery-in-dress.originalText: What then makes a man beautiful? Is it not the possession of the excellence of a man? And do you then, if you wish to be beautiful, young man, labor at this, the acquisition of human excellence? But what is this? Observe whom you yourself praise, when you praise many persons without partiality: do you praise the just or the unjust? The just. Whether do you praise the moderate or the immoderate? The moderate. And the temperate or the intemperate? The temperate. If then you make yourself such a person, you will know that you will make yourself beautiful; but so long as you neglect these things, you must be ugly, even though you contrive all you can to appear beautiful.
discourses_of-finery-in-dress.plainEnglish: What makes a man beautiful? Having the excellence that makes someone truly human. So if you want to be beautiful, young man, work on this — getting human excellence. But what is that? Look at who you praise when you judge people fairly. Do you praise the just person or the unjust? The just. Do you praise the moderate person or the immoderate? The moderate. The self-controlled or the uncontrolled? The self-controlled. If you make yourself that kind of person, you'll know you've made yourself beautiful. But as long as you ignore these things, you'll be ugly — no matter how hard you try to appear beautiful.

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: There are three things (topics, [Greek: topoi]) in which a man ought to exercise himself who would be wise and good. The first concerns the desires and the aversions, that a man may not fail to get what he desires, and that he may not fall into that which he does not desire. The second concerns the movements towards an object and the movements from an object, and generally in doing what a man ought to do, that he may act according to order, to reason, and not carelessly. The third thing concerns freedom from deception and rashness in judgment, and generally it concerns the assents ([Greek: sugchatatheseis]).
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: There are three areas you need to work on if you want to be wise and good. First, manage your desires and what you want to avoid. Learn to get what you truly want and stay away from what you don't want. Second, control your actions and impulses. Do what you should do in the right way, with reason, not carelessly. Third, avoid being fooled or making hasty judgments. Be careful about what you agree with or believe.

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: Of these topics the chief and the most urgent is that which relates to the affects ([Greek: ta pathae] perturbations); for an affect is produced in no other way than by a failing to obtain that which a man desires or falling into that which a man would wish to avoid. This is that which brings in perturbations, disorders, bad fortune, misfortunes, sorrows, lamentations, and envy; that which makes men envious and jealous; and by these causes we are unable even to listen to the precepts of reason. The second topic concerns the duties of a man; for I ought not to be free from affects ([Greek: apathae]) like a statue, but I ought to maintain the relations ([Greek: scheseis]) natural and acquired, as a pious man, as a son, as a father, as a citizen.
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: The most important and urgent topic is dealing with strong emotions. You get upset only when you fail to get what you want or when you end up with what you're trying to avoid. This is what causes disturbances, chaos, bad luck, misfortunes, grief, complaints, and envy. It makes people envious and jealous. When you're caught up in all this, you can't even listen to reason. The second topic is about your duties as a person. You shouldn't be emotionless like a statue. You need to fulfill your natural and social relationships — as a religious person, as a child, as a parent, as a citizen.

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: The third topic is that which immediately concerns those who are making proficiency, that which concerns the security of the other two, so that not even in sleep any appearance unexamined may surprise us, nor in intoxication, nor in melancholy. This, it may be said, is above our power. But the present philosophers neglecting the first topic and the second (the affects and duties), employ themselves on the third, using sophistical arguments ([Greek: metapiptontas]), making conclusions from questioning, employing hypotheses, lying. For a man must, it is said, when employed on these matters, take care that he is not deceived. Who must? The wise and good man. This then is all that is wanting to you. Have you successfully worked out the rest? Are you free from deception in the matter of money? If you see a beautiful girl do you resist the appearance? If your neighbor obtains an estate by will, are you not vexed? Now is there nothing else wanting to you except unchangeable firmness of mind ([Greek: ametaptosia])?
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: The third area of study is for those who are already making progress. It's about securing the first two areas so that not even in sleep or when drunk or depressed can any false impression catch us off guard. You might say this is beyond our power. But today's philosophers ignore the first and second topics (emotions and duties). Instead, they focus on the third, using tricky arguments, drawing conclusions from questions, and working with assumptions — basically lying. They say a person working on these things must be careful not to be deceived. Who must? The wise and good person. So that's all you need, right? Have you mastered everything else? Are you free from being fooled about money? When you see a beautiful woman, do you resist the temptation? When your neighbor inherits an estate, are you not bothered? Is the only thing you're missing an unshakeable mind?

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: Wretch, you hear these very things with fear and anxiety that some person may despise you, and with inquiries about what any person may say about you. And if a man come and tell you that in a certain conversation in which the question was, Who is the best philosopher, a man who was present said that a certain person was the chief philosopher, your little soul which was only a finger's length stretches out to two cubits. But if another who is present says, You are mistaken; it is not worth while to listen to a certain person, for what does he know? he has only the first principles, and no more?
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: You pathetic fool, you listen to these teachings with fear and worry that someone might look down on you. You obsess over what people might say about you. If someone comes and tells you that in some conversation about who the best philosopher is, someone mentioned a particular person as the top philosopher, your tiny soul that was only finger-sized suddenly swells to arm's length. But if someone else who was there says, 'You're wrong — that person isn't worth listening to. What does he really know? He only has the basics and nothing more,' what happens then?

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: then you are confounded, you grow pale, you cry out immediately, I will show him who I am, that I am a great philosopher. It is seen by these very things: why do you wish to show it by others? Do you not know that Diogenes pointed out one of the sophists in this way by stretching out his middle finger? And then when the man was wild with rage, This, he said, is the certain person: I have pointed him out to you. For a man is not shown by the finger, as a stone or a piece of wood; but when any person shows the man's principles, then he shows him as a man.
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: Then you get confused, you turn pale, you immediately shout, "I'll show him who I am — I'm a great philosopher!" But this very reaction shows who you are. Why do you need to prove it with other things? Don't you know how Diogenes exposed one of the sophists? He just held up his middle finger. When the sophist flew into a rage, Diogenes said, "There he is — that's the man. I've pointed him out to you." You can't show a person's true nature by pointing at them like you would at a stone or a piece of wood. But when someone reveals a person's principles, then they show who that person really is.

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: Let us look at your principles also. For is it not plain that you value not at all your own will ([Greek: proairesis]), but you look externally to things which are independent of your will? For instance, what will a certain person say? and what will people think of you? Will you be considered a man of learning; have you read Chrysippus or Antipater? for if you have read Archedamus also, you have every thing (that you can desire). Why you are still uneasy lest you should not show us who you are? Would you let me tell you what manner of man you have shown us that you are? You have exhibited yourself to us as a mean fellow, querulous, passionate, cowardly, finding fault with everything, blaming everybody, never quiet, vain: this is what you have exhibited to us. Go away now and read Archedamus; then if a mouse should leap down and make a noise, you are a dead man. For such a death awaits you as it did—what was the man's name—Crinis; and he too was proud, because he understood Archedamus.
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: Let's look at your principles too. Isn't it obvious that you don't value your own choices at all? Instead, you look outside to things you can't control. For example: What will someone say? What will people think of you? Will they think you're learned? Have you read Chrysippus or Antipater? If you've also read Archedamus, you think you have everything you need. Why are you still anxious about proving to us who you are? Want me to tell you what kind of person you've already shown us? You've shown yourself to be petty, whining, angry, cowardly, criticizing everything, blaming everyone, never at peace, and vain. That's what you've shown us. Go read Archedamus now. Then when a mouse jumps down and makes a noise, you'll drop dead from fear. That's the kind of death waiting for you — just like what's-his-name, Crinis. He was proud too because he understood Archedamus.

discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.originalText: Wretch, will you not dismiss these things that do not concern you at all? These things are suitable to those who are able to learn them without perturbation, to those who can say: "I am not subject to anger, to grief, to envy: I am not hindered, I am not restrained. What remains for me? I have leisure, I am tranquil: let us see how we must deal with sophistical arguments; let us see how when a man has accepted an hypothesis he shall not be led away to any thing absurd." To them such things belong. To those who are happy it is appropriate to light a fire, to dine; if they choose, both to sing and to dance. But when the vessel is sinking, you come to me and hoist the sails.
discourses_in-what-a-man-ought-to-be-exe.plainEnglish: You fool, stop wasting time on things that don't matter to you at all! These fancy debates are for people who can handle them without getting upset. They can say: "I don't get angry, sad, or jealous. Nothing blocks me or holds me back. What's left for me to do? I have free time and I'm calm. Let's see how to handle tricky arguments. Let's see how someone can accept an idea without being led to something ridiculous." That stuff is for them. Happy people can light a fire and eat dinner. If they want, they can sing and dance. But when the ship is going down, you come to me wanting to raise the sails.

discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.originalText: The material for the wise and good man is his own ruling faculty: and the body is the material for the physician and the aliptes (the man who oils persons); the land is the matter for the husbandman. The business of the wise and good man is to use appearances conformably to nature: and as it is the nature of every soul to assent to the truth, to dissent from the false, and to remain in suspense as to that which is uncertain; so it is its nature to be moved towards the desire for the good, and to aversion from the evil; and with respect to that which is neither good nor bad it feels indifferent.
discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.plainEnglish: The wise and good person works with their own mind. The doctor works with the body. The trainer works with athletes. The farmer works with land. The job of the wise and good person is to handle their impressions the right way. It's natural for every soul to agree with what's true, reject what's false, and stay undecided about what's uncertain. It's also natural to want good things and avoid bad things. And when something is neither good nor bad, you should feel neutral about it.

discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.originalText: For as the money-changer (banker) is not allowed to reject Cæsar's coin, nor the seller of herbs, but if you show the coin, whether he chooses or not, he must give up what is sold for the coin; so it is also in the matter of the soul. When the good appears, it immediately attracts to itself; the evil repels from itself. But the soul will never reject the manifest appearance of the good, any more than persons will reject Cæsar's coin. On this principle depends every movement both of man and God.
discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.plainEnglish: A money-changer can't refuse Caesar's coin. Neither can someone selling vegetables. If you show them the coin, they have to give you what you're buying — whether they want to or not. The same thing happens with your soul. When something truly good appears, it pulls you toward it automatically. When something bad appears, it pushes you away. Your soul can never reject what is clearly good, just like people can never reject Caesar's coin. This is how all movement works — for humans and for God.

discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.originalText: Against (or with respect to) this kind of thing chiefly a man should exercise himself. As soon as you go out in the morning, examine every man whom you see, every man whom you hear; answer as to a question, What have you seen? A handsome man or woman? Apply the rule. Is this independent of the will, or dependent? Independent. Take it away. What have you seen? A man lamenting over the death of a child. Apply the rule. Death is a thing independent of the will. Take it away. Has the proconsul met you? Apply the rule. What kind of a thing is a proconsul's office? Independent of the will or dependent on it? Independent. Take this away also; it does not stand examination; cast it away; it is nothing to you.
discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.plainEnglish: This is the main thing you should practice. Every morning when you go out, examine every person you see and hear. Ask yourself: What did you just see? A beautiful man or woman? Apply the rule. Is this something you control or not? You don't control it. Dismiss it. What did you see? Someone grieving a dead child? Apply the rule. Death is not something you control. Dismiss it. Did you meet a government official? Apply the rule. What is a government position? Do you control it or not? You don't control it. Dismiss this too. It doesn't pass the test. Throw it out. It's nothing to you.

discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.originalText: If we practised this and exercised ourselves in it daily from morning to night, something indeed would be done. But now we are forthwith caught half asleep by every appearance, and it is only, if ever, that in the school we are roused a little. Then when we go out, if we see a man lamenting, we say, He is undone. If we see a consul, we say, He is happy. If we see an exiled man, we say, He is miserable. If we see a poor man, we say, He is wretched; he has nothing to eat.
discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.plainEnglish: If we practiced this and worked on it every day from morning to night, we'd actually get somewhere. But instead, we get caught off guard by every little thing that happens — half asleep, not thinking clearly. Maybe we wake up a bit when we're in class. But then we go outside and see someone crying, and we say, 'That guy is ruined.' We see someone with a fancy government job and say, 'He's got it made.' We see someone in exile and say, 'Poor guy, he's miserable.' We see someone without money and say, 'How awful — he has nothing to eat.'

discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.originalText: We ought then to eradicate these bad opinions, and to this end we should direct all our efforts. For what is weeping and lamenting? Opinion. What is bad fortune? Opinion. What is civil sedition, what is divided opinion, what is blame, what is accusation, what is impiety, what is trifling? All these things are opinions, and nothing more, and opinions about things independent of the will, as if they were good and bad. Let a man transfer these opinions to things dependent on the will, and I engage for him that he will be firm and constant, whatever may be the state of things around him. Such as is a dish of water, such is the soul. Such as is the ray of light which falls on the water, such are the appearances. When the water is moved, the ray also seems to be moved, yet it is not moved. And when then a man is seized with giddiness, it is not the arts and the virtues which are confounded, but the spirit (the nervous power) on which they are impressed; but if the spirit be restored to its settled state, those things also are restored.
discourses_what-is-the-matter-on-which-a.plainEnglish: We need to get rid of these bad opinions. That's where we should focus all our effort. What is crying and complaining? Opinion. What is misfortune? Opinion. What is political chaos, what is disagreement, what is blame, what is accusation, what is godlessness, what is pettiness? All these things are opinions, nothing more. They're opinions about things outside your control, as if those things were good or bad. Let someone shift these opinions to things that are actually within their control. I promise you they'll stay steady and firm, no matter what's happening around them. Think of a bowl of water — that's like your soul. Think of a ray of light hitting the water — that's like your impressions. When the water moves, the light ray seems to move too, but it's not actually moving. When someone gets dizzy, their skills and virtues aren't really scrambled. It's just the mind they're written on that gets shaken. When the mind settles down, those things settle down too.

discourses_miscellaneous.originalText: It is not easy to exhort weak young men; for neither is it easy to hold (soft) cheese with a hook. But those who have a good natural disposition, even if you try to turn them aside, cling still more to reason.
discourses_miscellaneous.plainEnglish: It's hard to motivate weak young men. You can't grab soft cheese with a hook. But those with good character will stick to reason even more when you try to pull them away from it.

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: When the administrator came to visit him, and the man was an Epicurean, Epictetus said, It is proper for us who are not philosophers to inquire of you who are philosophers, as those who come to a strange city inquire of the citizens and those who are acquainted with it, what is the best thing in the world, in order that we also after inquiry may go in quest of that which is best and look at it, as strangers do with the things in cities. For that there are three things which relate to man—soul, body, and things external, scarcely any man denies. It remains for you philosophers to answer what is the best.
discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.plainEnglish: When an administrator came to visit him — this man was an Epicurean — Epictetus said: "Those of us who aren't philosophers should ask you philosophers the same way travelers ask locals when they visit a strange city. We want to know: what's the best thing in the world? Then we can go look for it and examine it, just like tourists examine the sights in cities. Almost everyone agrees that humans deal with three things: the soul, the body, and external things. So it's up to you philosophers to tell us which one is best."

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: What shall we say to men? Is the flesh the best? and was it for this that Maximus sailed as far as Cassiope in winter (or bad weather) with his son, and accompanied him that he might be gratified in the flesh? When the man said that it was not, and added, Far be that from him. Is it not fit then, Epictetus said, to be actively employed about the best? It is certainly of all things the most fit. What then do we possess which is better than the flesh? The soul, he replied. And the good things of the best, are they better, or the good things of the worse? The good things of the best.
