discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.plainEnglish: So what should we tell people? That the body is the most important thing? Is that why Maximus sailed all the way to Cassiope in winter storms with his son — so the boy could enjoy bodily pleasures? When the man said no, that wasn't the reason at all, Epictetus asked: "Then shouldn't we focus our energy on what's most important?" The man agreed that made perfect sense. "So what do we have that's better than the body?" "The soul," he replied. "And when it comes to the best thing we have, aren't its good qualities better than the good qualities of lesser things?" "Yes, the good qualities of the best thing are better."

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: And are the good things of the best within the power of the will or not within the power of the will? They are within the power of the will. Is then the pleasure of the soul a thing within the power of the will? It is, he replied. And on what shall this pleasure depend? On itself? But that cannot be conceived; for there must first exist a certain substance or nature ([Greek: ousia]) of good, by obtaining which we shall have pleasure in the soul. He assented to this also. On what then shall we depend for this pleasure of the soul?
discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.plainEnglish: Are the best good things under the will's control or not? They are under the will's control. So is the soul's pleasure something the will controls? Yes, he said. But what does this pleasure depend on? On itself? That's impossible. There must first be some actual substance or nature of good that exists. By getting that, we'll have pleasure in the soul. He agreed with this too. So what should we depend on for this pleasure of the soul?

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: for if it shall depend on things of the soul, the substance (nature) of the good is discovered; for good cannot be one thing, and that at which we are rationally delighted another thing; nor if that which precedes is not good, can that which comes after be good, for in order that the thing which comes after may be good, that which precedes must be good. But you would not affirm this, if you are in your right mind, for you would then say what is inconsistent both with Epicurus and the rest of your doctrines. It remains then that the pleasure of the soul is in the pleasure from things of the body; and again that those bodily things must be the things which precede and the substance (nature) of the good.
discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.plainEnglish: If good depends on things of the soul, then we've found what good really is. Because good can't be one thing while what we reasonably enjoy is something else. And if what comes first isn't good, then what follows can't be good either. For the thing that follows to be good, the thing that comes first must also be good. But you wouldn't say this if you're thinking clearly. You'd be contradicting both Epicurus and your own beliefs. So you're left saying that the soul's pleasure comes from bodily pleasure. And that means bodily things must come first and be the real nature of good.

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: Seek for doctrines which are consistent with what I say, and by making them your guide you will with pleasure abstain from things which have such persuasive power to lead us and overpower us. But if to the persuasive power of these things, we also devise such a philosophy as this which helps to push us on towards them and strengthens us to this end, what will be the consequence? In a piece of toreutic art which is the best part? the silver or the workmanship? The substance of the hand is the flesh; but the work of the hand is the principal part (that which precedes and leads the rest). The duties then are also three: those which are directed towards the existence of a thing; those which are directed towards its existence in a particular kind; and third, the chief or leading things themselves.
discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.plainEnglish: Look for teachings that match what I'm telling you. Use them as your guide. Then you'll gladly stay away from things that have such strong power to tempt and control us. But what if we create a philosophy that actually pushes us toward these tempting things and makes us weaker? What happens then? Think about a piece of fine metalwork — which part is better, the silver or the craftsmanship? Your hand is made of flesh, but the real value is in what your hand can do. So there are three kinds of duties: those about whether something exists, those about what kind of thing it is, and third, the most important duties of all.

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: So also in man we ought not to value the material, the poor flesh, but the principal (leading things, [Greek: ta proaegoumena]). What are these? Engaging in public business, marrying, begetting children, venerating God, taking care of parents, and generally, having desires, aversions ([Greek: echchlinein]), pursuits of things and avoidances, in the way in which we ought to do these things, and according to our nature. And how are we constituted by nature? Free, noble, modest; for what other animal blushes? what other is capable of receiving the appearance (the impression) of shame? and we are so constituted by nature as to subject pleasure to these things, as a minister, a servant, in order that it may call forth our activity, in order that it may keep us constant in acts which are conformable to nature.
discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.plainEnglish: In humans, we shouldn't value the material stuff — the weak flesh. We should value what's most important. What are those things? Taking part in public life, getting married, having children, honoring God, caring for your parents. And in general, having desires and aversions, pursuing some things and avoiding others — but doing all of this the right way, according to our nature. And how are we built by nature? We're free, noble, and modest. What other animal blushes? What other can feel shame? We're built so that pleasure serves these higher things like a servant. Pleasure should motivate us to act and keep us steady in doing what's natural for us.

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: HOW WE MUST EXERCISE OURSELVES AGAINST APPEARANCES ([Greek: phantasias]).—As we exercise ourselves against sophistical questions, so we ought to exercise ourselves daily against appearances; for these appearances also propose questions to us. A certain person's son is dead. Answer; the thing is not within the power of the will: it is not an evil. A father has disinherited a certain son. What do you think of it? It is a thing beyond the power of the will, not an evil. Cæsar has condemned a person. It is a thing beyond the power of the will, not an evil. The man is afflicted at this. Affliction is a thing which depends on the will: it is an evil. He has borne the condemnation bravely. That is a thing within the power of the will: it is a good.
discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.plainEnglish: HOW WE MUST TRAIN OURSELVES AGAINST FALSE IMPRESSIONS.—We practice answering tricky logical questions. We should practice the same way with our impressions every day. These impressions ask us questions too. Someone's son dies. Answer: this is not up to your will. It's not an evil. A father cuts his son out of his inheritance. What do you think? This is beyond your will's power. Not an evil. Caesar condemns someone. This is beyond your will's power. Not an evil. The person gets upset about this. Getting upset depends on your will. That's an evil. He handles the condemnation with courage. That depends on your will. That's a good.

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: If we train ourselves in this manner, we shall make progress; for we shall never assent to anything of which there is not an appearance capable of being comprehended. Your son is dead. What has happened? Your son is dead. Nothing more? Nothing. Your ship is lost. What has happened? Your ship is lost. A man has been led to prison. What has happened? He has been led to prison. But that herein he has fared badly, every man adds from his own opinion. But Zeus, you say, does not do right in these matters. Why? because he has made you capable of endurance? because he has made you magnanimous? because he has taken from that which befalls you the power of being evils? because it is in your power to be happy while you are suffering what you suffer? because he has opened the door to you, when things do not please you? Man, go out and do not complain!
discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.plainEnglish: If you train yourself this way, you'll make progress. You'll never accept anything unless you can clearly understand it. Your son is dead. What happened? Your son is dead. Nothing more? Nothing. Your ship is lost. What happened? Your ship is lost. A man was thrown in prison. What happened? He was thrown in prison. But people add their own spin: 'This is terrible!' That extra judgment comes from your own opinion. But you say Zeus isn't being fair here. Why not? He made you capable of enduring hardship. He made you strong-hearted. He took away the power of events to truly harm you. He made it possible for you to be happy even while you suffer. When things don't go your way, he opened the door for you to leave. So leave — and stop complaining!

discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.originalText: Hear how the Romans feel towards philosophers, if you would like to know. Italicus, who was the most in repute of the philosophers, once when I was present, being vexed with his own friends and as if he was suffering something intolerable, said: "I cannot bear it, you are killing me; you will make me such as that man is," pointing to me.
discourses_to-the-administrator-of-the-f.plainEnglish: Want to know how Romans feel about philosophers? Let me tell you a story. Italicus was the most respected philosopher in Rome. One day, when I was there, he got frustrated with his own friends. He acted like they were torturing him. He said: "I can't stand this anymore. You're killing me. You're going to turn me into someone like him" — and he pointed right at me.

discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.originalText: When a certain person came to him, who was going up to Rome on account of a suit which had regard to his rank, Epictetus inquired the reason of his going to Rome, and the man then asked what he thought about the matter. Epictetus replied: If you ask me what you will do in Rome, whether you will succeed or fail, I have no rule ([Greek: theoraema]) about this. But if you ask me how you will fare, I can tell you: if you have right opinions ([Greek: dogmata]), you will fare well; if they are false, you will fare ill. For to every man the cause of his acting is opinion.
discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.plainEnglish: A man came to see Epictetus. He was heading to Rome for a lawsuit about his social status. Epictetus asked why he was going. The man asked what Epictetus thought about his case. Epictetus said: "If you're asking me what will happen in Rome — whether you'll win or lose — I have no system for predicting that. But if you're asking me how you'll handle whatever happens, I can tell you: If your thinking is right, you'll be fine. If your thinking is wrong, you'll suffer. Because what a person believes is what drives their actions."

discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.originalText: For what is the reason why you desired to be elected governor of the Cnossians? Your opinion. What is the reason that you are now going up to Rome? Your opinion. And going in winter, and with danger and expense? I must go. What tells you this? Your opinion. Then if opinions are the causes of all actions, and a man has bad opinions, such as the cause may be, such also is the effect! Have we then all sound opinions, both you and your adversary? And how do you differ? But have you sounder opinions than your adversary? Why? You think so. And so does he think that his opinions are better; and so do madmen. This is a bad criterion.
discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.plainEnglish: Why did you want to be elected governor of the Cnossians? Because of your opinion. Why are you going to Rome now? Your opinion. Why are you traveling in winter, facing danger and expense? "I have to go." What tells you that? Your opinion again. So if opinions drive all our actions, and someone has bad opinions, then bad actions follow. Do we all have good opinions — you and your opponent? How are you different from him? Do you have better opinions than your opponent? Why? Because you think so. Well, he thinks his opinions are better too. So do crazy people. That's not a good way to judge.

discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.originalText: But show to me that you have made some inquiry into your opinions and have taken some pains about them. And as now you are sailing to Rome in order to become governor of the Cnossians, and you are not content to stay at home with the honors which you had, but you desire something greater and more conspicuous, so when did you ever make a voyage for the purpose of examining your own opinions, and casting them out, if you have any that are bad? Whom have you approached for this purpose? What time have you fixed for it? What age?
discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.plainEnglish: But show me that you've actually examined your beliefs and put some real effort into it. Look — you're sailing to Rome right now to become governor of Cnossus. You weren't satisfied staying home with the honors you already had. You wanted something bigger and more impressive. So when did you ever take a trip to examine your own opinions and throw out the bad ones? Who did you go to for help with this? What time did you set aside for it? At what age?

discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.originalText: Go over the times of your life by yourself, if you are ashamed of me (knowing the fact) when you were a boy, did you examine your own opinions? and did you not then, as you do all things now, do as you did do? and when you were become a youth and attended the rhetoricians, and yourself practised rhetoric, what did you imagine that you were deficient in? And when you were a young man and engaged in public matters, and pleaded causes yourself, and were gaining reputation, who then seemed your equal? And when would you have submitted to any man examining and showing that your opinions are bad?
discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.plainEnglish: Think back through your whole life. If you're embarrassed by me pointing this out — when you were a boy, did you ever examine your own beliefs? Didn't you just do whatever you felt like doing, the same way you do everything now? When you became a young man and studied with the rhetoric teachers and practiced speaking, what did you think you were missing? When you got older and entered public life, arguing cases in court and building your reputation, who did you think was your equal? And when would you have let anyone examine your beliefs and show you they were wrong?

discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.originalText: What then do you wish me to say to you? Help me in this matter. I have no theorem (rule) for this. Nor have you, if you came to me for this purpose, come to me as a philosopher, but as to a seller of vegetables or a shoemaker. For what purpose then have philosophers theorems? For this purpose, that whatever may happen, our ruling faculty may be and continue to be conformable to nature. Does this seem to you a small thing? No; but the greatest. What then? does it need only a short time? and is it possible to seize it as you pass by? If you can, seize it.
discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.plainEnglish: So what do you want me to tell you? 'Help me with this problem.' I don't have a rule for that. And if that's why you came to me, you didn't come to a philosopher. You came to a vegetable seller or a shoemaker. So why do philosophers have rules at all? For this: so that whatever happens, your mind stays calm and works the way it should. Think that's a small thing? No. It's the biggest thing there is. So what — does it only take a little time? Can you just grab it as you walk by? If you can, go ahead and grab it.

discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.originalText: Then you will say, I met with Epictetus as I should meet with a stone or a statue: for you saw me and nothing more. But he meets with a man as a man, who learns his opinions, and in his turn shows his own. Learn my opinions: show me yours; and then say that you have visited me. Let us examine one another: if I have any bad opinion, take it away; if you have any, show it. This is the meaning of meeting with a philosopher. Not so (you say): but this is only a passing visit, and while we are hiring the vessel, we can also see Epictetus. Let us see what he says. Then you go away and say: Epictetus was nothing; he used solecisms and spoke in a barbarous way. For of what else do you come as judges?
discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.plainEnglish: Then you'll say, "I met Epictetus the same way I'd meet a rock or a statue. I saw him and that's it." But a real person meets another person as a human being. They learn what the other thinks. They share their own thoughts in return. Learn what I believe. Show me what you believe. Then you can say you actually visited me. Let's challenge each other. If I have a wrong idea, help me get rid of it. If you have one, admit it. That's what it means to meet with a philosopher. But no — you think this is just a quick tourist stop. "While we're renting the boat, we might as well go see Epictetus. Let's hear what he has to say." Then you leave and complain: "Epictetus was nothing special. He made grammar mistakes and talked like a barbarian." What else did you come here to judge?

discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.originalText: Well, but a man may say to me, if I attend to such matters (as you do), I shall have no land as you have none; I shall have no silver cups as you have none, nor fine beasts as you have none. In answer to tins it is perhaps sufficient to say: I have no need of such things; but if you possess many things you have need of others: whether you choose or not, you are poorer than I am. What then have I need of? Of that which you have not? of firmness, of a mind which is conformable to nature, of being free from perturbation.
discourses_to-a-certain-rhetorician-who-.plainEnglish: Someone might say to me: "If I focus on the things you focus on, I won't have any land like you. I won't have silver cups like you. I won't have fine animals like you." Here's my answer: I don't need those things. But if you own a lot of stuff, you need even more stuff. Whether you want to admit it or not, you're poorer than I am. So what do I need? Things you don't have. I need strength of character. I need a mind that works with nature, not against it. I need freedom from worry and anxiety.

discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.originalText:
When the need of each opinion comes, we ought to have it in readiness: on the occasion of breakfast, such opinions as relate to breakfast; in the bath, those that concern the bath; in bed, those that concern bed.

Let sleep not come upon thy languid eyes
Before each daily action thou hast scann'd;
What's done amiss, what done, what left undone;
From first to last examine all, and then
Blame what is wrong, in what is right rejoice.

And we ought to retain these verses in such way that we may use them, not that we may utter them aloud, as when we exclaim, "Paean Apollo."
discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.plainEnglish:
When you need a particular way of thinking, you should have it ready. At breakfast, use thoughts that help with breakfast. In the bath, use thoughts about bathing. In bed, use thoughts about sleeping.

Don't let sleep close your tired eyes before you've looked at each thing you did that day. What did you do wrong? What did you do right? What did you leave undone? Go through everything from start to finish. Then feel bad about what was wrong and feel good about what was right.

You should memorize these lines so you can use them — not so you can recite them out loud like shouting "Praise Apollo!"

discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.originalText: Again in fever we should have ready such opinions as concern a fever; and we ought not, as soon as the fever begins, to lose and forget all. A man who has a fever may say: If I philosophize any longer, may I be hanged: wherever I go, I must take care of the poor body, that a fever may not come. But what is philosophizing? Is it not a preparation against events which may happen? Do you not understand that you are saying something of this kind? "If I shall still prepare myself to bear with patience what happens, may I be hanged." But this is just as if a man after receiving blows should give up the Pancratium. In the Pancratium it is in our power to desist and not to receive blows. But in the other matter if we give up philosophy, what shall we gain?
discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.plainEnglish: When you get a fever, you should have your philosophical principles ready to help you through it. Don't throw away everything you've learned the moment you start feeling sick. A sick person might say: "If I keep thinking about philosophy while I'm this sick, I'll go crazy. I need to focus on taking care of my body so I don't get sicker." But what is philosophy anyway? It's preparation for whatever might happen to you. Don't you see what you're really saying? "If I keep preparing myself to handle whatever comes with patience, I'll go crazy." That's like a fighter quitting the sport after getting punched a few times. In fighting, you can choose to quit and avoid getting hit. But in life, if you give up philosophy, what do you gain?

discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.originalText: What then should a man say on the occasion of each painful thing? It was for this that I exercised myself, for this I disciplined myself. God says to you: Give me a proof that you have duly practised athletics, that you have eaten what you ought, that you have been exercised, that you have obeyed the aliptes (the oiler and rubber). Then do you show yourself weak when the time for action comes? Now is the time for the fever. Let it be borne well. Now is the time for thirst, bear it well. Now is the time for hunger, bear it well. Is it not in your power? Who shall hinder you? The physician will hinder you from drinking; but he cannot prevent you from bearing thirst well: and he will hinder you from eating; but he cannot prevent you from bearing hunger well.
discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.plainEnglish: What should you say when something painful happens? "This is what I trained for. This is why I disciplined myself." God says to you: "Show me proof that you've practiced properly, that you've eaten right, that you've exercised, that you've followed your trainer." So will you be weak when it's time to perform? Now you have a fever. Bear it well. Now you're thirsty. Bear it well. Now you're hungry. Bear it well. Isn't this in your power? Who can stop you? The doctor will stop you from drinking, but he can't stop you from handling thirst well. He'll stop you from eating, but he can't stop you from handling hunger well.

discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.originalText: But I cannot attend to my philosophical studies. And for what purpose do you follow them? Slave, is it not that you may be happy, that you may be constant, is it not that you may be in a state conformable to nature and live so? What hinders you when you have a fever from having your ruling faculty conformable to nature? Here is the proof of the thing, here is the test of the philosopher. For this also is a part of life, like walking, like sailing, like journeying by land, so also is fever. Do you read when you are walking? No. Nor do you when you have a fever. But if you walk about well, you have all that belongs to a man who walks. If you bear a fever well, you have all that belongs to a man in a fever.
discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.plainEnglish: "But I can't focus on my philosophy studies." What are you studying philosophy for anyway? Fool, isn't it so you can be happy? So you can be steady? So you can live according to your nature? What stops you from keeping your mind right when you have a fever? This is your proof. This is your test as a philosopher. Fever is part of life, just like walking, sailing, or traveling. Do you read while you're walking? No. Do you read when you have a fever? No. But if you walk well, you're doing everything a walking person should do. If you handle a fever well, you're doing everything a sick person should do.

discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.originalText: What is it to bear a fever well? Not to blame God or man; not to be afflicted at that which happens, to expect death well and nobly, to do what must be done: when the physician comes in, not to be frightened at what he says; nor if he says you are doing well, to be overjoyed. For what good has he told you? and when you were in health, what good was that to you? And even if he says you are in a bad way, do not despond. For what is it to be ill? is it that you are near the severance of the soul and the body? what harm is there in this?
discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.plainEnglish: What does it mean to handle a fever well? Don't blame God or other people. Don't get upset about what's happening. Face death with courage and dignity. Do what needs to be done. When the doctor visits, don't panic at his words. And if he says you're doing well, don't get too excited. What good news has he really given you? When you were healthy, how much good did that do you? Even if he says you're in bad shape, don't lose hope. What does being sick actually mean? It means your soul and body might separate soon. What's the harm in that?

discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.originalText: If you are not near now, will you not afterwards be near? Is the world going to be turned upside down when you are dead? Why then do you flatter the physician? Why do you say if you please, master, I shall be well? Why do you give him an opportunity of raising his eyebrows (being proud; or showing his importance)? Do you not value a physician, as you do a shoemaker when he is measuring your foot, or a carpenter when he is building your house, and so treat the physician as to the body which is not yours, but by nature dead?
discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.plainEnglish: If you're not close to your goal now, will you be closer later? Is the world going to flip upside down when you die? So why do you flatter your doctor? Why do you say 'Please, doctor, make me well'? Why do you give him a chance to act important? Why don't you treat your doctor the way you treat a shoemaker measuring your foot or a carpenter building your house? Treat the doctor as someone working on your body — which isn't really yours anyway, but is naturally meant to die.

discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.originalText: He who has a fever has an opportunity of doing this: if he does these things, he has what belongs to him. For it is not the business of a philosopher to look after these externals, neither his wine nor his oil nor his poor body, but his own ruling power. But as to externals how must he act? so far as not to be careless about them. Where then is there reason for fear? where is there then still reason for anger, and of fear about what belongs to others, about things which are of no value? For we ought to have these two principles in readiness, that except the will nothing is good nor bad; and that we ought not to lead events, but to follow them. My brother ought not to have behaved thus to me. No, but he will see to that; and, however he may behave, I will conduct myself towards him as I ought. For this is my own business; that belongs to another: no man can prevent this, the other thing can be hindered.
discourses_in-what-manner-we-ought-to-be.plainEnglish: When someone has a fever, they have a chance to practice this: if they do what they should, they keep what's truly theirs. A philosopher's job isn't to worry about external things — not his wine, his oil, or even his body. His job is to manage his own mind. But how should he handle externals? Just don't be careless with them. So where's the reason for fear? Where's the reason for anger about things that belong to others, things that don't matter? Keep these two principles ready: nothing is good or bad except your will. And don't try to control events — follow them instead. "My brother shouldn't have treated me this way." Well, that's his problem. However he acts, I'll act toward him as I should. That's my business. What he does is his business. No one can stop me from doing my part. They can only stop his part.

discourses_about-exercise.originalText: We ought not to make our exercises consist in means contrary to nature and adapted to cause admiration, for if we do so, we who call ourselves philosophers, shall not differ at all from jugglers. For it is difficult even to walk on a rope; and not only difficult, but it is also dangerous. Ought we for this reason to practice walking on a rope, or setting up a palm-tree, or embracing statues? By no means. Every thing which is difficult and dangerous is not suitable for practice; but that is suitable which conduces to the working out of that which is proposed to us.
discourses_about-exercise.plainEnglish: Don't make your training about doing weird, unnatural things just to impress people. If we do that, we philosophers will be no different from circus performers. Sure, walking on a tightrope is hard. It's also dangerous. But should we practice tightrope walking for that reason? Should we practice climbing palm trees or hugging statues? Of course not. Not everything difficult and dangerous is worth practicing. Only practice what helps you work toward your actual goals.

discourses_about-exercise.originalText: And what is that which is proposed to us as a thing to be worked out? To live with desire and aversion (avoidance of certain things) free from restraint. And what is this? Neither to be disappointed in that which you desire, nor to fall into anything which you would avoid. Towards this object then exercise (practice) ought to tend.
discourses_about-exercise.plainEnglish: So what's the goal we're working toward? To live without being controlled by our desires and fears. What does that mean? Never being disappointed when you want something, and never ending up with what you're trying to avoid. That's what all your practice should aim for.

discourses_about-exercise.originalText: For since it is not possible to have your desire not disappointed and your aversion free from falling into that which you would avoid, without great and constant practice, you must know that if you allow your desire and aversion to turn to things which are not within the power of the will, you will neither have your desire capable of attaining your object, nor your aversion free from the power of avoiding that which you would avoid.
discourses_about-exercise.plainEnglish: You need lots of practice to get what you want and avoid what you don't want. But here's the thing: if you focus your desires and fears on things outside your control, you'll fail. You won't get what you want, and you won't avoid what you're trying to escape.

discourses_about-exercise.originalText: And since strong habit leads (prevails), and we are accustomed to employ desire and aversion only to things which are not within the power of our will, we ought to oppose to this habit a contrary habit, and where there is great slipperiness in the appearances, there to oppose the habit of exercise. Then at last, if occasion presents itself, for the purpose of trying yourself at a proper time you will descend into the arena to know if appearances overpower you as they did formerly. But at first fly far from that which is stronger than yourself; the contest is unequal between a charming young girl and a beginner in philosophy. The earthen pitcher, as the saying is, and the rock do not agree.
discourses_about-exercise.plainEnglish: We have strong habits. We're used to wanting and avoiding things that are outside our control. We need to build opposite habits to fight this. When appearances are really tempting, that's where we need to practice the most. Once you've trained enough, you can test yourself at the right time. Then you'll enter the arena to see if appearances still overpower you like they used to. But at first, stay far away from what's too strong for you. It's not a fair fight between a charming young woman and a philosophy beginner. As the saying goes, the clay pot and the rock don't get along.

discourses_what-solitude-is-and-what-kin.originalText: Solitude is a certain condition of a helpless man. For because a man is alone, he is not for that reason also solitary; just as though a man is among numbers, he is not therefore not solitary. When then we have lost either a brother, or a son, or a friend on whom we were accustomed to repose, we say that we are left solitary, though we are often in Rome, though such a crowd meet us, though so many live in the same place, and sometimes we have a great number of slaves. For the man who is solitary, as it is conceived, is considered to be a helpless person and exposed to those who wish to harm him. For this reason when we travel, then especially do we say that we are lonely when we fall among robbers, for it is not the sight of a human creature which removes us from solitude, but the sight of one who is faithful and modest and helpful to us.
discourses_what-solitude-is-and-what-kin.plainEnglish: Being alone and being isolated are two different things. You can be alone without being isolated. You can be surrounded by people and still feel isolated. When we lose a brother, son, or friend we relied on, we say we feel alone. This happens even in Rome with crowds around us, even when many people live nearby, even when we have many servants. The person who feels truly isolated is helpless and vulnerable to anyone who wants to hurt them. That's why when we travel, we especially feel lonely if we run into bandits. It's not seeing another human being that removes our isolation. It's seeing someone who is loyal, decent, and willing to help us.

discourses_what-solitude-is-and-what-kin.originalText: For if being alone is enough to make solitude, you may say that even Zeus is solitary in the conflagration and bewails himself saying, Unhappy that I am who have neither Hera, nor Athena, nor Apollo, nor brother, nor son, nor descendant, nor kinsman. This is what some say that he does when he is alone at the conflagration. For they do not understand how a man passes his life when he is alone, because they set out from a certain natural principle, from the natural desire of community and mutual love and from the pleasure of conversation among men. But none the less a man ought to be prepared in a manner for this also (being alone), to be able to be sufficient for himself and to be his own companion.
discourses_what-solitude-is-and-what-kin.plainEnglish: If being physically alone makes you truly lonely, then even Zeus would be miserable when he destroys and recreates the world. He'd cry and say, 'Poor me! I have no Hera, no Athena, no Apollo, no brother, no son, no family, no friends.' Some people claim this is what Zeus does when he's alone during the world's destruction. But they don't understand how someone can live well when alone. They start from the natural human need for community, love, and conversation. Still, you should be ready for solitude too. You should be able to rely on yourself and be your own good company.

discourses_what-solitude-is-and-what-kin.originalText: For as Zeus dwells with himself, and is tranquil by himself, and thinks of his own administration and of its nature, and is employed in thoughts suitable to himself; so ought we also to be able to talk with ourselves, not to feel the want of others also, not to be unprovided with the means of passing our time; to observe the divine administration, and the relation of ourselves to everything else; to consider how we formerly were affected towards things that happened and how at present; what are still the things which give us pain; how these also can be cured and how removed; if any things require improvement, to improve them according to reason.
discourses_what-solitude-is-and-what-kin.plainEnglish: Zeus lives at peace with himself. He stays calm on his own. He thinks about how he runs things and what that means. His thoughts match who he is. We should be the same way. We should be able to talk to ourselves without needing other people around all the time. We shouldn't depend on others to keep us busy. Instead, we should watch how the universe works. We should think about how we fit into everything else. We should look at how we used to react to things that happened, and how we react now. What still causes us pain? How can we heal those things? How can we get rid of them? If anything about us needs to get better, we should improve it using reason.

discourses_what-solitude-is-and-what-kin.originalText: Well then, if some man should come upon me when I am alone and murder me? Fool, not murder You, but your poor body. What kind of solitude then remains? what want? why do we make ourselves worse than children; and what do children do when they are left alone? They take up shells and ashes, and they build something, then pull it down, and build something else, and so they never want the means of passing the time. Shall I then, if you sail away, sit down and weep, because I have been left alone and solitary? Shall I then have no shells, no ashes? But children do what they do through want of thought (or deficiency in knowledge), and we through knowledge are unhappy.
discourses_what-solitude-is-and-what-kin.plainEnglish: What if someone finds me alone and murders me? Fool — they can't murder you, only your poor body. So what kind of loneliness is left? What lack? Why do we make ourselves worse than children? What do children do when left alone? They pick up shells and dirt. They build something, knock it down, then build something else. They never run out of ways to pass the time. So if you sail away, should I sit down and cry because I've been left alone? Do I have no shells, no dirt? Children do what they do because they don't think much. We have knowledge, and it makes us miserable.

discourses_what-solitude-is-and-what-kin.originalText: Every great power (faculty) is dangerous to beginners. You must then bear such things as you are able, but conformably to nature: but not ... Practise sometimes a way of living like a person out of health that you may at some time live like a man in health.
discourses_what-solitude-is-and-what-kin.plainEnglish: Every great power is dangerous to beginners. You must handle only what you can manage, and do it in a way that fits your nature. Practice sometimes living like a sick person so that you can eventually live like a healthy person.

meaningCheck.verification_notes: The original text appears incomplete with 'but not ...' - translated the clear portions faithfully

discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.originalText: As bad tragic actors cannot sing alone, but in company with many, so some persons cannot walk about alone. Man, if you are anything, both walk alone and talk to yourself, and do not hide yourself in the chorus. Examine a little at last, look around, stir yourself up, that you may know who you are.
discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.plainEnglish: Bad actors in tragedies can't sing solo — they need a whole chorus to hide behind. Some people are the same way. They can't walk around alone. But if you're worth anything, you should be able to walk by yourself and talk to yourself. Don't hide in the crowd. Take some time to examine yourself. Look around. Wake yourself up. Figure out who you really are.

discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.originalText: You must root out of men these two things, arrogance (pride) and distrust. Arrogance then is the opinion that you want nothing (are deficient in nothing); but distrust is the opinion that you cannot be happy when so many circumstances surround you. Arrogance is removed by confutation; and Socrates was the first who practised this. And (to know) that the thing is not impossible inquire and seek. This search will do you no harm; and in a manner this is philosophizing, to seek how it is possible to employ desire and aversion ([Greek: echchlisis]) without impediment.
discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.plainEnglish: You must pull out two things from people: arrogance and distrust. Arrogance is thinking you don't need anything. Distrust is thinking you can't be happy because of all the difficult things around you. You get rid of arrogance by proving it wrong. Socrates was the first to do this well. To know that happiness isn't impossible, ask questions and search for answers. This searching won't hurt you. In fact, this is what philosophy is — figuring out how to want things and avoid things without getting blocked.

discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.originalText: I am superior to you, for my father is a man of consular rank. Another says, I have been a tribune, but you have not. If we were horses, would you say, My father was swifter? I have much barley and fodder, or elegant neck ornaments. If then you were saying this, I said, Be it so: let us run then. Well, is there nothing in a man such as running in a horse, by which it will be known which is superior and inferior? Is there not modesty ([Greek: aidos]), fidelity, justice? Show yourself superior in these, that you may be superior as a man. If you tell me that you can kick violently, I also will say to you, that you are proud of that which is the act of an ass.
discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.plainEnglish: "I'm better than you because my father was a consul." Another person says, "I was a tribune, but you weren't." If we were horses, would you say, "My father was faster? I have lots of barley and feed, or fancy decorations around my neck?" If you said that, I'd respond, "Fine, let's race then." Well, isn't there something in a human being like speed in a horse that shows who is superior and who is inferior? Isn't there respect, loyalty, and justice? Show yourself superior in these things if you want to be superior as a human being. If you tell me you can kick hard, I'll tell you that you're bragging about something that makes you like a donkey.

discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.originalText: THAT WE OUGHT TO PROCEED WITH CIRCUMSPECTION TO EVERYTHING.—In every act consider what precedes and what follows, and then proceed to the act. If you do not consider, you will at first begin with spirit, since you have not thought at all of the things which follow; but afterwards when some consequences have shown themselves, you will basely desist (from that which you have begun).—I wish to conquer at the Olympic games.—(And I too, by the gods; for it is a fine thing.) But consider here what precedes and what follows; and then, if it is for your good, undertake the thing. You must act according to rules, follow strict diet, abstain from delicacies, exercise yourself by compulsion at fixed times, in heat, in cold; drink no cold water, nor wine, when there is opportunity of drinking it. In a word, you must surrender yourself to the trainer, as you do to a physician. Next in the contest, you must be covered with sand, sometimes dislocate a hand, sprain an ankle, swallow a quantity of dust, be scourged with the whip; and after undergoing all this, you must sometimes be conquered.
discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.plainEnglish:
Think carefully before you do anything. In every action, consider what comes before and what comes after. Then act. If you don't think it through, you'll start with enthusiasm because you haven't thought about the consequences. But when those consequences show up, you'll quit in shame.

"I want to win at the Olympic games." (And I do too, by the gods — it's a great thing.) But think about what comes before and after. Then, if it's good for you, go for it. You must follow strict rules. You must diet strictly. No fancy foods. You must train at set times whether you want to or not — in heat, in cold. No cold water or wine when you want them. You must give yourself completely to your trainer, like you would to a doctor. In competition, you'll get covered in sand. You might dislocate your hand or sprain your ankle. You'll swallow dust. You'll get whipped. After all that, you might still lose.

discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.originalText: After reckoning all these things, if you have still an inclination, go to the athletic practice. If you do not reckon them, observe you will behave like children who at one time play as wrestlers, then as gladiators, then blow a trumpet, then act a tragedy, when they have seen and admired such things. So you also do: you are at one time a wrestler (athlete), then a gladiator, then a philosopher, then a rhetorician; but with your whole soul you are nothing: like the ape you imitate all that you see; and always one thing after another pleases you, but that which becomes familiar displeases you. For you have never undertaken anything after consideration, nor after having explored the whole matter and put it to a strict examination; but you have undertaken it at hazard and with a cold desire. Thus some persons having seen a philosopher and having heard one speak like Euphrates—and yet who can speak like him?—wish to be philosophers themselves.
discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.plainEnglish: After you've thought through all this, if you still want to go into athletic training, go ahead. But if you don't think it through first, watch what happens. You'll act like children who play wrestler one day, then gladiator the next, then pretend to blow trumpets, then act out plays — just copying whatever they've seen and thought was cool. That's exactly what you do. One day you're an athlete, then a fighter, then a philosopher, then a speaker. But deep down, you're nothing. Like a monkey, you just copy whatever you see. Something new always catches your eye, but once it becomes familiar, you get bored with it. You never commit to anything after real thought. You never explore it fully or examine it carefully. You just jump in randomly with lukewarm interest. Some people hear a philosopher speak — someone like Euphrates, though who could speak like him? — and suddenly they want to be philosophers too.

discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.originalText: Man, consider first what the matter is (which you propose to do), then your own nature also, what it is able to bear. If you are a wrestler, look at your shoulders, your thighs, your loins: for different men are naturally formed for different things. Do you think that, if you do (what you are doing daily), you can be a philosopher? Do you think that you can eat as you do now, drink as you do now, and in the same way be angry and out of humor? You must watch, labor, conquer certain desires, you must depart from your kinsmen, be despised by your slaves, laughed at by those who meet you, in everything you must be in an inferior condition, as to magisterial office, in honors, in courts of justice.
discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.plainEnglish: Listen, first figure out what you're trying to do. Then look at yourself honestly — what can you actually handle? If you want to be a wrestler, check your shoulders, your thighs, your back. Different people are built for different things. Do you think you can keep living exactly like you do now and also be a philosopher? Do you think you can eat the same way, drink the same way, get angry the same way, and still make progress? You'll have to stay alert, work hard, and beat certain desires. You'll have to leave your family behind. Your servants will look down on you. People you meet will laugh at you. In every way, you'll be worse off when it comes to government jobs, honors, and court cases.

discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.originalText: When you have considered all these things completely, then, if you think proper, approach to philosophy, if you would gain in exchange for these things freedom from perturbations, liberty, tranquillity. If you have not considered these things, do not approach philosophy: do not act like children, at one time a philosopher, then a tax collector, then a rhetorician, then a procurator (officer) of Cæsar. These things are not consistent. You must be one man either good or bad; you must either labor at your own ruling faculty or at external things; you must either labor at things within or at external things; that is, you must either occupy the place of a philosopher or that of one of the vulgar.
discourses_certain-miscellaneous-matters.plainEnglish: Think through all of this completely first. Then, if you decide it's right for you, approach philosophy. You'll gain freedom from worry, liberty, and peace of mind in return. But if you haven't thought it through, don't approach philosophy at all. Don't act like children who play pretend — philosopher one day, tax collector the next, then public speaker, then Caesar's officer. These roles don't fit together. You must be one person, either good or bad. You must either work on your own mind or on external things. You must either work on what's within your control or on external things. In other words, you must either take the place of a philosopher or take the place of an ordinary person.

discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.originalText: If a man has frequent intercourse with others either for talk, or drinking together, or generally for social purposes, he must either become like them, or change them to his own fashion. For if a man places a piece of quenched charcoal close to a piece that is burning, either the quenched charcoal will quench the other, or the burning charcoal will light that which is quenched. Since then the danger is so great, we must cautiously enter into such intimacies with those of the common sort, and remember that it is impossible that a man can keep company with one who is covered with soot without being partaker of the soot himself.
discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.plainEnglish: If you spend a lot of time with people — talking, drinking, or just hanging out — one of two things will happen. Either you'll become like them, or you'll change them to be like you. Think of it like putting a cold piece of charcoal next to a burning one. Either the cold charcoal will put out the hot one, or the hot charcoal will light the cold one. Since the risk is so high, be careful about getting close to ordinary people. Remember: you can't hang around someone covered in soot without getting soot on yourself.

discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.originalText: For what will you do if a man speaks about gladiators, about horses, about athletes, or what is worse about men? Such a person is bad, such a person is good; this was well done, this was done badly. Further, if he scoff, or ridicule, or show an ill-natured disposition? Is any man among us prepared like a lute-player when he takes a lute, so that as soon as he has touched the strings, he discovers which are discordant, and tunes the instrument? Such a power as Socrates had who in all his social intercourse could lead his companions to his own purpose? How should you have this power? It is therefore a necessary consequence that you are carried about by the common kind of people.
discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.plainEnglish: What will you do when someone talks about gladiators, horses, athletes, or worse — gossips about people? 'This person is bad, that person is good. This was done well, that was done badly.' What if they mock you, ridicule you, or act mean-spirited? Are any of us prepared like a musician who picks up a lute? As soon as he touches the strings, he knows which ones are out of tune and fixes them. Do you have the kind of power Socrates had? He could steer any conversation toward what mattered. How could you possibly have that skill? So of course you get swept along by whatever ordinary people are talking about.

discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.originalText: Why then are they more powerful than you? Because they utter these useless words from their real opinions; but you utter your elegant words only from your lips; for this reason they are without strength and dead, and it is nauseous to listen to your exhortations and your miserable virtue, which is talked of everywhere (up and down). In this way the vulgar have the advantage over you; for every opinion ([Greek: dogma]) is strong and invincible. Until then the good ([Greek: chompsai]) sentiments ([Greek: hupolaepseis]) are fixed in you, and you shall have acquired a certain power for your security, I advise you to be careful in your association with common persons; if you are not, every day like wax in the sun there will be melted away whatever you inscribe on your minds in the school.
discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.plainEnglish: Why are they more powerful than you? Because they speak their useless words from real conviction. But you only speak your fancy words with your lips — that's why your words have no strength and are dead. It's sickening to listen to your preaching and your pathetic virtue that gets talked about everywhere. This is how ordinary people have the upper hand over you. Every real belief is strong and unshakeable. Until good thoughts are truly fixed in you, and you've built real strength to protect yourself, I advise you to be careful around common people. If you're not careful, whatever you write on your mind in school will melt away every day like wax in the sun.

discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.originalText: Withdraw then yourselves far from the sun so long as you have these waxen sentiments. For this reason also philosophers advise men to leave their native country, because ancient habits distract them and do not allow a beginning to be made of a different habit; nor can we tolerate those who meet us and say: See such a one is now a philosopher, who was once so and so. Thus also physicians send those who have lingering diseases to a different country and a different air; and they do right. Do you also introduce other habits than those which you have; fix you opinions and exercise yourselves in them.
discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.plainEnglish: Stay away from temptation while your resolve is still weak, like wax that melts in the sun. This is why philosophers tell people to leave their home country. Old habits distract you and prevent you from building new ones. You also can't stand people who see you and say, 'Look, there's so-and-so trying to be a philosopher now.' Doctors do the same thing — they send patients with chronic illnesses to different places with different air. And they're right to do it. You should do this too. Build new habits to replace your old ones. Set your beliefs and practice them.

discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.originalText: But you do not so; you go hence to a spectacle, to a show of gladiators, to a place of exercise ([Greek: chuston]), to a circus; then you come back hither, and again from this place you go to those places, and still the same persons. And there is no pleasing (good) habit, nor attention, nor care about self and observation of this kind. How shall I use the appearances presented to me? according to nature, or contrary to nature? how do I answer to them? as I ought, or as I ought not? Do I say to those things which are independent of the will, that they do not concern me? For if you are not yet in this state, fly from your former habits, fly from the common sort, if you intend ever to begin to be something.
discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.plainEnglish: But you don't do this. Instead, you go off to watch a show or gladiators or athletes or the circus. Then you come back here. Then you go back to those places again. Always the same people doing the same things. You never develop good habits. You never pay attention or take care of yourself or watch what you're doing. You never ask: How should I handle what happens to me? Should I respond naturally or unnaturally? Am I reacting the right way or the wrong way? Do I tell myself that things outside my control don't concern me? If you're not doing this yet, run from your old habits. Get away from ordinary people if you ever want to become something worthwhile.

discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.originalText: ON PROVIDENCE.-When you make any charge against Providence, consider, and you will learn that the thing has happened according to reason. Yes, but the unjust man has the advantage. In what? In money. Yes, for he is superior to you in this, that he flatters, is free from shame, and is watchful. What is the wonder? But see if he has the advantage over you in being faithful, in being modest; for you will not find it to be so; but wherein you are superior, there you will find that you have the advantage. And I once said to a man who was vexed because Philostorgus was fortunate: Would you choose to lie with Sura?
discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.plainEnglish: When you complain that life is unfair, stop and think. You'll see that things happen for good reasons. 'But the dishonest person gets ahead!' In what way? In money? Sure, because they're better than you at flattering people, having no shame, and staying alert to opportunities. So what? But check if they beat you at being trustworthy or decent. You won't find that they do. Where you're actually superior, that's where you have the real advantage. I once asked a man who was bitter about Philostorgus's success: Would you want to sleep with Sura?

discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.originalText: May it never happen, he replied, that this day should come? Why then are you vexed, if he receives something in return for that which he sells; or how can you consider him happy who acquires those things by such means as you abominate; or what wrong does Providence, if he gives the better things to the better men? Is it not better to be modest than to be rich? He admitted this. Why are you vexed then, man, when you possess the better thing? Remember then always and have in readiness the truth, that this is a law of nature, that the superior has an advantage over the inferior in that in which he is superior; and you will never be vexed.
discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.plainEnglish: "May that day never come," he said. Then why are you upset if he gets something back for what he's selling? How can you think someone is happy when they get things through methods you hate? What's wrong with Providence giving better things to better people? Isn't it better to be modest than to be rich? He agreed it was. Then why are you upset when you have the better thing? Always remember this truth and keep it ready: it's a law of nature that whoever is superior has an advantage in the area where they're superior. Remember this and you'll never be upset.

discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.originalText: But my wife treats me badly. Well, if any man asks you what this is, say, my wife treats me badly. Is there then nothing more? Nothing. My father gives me nothing. (What is this? my father gives me nothing. Is there nothing else then? Nothing); but to say that this is an evil is something which must be added to it externally, and falsely added. For this reason we must not get rid of poverty, but of the opinion about poverty, and then we shall be happy.
discourses_that-we-ought-with-caution-to.plainEnglish: But my wife treats me badly. Well, if someone asks you what this is, say: my wife treats me badly. Is there anything more to it? No. My father gives me nothing. What is this? My father gives me nothing. Is there anything else? No. But calling this an evil — that's something you add on top of it. And you add it wrongly. This is why we shouldn't try to get rid of poverty. We should get rid of our opinions about poverty. Then we'll be happy.

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText:
When one of his pupils inquired of Epictetus, and he was a person who appeared to be inclined to Cynicism, what kind of person a Cynic ought to be, and what was the notion ([Greek: prolaepsis]) of the thing, we will inquire, said Epictetus, at leisure; but I have so much to say to you that he who without God attempts so great a matter, is hateful to God, and has no other purpose than to act indecently in public.

In the first place, in the things which relate to yourself, you must not be in any respect like what you do now; you must not blame God or man; you must take away desire altogether, you must transfer avoidance ([Greek: echchlisis]) only to the things which are within the power of the will; you must not feel anger nor resentment or envy nor pity; a girl must not appear handsome to you, nor must you love a little reputation, nor be pleased with a boy or a cake.
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish:
A student asked Epictetus about becoming a Cynic philosopher. The student seemed drawn to that way of life. He wanted to know what kind of person a Cynic should be and what the whole idea meant. Epictetus said, "We'll talk about this more later. But I'll tell you this much: anyone who tries to take on such a huge responsibility without God's help is disgusting to God. They're just planning to make a fool of themselves in public.

First, you'd have to completely change how you handle your own life. You can't blame God or other people for anything. You must get rid of wanting things entirely. You can only avoid things that are actually under your control. You can't feel angry, resentful, jealous, or sorry for people. You can't think a girl is beautiful. You can't care about having a good reputation. You can't get excited about a attractive boy or even a piece of cake."

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText: For you ought to know that the rest of men throw walls around them and houses and darkness when they do any such things, and they have many means of concealment. A man shuts the door, he sets somebody before the chamber; if a person comes, say that he is out, he is not at leisure. But the Cynic instead of all these things must use modesty as his protection; if he does not, he will be indecent in his nakedness and under the open sky. This is his house, his door; this is the slave before his bedchamber; this is his darkness.
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish: You need to understand something. Most people hide behind walls, houses, and darkness when they do shameful things. They have many ways to conceal themselves. A man shuts his door. He posts someone outside his room. If someone comes by, he says "Tell them I'm out" or "Tell them I'm busy." But a Cynic has none of these hiding places. Instead of walls and doors, he must use self-respect as his only protection. If he doesn't, he'll act shamefully right out in the open for everyone to see. Self-respect is his house, his door, his guard, his privacy.

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText: For he ought not to wish to hide anything that he does; and if he does, he is gone, he has lost the character of a Cynic, of a man who lives under the open sky, of a free man; he has begun to fear some external thing, he has begun to have need of concealment, nor can he get concealment when he chooses. For where shall he hide himself and how? And if by chance this public instructor shall be detected, this pædagogue, what kind of things will he be compelled to suffer? when then a man fears these things, is it possible for him to be bold with his whole soul to superintend men? It cannot be: it is impossible.
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish: A Cynic shouldn't want to hide anything he does. If he does hide things, he's finished. He's lost what makes him a Cynic — someone who lives openly, a free person. He's started to fear something outside himself. He's started to need secrecy. But he can't get secrecy whenever he wants it. Where would he hide? How would he do it? And if this public teacher gets caught — this guide for others — what terrible things will happen to him? When someone fears these things, can he boldly lead other people with his whole heart? He can't. It's impossible.

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText: In the first place then you must make your ruling faculty pure, and this mode of life also. Now (you should say), to me the matter to work on is my understanding, as wood is to the carpenter, as hides to the shoemaker; and my business is the right use of appearances. But the body is nothing to me: the parts of it are nothing to me. Death? Let it come when it chooses, either death of the whole or of a part. Fly, you say. And whither; can any man eject me out of the world? He cannot. But wherever I go, there is the sun, there is the moon, there are the stars, dreams, omens, and the conversation ([Greek: omilia]) with gods.
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish: First, you must clean up your mind and your way of living. You should say: "My job is to work on my thinking, like wood is the carpenter's material or leather is the shoemaker's. My business is using my perceptions correctly. My body means nothing to me. Its parts mean nothing to me. Death? Let it come whenever it wants — death of my whole body or just a part of it. Run away, you say? Where to? Can anyone throw me out of the world? They can't. But wherever I go, there's the sun, the moon, the stars, dreams, signs, and conversation with the gods."

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText: Then, if he is thus prepared, the true Cynic cannot be satisfied with this; but he must know that he is sent a messenger from Zeus to men about good and bad things, to show them that they have wandered and are seeking the substance of good and evil where it is not, but where it is, they never think; and that he is a spy, as Diogenes was carried off to Philip after the battle of Chaeroneia as a spy. For in fact a Cynic is a spy of the things which are good for men and which are evil, and it is his duty to examine carefully and to come and report truly, and not to be struck with terror so as to point out as enemies those who are not enemies, nor in any other way to be perturbed by appearances nor confounded.
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish: If he's prepared like this, the true Cynic can't stop there. He must know that Zeus sent him as a messenger to people about good and bad things. His job is to show them that they've lost their way. They're looking for what's truly good and evil in the wrong places. Where it actually is, they never think to look. He's like a spy — just as Diogenes was captured by Philip after the battle of Chaeroneia and treated as a spy. A Cynic really is a spy. He scouts out what's truly good for people and what's truly harmful. His duty is to investigate carefully, then come back and report the truth. He can't let fear make him point to fake enemies. He can't let appearances disturb him or confuse him in any way.

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText: It is his duty then to be able with a loud voice, if the occasion should arise, and appearing on the tragic stage to say like Socrates: Men, whither are you hurrying, what are you doing, wretches? like blind people you are wandering up and down; you are going by another road, and have left the true road; you seek for prosperity and happiness where they are not, and if another shows you where they are, you do not believe him. Why do you seek it without? In the body? It is not there. If you doubt, look at Myro, look at Ophellius. In possessions? It is not there. But if you do not believe me, look at Croesus: look at those who are now rich, with what lamentations their life is filled. In power? It is not there. If it is, those must be happy who have been twice and thrice consuls; but they are not.
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish: So it's his job to be ready to speak up loudly when needed. He should be willing to stand on stage like Socrates and say: "People, where are you rushing to? What are you doing, you poor souls? You're wandering around like blind people. You've taken the wrong path and left the right one behind. You're looking for success and happiness in the wrong places. And when someone shows you where to really find them, you don't believe them. Why do you look for happiness outside yourself? In your body? It's not there. Don't believe me? Look at Myro, look at Ophellius. In your stuff? It's not there either. Still doubt me? Look at Croesus. Look at today's rich people — listen to how much they complain about their lives. In power? Nope, not there either. If it were, then people who've been consul two or three times would be happy. But they're not."

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText:
Whom shall we believe in these matters? You who from without see their affairs and are dazzled by an appearance, or the men themselves? What do they say? Hear them when they groan, when they grieve, when on account of these very consulships and glory and splendor they think that they are more wretched and in greater danger. Is it in royal power? It is not: if it were, Nero would have been happy, and Sardanapalus. But neither was Agamemnon happy, though he was a better man than Sardanapalus and Nero; but while others are snoring, what is he doing?

Much from his head he tore his rooted hair:
Iliad, x., 15.

and what does he say himself?

"I am perplexed," he says, "and
Disturb'd I am," and "my heart out of my bosom
Is leaping."
Iliad, x., 91.
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish:
Who should we believe about these things? You, watching from the outside and impressed by appearances? Or the people living it? What do they actually say? Listen to them groan and complain. They think their high offices, fame, and glory make them more miserable and put them in more danger.

Is happiness found in royal power? No. If it were, Nero would have been happy. So would Sardanapalus. But neither was Agamemnon happy, even though he was better than both of them. While everyone else sleeps soundly, what's he doing?

He's tearing his hair out. And what does he say? "I'm confused and disturbed. My heart is jumping out of my chest."

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText: Wretch, which of your affairs goes badly? Your possessions? No. Your body? No. But you are rich in gold and copper. What then is the matter with you? That part of you, whatever it is, has been neglected by you and is corrupted, the part with which we desire, with which we avoid, with which we move towards and move from things. How neglected? He knows not the nature of good for which he is made by nature and the nature of evil; and what is his own, and what belongs to another; and when anything that belongs to others goes badly, he says, Woe to me, for the Hellenes are in danger. Wretched is his ruling faculty, and alone neglected and uncared for.
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish: You fool, what part of your life is actually going wrong? Your stuff? No. Your body? No. You're loaded with gold and copper. So what's your problem? It's that part of you — whatever it is — that you've ignored and let rot. The part that wants things, avoids things, moves toward some things and away from others. How have you ignored it? You don't understand what's naturally good for you and what's naturally bad. You don't know what's yours and what belongs to other people. And when something bad happens to other people's business, you cry, "Poor me, the Greeks are in trouble!" Your mind is a wreck. It's the only thing you've abandoned and refuse to take care of.

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText: The Hellenes are going to die destroyed by the Trojans. And if the Trojans do not kill them, will they not die? Yes; but not all at once. What difference then does it make? For if death is an evil, whether men die altogether, or if they die singly, it is equally an evil. Is anything else then going to happen than the separation of the soul and the body? Nothing. And if the Hellenes perish, is the door closed, and is it not in your power to die? It is. Why then do you lament (and say), Oh, you are a king and have the sceptre of Zeus? An unhappy king does not exist more than an unhappy god. What then art thou?
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish: The Greeks are going to die, destroyed by the Trojans. And if the Trojans don't kill them, won't they still die? Yes — but not all at once. So what's the difference? If death is evil, then whether people die together or one by one, it's still equally evil. What else is going to happen besides the soul separating from the body? Nothing. And if the Greeks die out, is the door to death closed to you? Can't you still die? You can. So why do you cry and say, 'Oh, you are a king with Zeus's scepter'? There's no such thing as an unhappy king any more than there's an unhappy god. So what are you?

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText: In truth a shepherd: for you weep as shepherds do, when a wolf has carried off one of their sheep: and these who are governed by you are sheep. And why did you come hither? Was your desire in any danger? was your aversion ([Greek: echchlisis])? was your movement (pursuits)? was your avoidance of things? He replies, No; but the wife of my brother was carried off. Was it not then a great gain to be deprived of an adulterous wife? Shall we be despised then by the Trojans? What kind of people are the Trojans, wise or foolish? If they are wise, why do you fight with them? If they are fools, why do you care about them?
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish: You're acting like a shepherd who cries when a wolf takes one of his sheep. The people you rule are just sheep to you. So why did you come here? Was your desire threatened? Your ability to avoid what you don't want? Your goals? Your choices? He says no. But my brother's wife was taken! Wasn't it actually good to lose an unfaithful wife? But the Trojans will look down on us! What kind of people are these Trojans — wise or foolish? If they're wise, why are you fighting them? If they're fools, why do you care what they think?

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText: Do you possess the body then free or is it in servile condition? We do not know. Do you not know that it is the slave of fever, of gout, ophthalmia, dysentery, of a tyrant, of fire, of iron, of everything which is stronger? Yes, it is a slave. How then is it possible that anything which belongs to the body can be free from hindrance? and how is a thing great or valuable which is naturally dead, or earth, or mud? Well then, do you possess nothing which is free? Perhaps nothing. And who is able to compel you to assent to that which appears false? No man.
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish: Do you own your body freely, or is it enslaved? We don't know. Actually, don't you know that it's a slave to fever, gout, eye infections, stomach problems, tyrants, fire, weapons — anything stronger than it? Yes, it's enslaved. So how can anything that belongs to the body be free from interference? And how can something be great or valuable when it's naturally dead matter — just earth or mud? So do you own nothing that is free? Maybe nothing. But who can force you to agree with something that seems false to you? No one.

discourses_about-cynicism.originalText: And who can compel you not to assent to that which appears true? No man. By this then you see that there is something in you naturally free. But to desire or to be averse from, or to move towards an object or to move from it, or to prepare yourself, or to propose to do anything, which of you can do this, unless he has received an impression of the appearance of that which is profitable or a duty? No man. You have then in these things also something which is not hindered and is free. Wretched men, work out this, take care of this, seek for good here.
discourses_about-cynicism.plainEnglish: Who can force you to agree with something that seems true to you? No one. This shows you have something naturally free inside you. But what about wanting something or avoiding it? What about moving toward something or away from it? What about getting ready to act or planning to do something? Can any of you do these things without first getting an impression that something is good for you or the right thing to do? No. So you also have something free and unhindered in these areas too. You miserable people — work on this! Take care of this! Look for what's good right here.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Let not that which in another is contrary to nature be an evil to you; for you are not formed by nature to be depressed with others nor to be unhappy with others, but to be happy with them. If a man is unhappy, remember that his unhappiness is his own fault; for God has made all men to be happy, to be free from perturbations. For this purpose he has given means to them, some things to each person as his own, and other things not as his own; some things subject to hindrance and compulsion and deprivation; and these things are not a man's own; but the things which are not subject to hindrances, are his own; and the nature of good and evil, as it was fit to be done by him who takes care of us and protects us like a father, he has made our own.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Don't let someone else's unnatural behavior become your problem. You weren't built to be miserable alongside others or to suffer when they suffer. You were built to be happy with them. If someone is unhappy, remember that their unhappiness is their own fault. God made all people to be happy and free from inner turmoil. He gave us the tools for this. Some things belong to each person. Other things don't. Some things can be blocked, forced, or taken away — these don't belong to you. But the things that can't be interfered with — those are yours. And whether something is good or evil? God made that yours too. He did this because he cares for us and protects us like a father.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: But you say, I have parted from a certain person, and he is grieved. Why did he consider as his own that which belongs to another? why, when he looked on you and was rejoiced, did he not also reckon that you are a mortal, that it is natural for you to part from him for a foreign country? Therefore he suffers the consequences of his own folly. But why do you or for what purpose bewail yourself? Is it that you also have not thought of these things? but like poor women who are good for nothing, you have enjoyed all things in which you took pleasure, as if you would always enjoy them, both places and men and conversation; and now you sit and weep because you do not see the same persons and do not live in the same places.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: But you say, "I left someone, and now they're upset." Why did they think you belonged to them? When they looked at you and felt happy, why didn't they also remember that you're mortal? That it's natural for you to leave for another country? They're suffering because of their own foolishness.
