But why are you crying? What's the point of feeling sorry for yourself? Have you not thought about these things either? Like useless women, you enjoyed everything that gave you pleasure as if it would last forever — places, people, conversations. And now you sit there weeping because you don't see the same faces or live in the same places.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Indeed you deserve this, to be more wretched than crows and ravens who have the power of flying where they please and changing their nests for others, and crossing the seas without lamenting or regretting their former condition. Yes, but this happens to them because they are irrational creatures. Was reason then given to us by the gods for the purpose of unhappiness and misery, that we may pass our lives in wretchedness and lamentation? Must all persons be immortal and must no man go abroad, and must we ourselves not go abroad, but remain rooted like plants; and if any of our familiar friends goes abroad, must we sit and weep; and on the contrary, when he returns, must we dance and clap our hands like children?
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: You deserve to be more miserable than crows and ravens. They can fly wherever they want. They can change nests. They can cross oceans without crying or regretting what they left behind. But wait — they do this because they don't think like we do. So did the gods give us reason just to make us unhappy and miserable? Are we supposed to spend our lives being wretched and complaining? Should everyone live forever? Should no one ever travel? Should we never leave home but stay rooted like plants? And when a friend travels, should we sit around crying? Then when they come back, should we dance and clap like little children?

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: But my mother laments when she does not see me. Why has she not learned these principles? and I do not say this, that we should not take care that she may not lament, but I say that we ought not to desire in every way what is not our own. And the sorrow of another is another's sorrow; but my sorrow is my own. I then will stop my own sorrow by every means, for it is in my power; and the sorrow of another I will endeavor to stop as far as I can; but I will not attempt to do it by every means; for if I do, I shall be fighting against God, I shall be opposing Zeus and shall be placing myself against him in the administration of the universe; and the reward (the punishment) of this fighting against God and of this disobedience not only will the children of my children pay, but I also shall myself, both by day and by night, startled by dreams, perturbed, trembling at every piece of news, and having my tranquillity depending on the letters of others.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: But my mother grieves when she doesn't see me. Why hasn't she learned these principles? I'm not saying we shouldn't try to prevent her grief. I'm saying we shouldn't desperately want to control what isn't ours to control. Another person's sorrow belongs to them. My sorrow belongs to me. I'll stop my own sorrow by any means necessary, because that's in my power. I'll try to help with another person's sorrow as much as I reasonably can. But I won't try to control it completely. If I do that, I'll be fighting against God. I'll be opposing Zeus and setting myself against the way the universe works. The punishment for this fight against God and this disobedience won't just fall on my children's children. I'll pay for it myself, day and night. I'll be startled by dreams, disturbed, trembling at every bit of news, and my peace of mind will depend on other people's letters.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Some person has arrived from Rome. I only hope there is no harm. But what harm can happen to you, where you are not? From Hellas (Greece) some one is come; I hope that there is no harm. In this way every place may be the cause of misfortune to you. Is it not enough for you to be unfortunate there where you are, and must you be so even beyond sea, and by the report of letters? Is this the way in which your affairs are in a state of security? Well then suppose that my friends have died in the places which are far from me. What else have they suffered than that which is the condition of mortals? Or how are you desirous at the same time to live to old age, and at the same time not to see the death of any person whom you love?
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Someone has come from Rome. I just hope nothing bad happened. But what harm can reach you when you're not even there? Someone comes from Greece. I hope nothing bad happened there either. This way, every place in the world becomes a source of worry for you. Isn't it enough to be miserable where you actually are? Do you have to be miserable about places across the sea too, just because of some letter? Is this what you call having your life under control? So suppose my friends died in distant places. What happened to them except what happens to all humans? How can you want to live to old age and also never see anyone you love die?

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Know you not that in the course of a long time many and various kinds of things must happen; that a fever shall overpower one, a robber another, and a third a tyrant? Such is the condition of things around us, such are those who live with us in the world; cold and heat, and unsuitable ways of living, and journeys by land, and voyages by sea, and winds, and various circumstances which surround us, destroy one man, and banish another, and throw one upon an embassy and another into an army. Sit down then in a flutter at all these things, lamenting, unhappy, unfortunate, dependent on another, and dependent not on one or two, but on ten thousands upon ten thousands.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Don't you know that over a long life, all kinds of things will happen? Fever will kill one person. A robber will kill another. A tyrant will kill someone else. This is how the world works. This is what the people around us face. Cold and heat, unhealthy living, travel by land and sea, storms, and countless other circumstances — they destroy one person, exile another, send one on a diplomatic mission and another to war. So don't sit there panicking about all these things. Don't sit there crying, miserable, calling yourself unlucky, depending on others — and not just one or two people, but thousands and thousands of them.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Did you hear this when you were with the philosophers? did you learn this? do you not know that human life is a warfare? that one man must keep watch, another must go out as a spy, and a third must fight? and it is not possible that all should be in one place, nor is it better that it should be so. But you neglecting to do the commands of the general complain when anything more hard than usual is imposed on you, and you do not observe what you make the army become as far as it is in your power; that if all imitate you, no man will dig a trench, no man will put a rampart round, nor keep watch, nor expose himself to danger, but will appear to be useless for the purposes of an army.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Didn't you hear this when you studied with the philosophers? Didn't you learn this? Don't you know that human life is like being at war? One person has to stand guard. Another has to go out and spy. A third has to fight. Not everyone can be in the same place. And it wouldn't be better if they were. But you ignore the general's orders. Then you complain when something harder than usual gets assigned to you. You don't see what you're doing to the army. If everyone copies you, no one will dig trenches. No one will build walls. No one will keep watch or put themselves in danger. Everyone will be useless as soldiers.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Again, in a vessel if you go as a sailor, keep to one place and stick to it. And if you are ordered to climb the mast, refuse; if to run to the head of the ship, refuse; and what master of a ship will endure you? and will he not pitch you overboard as a useless thing, an impediment only and bad example to the other sailors? And so it is here also: every man's life is a kind of warfare, and it is long and diversified. You must observe the duty of a soldier and do every thing at the nod of the general; if it is possible, divining what his wishes are; for there is no resemblance between that general and this, neither in strength nor in superiority of character.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Say you're on a ship as a sailor. You can't just stay in one spot and refuse to move. If the captain orders you to climb the mast, you can't refuse. If he tells you to run to the front of the ship, you can't refuse. What ship captain would put up with you? He'd throw you overboard as a useless burden and a bad example to the other sailors. Life works the same way. Everyone's life is like being at war — a long war with many battles. You must do your duty like a soldier. Follow every command from your general. If you can, try to figure out what he wants before he even asks. But this general we serve in life is nothing like an earthly general. He's far stronger and far superior in character.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Know you not that a good man does nothing for the sake of appearance, but for the sake of doing right? What advantage is it then to him to have done right? And what advantage is it to a man who writes the name of Dion to write it as he ought? The advantage is to have written it. Is there no reward then? Do you seek a reward for a good man greater than doing what is good and just? At Olympia you wish for nothing more, but it seems to you enough to be crowned at the games. Does it seem to you so small and worthless a thing to be good and happy? For these purposes being introduced by the gods into this city (the world), and it being now your duty to undertake the work of a man, do you still want nurses also and a mamma, and do foolish women by their weeping move you and make you effeminate? Will you thus never cease to be a foolish child? know you not that he who does the acts of a child, the older he is, the more ridiculous he is?
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Don't you know that a good person doesn't act for show? They act because it's right. What's the benefit of doing the right thing? What's the benefit to someone who writes the name 'Dion' correctly? The benefit is that they wrote it correctly. Isn't there a reward then? Do you want a bigger reward for being good than simply doing what's good and just? At the Olympics, you don't want anything more than winning. Being crowned at the games seems like enough. Does being good and happy seem like such a small, worthless thing to you? The gods brought you into this world for these purposes. Now it's your job to do the work of an adult. Do you still want nurses and mommy? Will you let foolish women make you weak with their crying? Will you never stop being a foolish child? Don't you know that the older someone gets, the more ridiculous they look acting like a child?

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: So in this matter also: if you kiss your own child, or your brother or friend, never give full license to the appearance ([Greek: phantasian]), and allow not your pleasure to go as far as it chooses; but check it, and curb it as those who stand behind men in their triumphs and remind them that they are mortal. Do you also remind yourself in like manner, that he whom you love is mortal, and that what you love is nothing of your own; it has been given to you for the present, not that it should not be taken from you, nor has it been given to you for all time, but as a fig is given to you or a bunch of grapes at the appointed season of the year. But if you wish for these things in winter, you are a fool. So if you wish for your son or friend when it is not allowed to you, you must know that you are wishing for a fig in winter. For such as winter is to a fig, such is every event which happens from the universe to the things which are taken away according to its nature.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Here's how to handle this: when you kiss your child, your brother, or your friend, don't let your feelings run wild. Don't let your joy go wherever it wants. Hold it back. Control it like those people who stand behind generals during victory parades and whisper "remember, you're mortal." You do the same thing. Remind yourself that the person you love will die. What you love doesn't really belong to you. It's been given to you for now — not permanently, and not forever. It's like a fig or grapes that come in their season. If you want figs in winter, you're being foolish. So if you want your son or friend when they're gone, know that you're asking for figs in winter. Winter is to figs what death is to the people we lose — it's just the natural order.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: And further, at the times when you are delighted with a thing, place before yourself the contrary appearances. What harm is it while you are kissing your child to say with a lisping voice: To-morrow you will die; and to a friend also: To-morrow you will go away or I shall, and never shall we see one another again? But these are words of bad omen—and some incantations also are of bad omen; but because they are useful, I don't care for this; only let them be useful. But do you call things to be of bad omen except those which are significant of some evil? Cowardice is a word of bad omen, and meanness of spirit, and sorrow, and grief, and shamelessness. These words are of bad omen; and yet we ought not to hesitate to utter them in order to protect ourselves against the things. Do you tell me that a name which is significant of any natural thing is of evil omen?
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Here's another thing: when you're enjoying something, remind yourself it won't last forever. What's wrong with kissing your child and whispering, "Tomorrow you might die"? Or saying to a friend, "Tomorrow one of us will leave and we'll never see each other again"? You say these are unlucky words. Some spells are unlucky too. But if they help us, who cares? As long as they're useful. What makes words unlucky anyway — just that they point to something bad? Cowardice is an unlucky word. So is pettiness, sadness, grief, and shamelessness. These are all unlucky words. But we shouldn't be afraid to say them if they protect us from the actual things. Are you telling me that any word describing something natural is bad luck?

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: say that even for the ears of corn to be reaped is of bad omen, for it signifies the destruction of the ears, but not of the world. Say that the falling of the leaves also is of bad omen, and for the dried fig to take the place of the green fig, and for raisins to be made from the grapes. For all these things are changes from a former state into other states; not a destruction, but a certain fixed economy and administration. Such is going away from home and a small change: such is death, a greater change, not from the state which now is to that which is not, but to that which is not now. Shall I then no longer exist? You will not exist, but you will be something else, of which the world now has need; for you also came into existence not when you chose, but when the world had need of you.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Say that even harvesting corn is a bad sign, because it means destroying the ears of corn — but not destroying the world. Say that leaves falling is also a bad sign. Say that dried figs replacing fresh figs is bad, and grapes becoming raisins is bad. All these things are just changes from one state to another. They're not destruction — they're part of a fixed system and natural order. Going away from home is like this — a small change. Death is like this too — a bigger change. You don't go from existing to not existing. You go from what you are now to something you're not now. Will I stop existing then? You won't exist as you are, but you'll become something else that the world needs. You didn't choose when to come into existence either. You came when the world needed you.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Let these thoughts be ready to hand by night and by day; these you should write, these you should read; about these you should talk to yourself and to others. Ask a man: Can you help me at all for this purpose? and further, go to another and to another. Then if anything that is said be contrary to your wish, this reflection first will immediately relieve you, that it is not unexpected. For it is a great thing in all cases to say: I knew that I begot a son who is mortal.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Keep these ideas ready at all times — day and night. Write them down. Read them. Talk about them with yourself and others. Ask people: Can you help me with this? Then go ask someone else, and someone else. When something happens that you don't like, this thought will help you right away: it's not a surprise. It makes a huge difference to be able to say: I knew I had a mortal son.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: For so you also will say: I knew that I am mortal, I knew that I may leave my home, I knew that I may be ejected from it, I knew that I may be led to prison. Then if you turn round and look to yourself, and seek the place from which comes that which has happened, you will forthwith recollect that it comes from the place of things which are out of the power of the will, and of things which are not my own. What then is it to me? Then, you will ask, and this is the chief thing: And who is it that sent it? The leader, or the general, the state, the law of the state. Give it me then, for I must always obey the law in everything.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: You'll say to yourself: I knew I would die someday. I knew I might have to leave home. I knew I could be kicked out. I knew I might go to prison. When you turn around and look at yourself, ask where this thing that happened came from. You'll quickly remember it comes from things outside your control — things that aren't really yours. So what is it to me? Then you'll ask the most important question: Who sent this? The leader? The general? The state? The law? Give it to me then. I must always obey the law in everything.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Then, when the appearance (of things) pains you, for it is not in your power to prevent this, contend against it by the aid of reason, conquer it: do not allow it to gain strength nor to lead you to the consequences by raising images such as it pleases and as it pleases. If you be in Gyara, do not imagine the mode of living at Rome, and how many pleasures there were for him who lived there and how many there would be for him who returned to Rome; but fix your mind on this matter, how a man who lives in Gyara ought to live in Gyara like a man of courage. And if you be in Rome, do not imagine what the life in Athens is, but think only of the life in Rome.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: When something looks bad and upsets you — and you can't stop that first reaction — fight back with reason. Beat it. Don't let it grow stronger or drag you into its consequences by painting whatever pictures it wants in your mind. If you're stuck in Gyara, don't fantasize about the good life in Rome. Don't think about all the pleasures someone had there or all the pleasures you'd have if you went back. Focus on this: how should a brave person live in Gyara? Live like that. And if you're in Rome, don't daydream about life in Athens. Think only about life in Rome.

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Then in the place of all other delights substitute this, that of being conscious that you are obeying God, that not in word, but in deed you are performing the acts of a wise and good man. For what a thing it is for a man to be able to say to himself: Now whatever the rest may say in solemn manner in the schools and may be judged to be saying in a way contrary to common opinion (or in a strange way), this I am doing; and they are sitting and are discoursing of my virtues and inquiring about me and praising me; and of this Zeus has willed that I shall receive from myself a demonstration, and shall myself know if he has a soldier such as he ought to have, a citizen such as he ought to have, and if he has chosen to produce me to the rest of mankind as a witness of the things which are independent of the will: See that you fear without reason, that you foolishly desire what you do desire; seek not the good in things external; seek it in yourselves: if you do not, you will not find it.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Instead of chasing other pleasures, focus on this one: knowing that you're obeying God. Not just talking about it, but actually doing what a wise and good person does. What a feeling it is to say to yourself: "Right now, while others sit in schools talking seriously about virtue and saying things that sound strange to most people, I'm actually living it. They sit around discussing my good qualities, asking about me, praising me. And Zeus wanted me to prove something to myself — to know for myself whether he has the kind of soldier he needs, the kind of citizen he needs. He's chosen me to show the rest of humanity something about the things beyond our control: Look, you're afraid for no reason. You foolishly want what you want. Don't look for good things in external stuff. Look for it in yourselves. If you don't, you won't find it."

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: For this purpose he leads me at one time hither, at another time sends me thither, shows me to men as poor, without authority, and sick; sends me to Gyara, leads me into prison, not because he hates me—far from him be such a meaning, for who hates the best of his servants? nor yet because he cares not for me, for he does not neglect any even of the smallest things; but he does this for the purpose of exercising me and making use of me as a witness to others. Being appointed to such a service, do I still care about the place in which I am, or with whom I am, or what men say about me? and do I not entirely direct my thoughts to God and to his instructions and commands?
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: God leads me here and there for a purpose. Sometimes he shows me to people as poor, powerless, and sick. He sends me to exile, throws me in prison. But not because he hates me — God could never hate his best servants. And not because he doesn't care about me — he doesn't neglect even the smallest things. He does this to train me and to use me as an example for others. Since I'm appointed to this job, why should I care where I am? Or who I'm with? Or what people say about me? Shouldn't I focus completely on God and his instructions and commands?

discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.originalText: Having these things (or thoughts) always in hand, and exercising them by yourself, and keeping them in readiness, you will never be in want of one to comfort you and strengthen you. For it is not shameful to be without something to eat, but not to have reason sufficient for keeping away fear and sorrow. But if once you have gained exemption from sorrow and fear, will there any longer be a tyrant for you, or a tyrant's guard, or attendants on Cæsar? Or shall any appointment to offices at court cause you pain, or shall those who sacrifice in the Capitol on the occasion of being named to certain functions, cause pain to you who have received so great authority from Zeus? Only do not make a proud display of it, nor boast of it; but show it by your acts; and if no man perceives it, be satisfied that you are yourself in a healthy state and happy.
discourses_that-we-ought-not-to-be-moved.plainEnglish: Keep these ideas always ready. Practice them by yourself. Keep them sharp. Then you'll never lack something to comfort and strengthen you. It's not shameful to go without food. But it is shameful not to have enough reason to keep away fear and sadness. Once you're free from sadness and fear, what tyrant can touch you? What can his guards do? What about Caesar's attendants? Will getting some court appointment still hurt you? Will you feel pain watching others sacrifice at the Capitol when they get promoted — you who have received such great authority from Zeus? Just don't show off about it or brag. Show it through your actions. And if no one notices, be satisfied that you yourself are healthy and happy.

discourses_to-those-who-fall-off-desist-.originalText: Consider as to the things which you proposed to yourself at first, which you have secured, and which you have not; and how you are pleased when you recall to memory the one, and are pained about the other; and if it is possible, recover the things wherein you failed. For we must not shrink when we are engaged in the greatest combat, but we must even take blows.
discourses_to-those-who-fall-off-desist-.plainEnglish: Think about the goals you set for yourself at the start. Which ones did you achieve? Which ones didn't you achieve? Notice how remembering your successes makes you happy, while thinking about your failures hurts. If you can, try to recover what you failed at. Don't back down when you're fighting the biggest battle of your life. You have to be willing to take some hits.

discourses_to-those-who-fall-off-desist-.originalText: For the combat before us is not in wrestling and the Pancration, in which both the successful and the unsuccessful may have the greatest merit, or may have little, and in truth may be very fortunate or very unfortunate; but the combat is for good fortune and happiness themselves.
discourses_to-those-who-fall-off-desist-.plainEnglish: The fight we're facing isn't like wrestling or mixed martial arts, where winners and losers can both be highly skilled or completely worthless, and where luck plays a huge role. Our fight is for good fortune and happiness itself.

discourses_to-those-who-fall-off-desist-.originalText: Well then, even if we have renounced the contest in this matter (for good fortune and happiness), no man hinders us from renewing the combat again, and we are not compelled to wait for another four years that the games at Olympia may come again; but as soon as you have recovered and restored yourself, and employ the same zeal, you may renew the combat again; and if again you renounce it, you may again renew it; and if you once gain the victory, you are like him who has never renounced the combat. Only do not through a habit of doing the same thing (renouncing the combat), begin to do it with pleasure, and then like a bad athlete go about after being conquered in all the circuit of the games like quails who have run away.
discourses_to-those-who-fall-off-desist-.plainEnglish: So what if you've given up the fight for a good life and happiness? Nobody's stopping you from starting again. You don't have to wait four years for the next Olympic Games. As soon as you've recovered your strength and found your passion again, you can jump back into the fight. If you quit again, you can start again. If you finally win, you're just like someone who never quit in the first place. Just don't make quitting a habit. Don't start enjoying it. Don't become like a lousy athlete who gets beaten at every competition and runs around like a coward who fled the fight.

discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.originalText:
Are you not ashamed at being more cowardly and more mean than fugitive slaves? How do they when they run away leave their masters? on what estates do they depend, and what domestics do they rely on? Do they not after stealing a little, which is enough for the first days, then afterwards move on through land or through sea, contriving one method after another for maintaining their lives? And what fugitive slave ever died of hunger? But you are afraid lest necessary things should fail you, and are sleepless by night. Wretch, are you so blind, and don't you see the road to which the want of necessaries leads?—Well, where does it lead?—to the same place to which a fever leads, or a stone that falls on you, to death. Have you not often said this yourself to your companions? have you not read much of this kind, and written much? and how often have you boasted that you were easy as to death?

Learn then first what are the things which are shameful, and then tell us that you are a philosopher: but at present do not, even if any other man calls you so, allow it.
discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.plainEnglish:
Aren't you ashamed of being more cowardly and pathetic than runaway slaves? When they escape, how do they leave their masters? What property do they count on? What servants help them? They steal just a little bit — enough for a few days — then they figure out how to survive as they go. They cross land and sea. They come up with one plan after another to stay alive. Has any runaway slave ever starved to death? But you're terrified that you won't have what you need. You lose sleep over it. You fool, are you so blind that you can't see where this fear of lacking necessities leads? Where does it lead? To the same place that fever leads, or a falling stone — to death. Haven't you said this to your friends countless times? Haven't you read and written about this very thing? How often have you bragged that you were comfortable with death?

So learn first what things are truly shameful. Then come tell us you're a philosopher. But right now, don't claim that title — not even if someone else calls you one.

discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.originalText: Is that shameful to you which is not your own act, that of which you are not the cause, that which has come to you by accident, as a headache, as a fever? If your parents were poor, and left their property to others, and if while they live, they do not help you at all, is this shameful to you? Is this what you learned with the philosophers? Did you never hear that the thing which is shameful ought to be blamed, and that which is blamable is worthy of blame? Whom do you blame for an act which is not his own, which he did not do himself? Did you then make your father such as he is, or is it in your power to improve him? Is this power given to you? Well then, ought you to wish the things which are not given to you, or to be ashamed if you do not obtain them?
discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.plainEnglish: Are you ashamed of things that aren't your doing? Things you didn't cause? Things that just happened to you, like a headache or fever? If your parents were poor and left their money to someone else, if they don't help you while they're alive — is that shameful for you? Is this what you learned from the philosophers? Didn't you ever hear that only shameful acts deserve blame? And only things worthy of blame should be blamed? Who do you blame for something they didn't do themselves? Did you make your father the way he is? Can you change him? Do you have that power? No. So why wish for things you can't have? Why be ashamed when you don't get them?

discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.originalText: And have you also been accustomed while you were studying philosophy to look to others and to hope for nothing from yourself? Lament then and groan and eat with fear that you may not have food to-morrow. Tremble about your poor slaves lest they steal, lest they run away, lest they die. So live, and continue to live, you who in name only have approached philosophy, and have disgraced its theorems as far as you can by showing them to be useless and unprofitable to those who take them up; you who have never sought constancy, freedom from perturbation, and from passions; you who have not sought any person for the sake of this object, but many for the sake of syllogisms; you who have never thoroughly examined any of these appearances by yourself, Am I able to bear, or am I not able to bear? What remains for me to do?
discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.plainEnglish: And have you gotten used to studying philosophy while looking to other people for help? Have you learned to expect nothing from yourself? Then go ahead and complain and moan. Eat your meals in fear that you won't have food tomorrow. Shake with worry about your poor slaves — that they might steal from you, run away, or die. Live like this. Keep living like this. You who have only pretended to study philosophy. You who have made its teachings look as worthless as possible by proving they don't help anyone who tries to use them. You never looked for inner strength, peace of mind, or freedom from destructive emotions. You never sought out anyone to help you with these goals. You only looked for people who could teach you clever arguments. You never seriously asked yourself any of these key questions: Can I handle this, or can't I? What should I do next?

discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.originalText: But as if all your affairs were well and secure, you have been resting on the third topic, that of things being unchanged, in order that you may possess unchanged—what? cowardice, mean spirit, the admiration of the rich, desire without attaining any end, and avoidance ([Greek: echchlisin]) which fails in the attempt? About security in these things you have been anxious.
discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.plainEnglish: But you act like everything in your life is fine and secure. So you've been focusing on the third topic — keeping things unchanged so you can hold onto what? Your cowardice, your petty spirit, your worship of rich people, your endless wanting without getting anything, and your failed attempts to avoid what you don't like? That's what you're trying to make secure.

discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.originalText: Ought you not to have gained something in addition from reason, and then to have protected this with security? And whom did you ever see building a battlement all around and encircling it with a wall? And what doorkeeper is placed with no door to watch? But you practise in order to be able to prove—what? You practise that you may not be tossed as on the sea through sophisms, and tossed about from what? Show me first what you hold, what you measure, or what you weigh; and show me the scales or the medimnus (the measure); or how long will you go on measuring the dust? Ought you not to demonstrate those things which make men happy, which make things go on for them in the way as they wish, and why we ought to blame no man, accuse no man, and acquiesce in the administration of the universe?
discourses_to-those-who-fear-want.plainEnglish: Shouldn't you have gained something extra from all your reasoning? And then protected it properly? Have you ever seen anyone build a wall around nothing? What's the point of posting a guard at a door that doesn't exist? You practice so you can prove things — but prove what exactly? You practice so sophisms won't toss you around like waves at sea. But tossed around from what secure position? First show me what you actually hold onto, what you measure, what you weigh. Show me your scales or your measuring cup. How long will you keep measuring dust? Shouldn't you be demonstrating the things that make people happy? The things that help life go the way they want? Why we shouldn't blame anyone or accuse anyone, and why we should accept how the universe works?

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: He is free who lives as he wishes to live; who is neither subject to compulsion nor to hindrance, nor to force; whose movements to action ([Greek: hormai]) are not impeded, whose desires attain their purpose, and who does not fall into that which he would avoid ([Greek: echchliseis aperiptotoi]). Who then chooses to live in error? No man. Who chooses to live deceived, liable to mistake, unjust, unrestrained, discontented, mean? No man. Not one then of the bad lives as he wishes; nor is he then free. And who chooses to live in sorrow, fear, envy, pity, desiring and failing in his desires, attempting to avoid something and falling into it? Not one. Do we then find any of the bad free from sorrow, free from fear, who does not fall into that which he would avoid, and does not obtain that which he wishes? Not one; nor then do we find any bad man free.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: A free person lives the way they want to live. They're not forced around or blocked or pushed. Their impulses aren't stopped. They get what they want and avoid what they don't want. Now, who chooses to live in error? Nobody. Who chooses to live deceived, prone to mistakes, unjust, out of control, unhappy, or petty? Nobody. So none of the bad people live as they wish. That means they're not free. And who chooses to live in sorrow, fear, envy, or pity? Who chooses to want things and not get them, or to try avoiding something and fall right into it? Nobody. Do we find any bad people who are free from sorrow and fear? Do we find any who avoid what they don't want and get what they do want? Not one. So we don't find any bad person who is free.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: Further, then, answer me this question, also: does freedom seem to you to be something great and noble and valuable? How should it not seem so? Is it possible then when a man obtains anything so great and valuable and noble to be mean? It is not possible. When then you see any man subject to another or flattering him contrary to his own opinion, confidently affirm that this man also is not free; and not only if he do this for a bit of supper, but also if he does it for a government (province) or a consulship; and call these men little slaves who for the sake of little matters do these things, and those who do so for the sake of great things call great slaves, as they deserve to be. This is admitted also. Do you think that freedom is a thing independent and self-governing? Certainly. Whomsoever then it is in the power of another to hinder and compel, declare that he is not free.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: Now answer this: Does freedom seem great and noble and valuable to you? Of course it does. So is it possible for someone who has something so great and valuable to act in petty ways? No, it's not possible. When you see someone bowing down to another person or flattering them against their own beliefs, say confidently that this person is not free. This applies whether they do it for a free meal or for a government position or high office. Call the people who do this for small rewards 'little slaves.' Call those who do it for big rewards 'great slaves' — that's what they deserve to be called. You agree with this, right? Do you think freedom means being independent and self-governing? Absolutely. Then whoever can be stopped or forced by another person — declare that person is not free.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: And do not look, I entreat you, after his grandfathers and great-grandfathers, or inquire about his being bought or sold, but if you hear him saying from his heart and with feeling, "Master," even if the twelve fasces precede him (as consul), call him a slave. And if you hear him say, "Wretch that I am, how much I suffer," call him a slave. If, finally, you see him lamenting, complaining, unhappy, call him a slave, though he wears a praetexta. If, then, he is doing nothing of this kind do not yet say that he is free, but learn his opinions, whether they are subject to compulsion, or may produce hindrance, or to bad fortune, and if you find him such, call him a slave who has a holiday in the Saturnalia; say that his master is from home; he will return soon, and you will know what he suffers.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: Don't worry about someone's family background or whether they were born into slavery. If you hear someone calling another person "Master" from the heart — even if that person holds the highest office — call him a slave. If you hear him say "Poor me, look how much I suffer," call him a slave. If you see him complaining, whining, or miserable, call him a slave, even if he wears the finest clothes. But if he doesn't do any of these things, don't assume he's free yet. Look at his opinions. Are they controlled by outside forces? Can they be blocked or ruined by bad luck? If so, call him a slave on vacation. His master is just away for now. When the master returns, you'll see what he really suffers.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: What then is that which makes a man free from hindrance and makes him his own master? For wealth does not do it, nor consulship, nor provincial government, nor royal power; but something else must be discovered. What then is that which when we write makes us free from hindrance and unimpeded? The knowledge of the art of writing. What then is it in playing the lute? The science of playing the lute. Therefore in life also it is the science of life. You have then heard in a general way; but examine the thing also in the several parts. Is it possible that he who desires any of the things which depend on others can be free from hindrance? No. Is it possible for him to be unimpeded? No. Therefore he cannot be free. Consider then, whether we have nothing which is in our own power only, or whether we have all things, or whether some things are in our own power, and others in the power of others.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: So what makes a person truly free and in control of their own life? Money doesn't do it. Neither does being a consul or governor or king. Something else must be the answer. What lets you write without obstacles or interference? Knowing how to write. What lets you play the lute without problems? Knowing how to play the lute. So in life, it must be knowing how to live. You've heard this in general terms. Now let's look at the details. Can someone who wants things that depend on other people be free from obstacles? No. Can they be unimpeded? No. So they can't be free. Think about this: do we have nothing that belongs only to us? Do we control everything? Or do we control some things while others control other things?

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: What do you mean? When you wish the body to be entire (sound) is it in your power or not? It is not in my power. When you wish it to be healthy? Neither is this in my power. When you wish it to be handsome? Nor is this. Life or death? Neither is this in my power. Your body then is another's, subject to every man who is stronger than yourself. It is. But your estate is it in your power to have it when you please, and as long as you please, and such as you please? No. And your slaves? No. And your clothes? No. And your house? No. And your horses? Not one of these things. And if you wish by all means your children to live, or your wife, or your brother, or your friends, is it in your power? This also is not in my power.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: What do you mean? When you want your body to be whole and healthy, is that up to you or not? It's not up to me. When you want it to be healthy? That's not up to me either. When you want it to be attractive? That's not up to me. Life or death? That's not up to me either. So your body belongs to someone else. It's subject to anyone stronger than you. That's right. But what about your property — can you have it when you want, for as long as you want, exactly as you want it? No. What about your slaves? No. Your clothes? No. Your house? No. Your horses? Not one of these things. And if you desperately want your children to live, or your wife, or your brother, or your friends — is that up to you? That's not up to me either.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: Whether then have you nothing which is in your own power, which depends on yourself only and cannot be taken from you, or have you anything of the kind? I know not. Look at the thing then thus, and examine it. Is any man able to make you assent to that which is false? No man. In the matter of assent then you are free from hindrance and obstruction. Granted. Well; and can a man force you to desire to move towards that to which you do not choose? He can, for when he threatens me with death or bonds he compels me to desire to move towards it. If then you despise death and bonds, do you still pay any regard to him? No. Is then the despising of death an act of your own or is it not yours? It is my act.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: So do you have nothing that belongs only to you? Nothing that depends entirely on yourself and can't be taken away? Or do you have something like that? I don't know. Look at it this way and think it through. Can anyone make you believe something that's false? No one can. So when it comes to what you believe, you're free. No one can block you or get in your way. Fair enough. Now, can someone force you to want to do something you don't want to do? Yes, he can. When he threatens me with death or prison, he makes me want to go along with it. But what if you don't fear death or prison? Do you still care what he says? No. So is despising death your own choice, or isn't it? It's my choice.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: When you have made this preparation, and have practised this discipline, to distinguish that which belongs to another from that which is your own, the things which are subject to hindrance from those which are not, to consider the things free from hindrance to concern yourself, and those which are not free not to concern yourself, to keep your desire steadily fixed to the things which do concern yourself, and turned from the things which do not concern yourself; do you still fear any man? No one. For about what will you be afraid? About the things which are your own, in which consists the nature of good and evil? and who has power over these things? who can take them away? who can impede them? No man can, no more than he can impede God. But will you be afraid about your body and your possessions, about things which are not yours, about things which in no way concern you?
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: Once you've done this work — once you've practiced telling the difference between what belongs to others and what belongs to you, between what can be blocked and what can't be blocked — then you focus only on what can't be blocked and ignore what can be blocked. You keep your desires fixed on what's actually your concern and turn away from what's not your concern. Do you still fear anyone? No. What would you be afraid of? The things that are truly yours — where good and evil actually exist? Who has power over those? Who can take them away? Who can stop them? No one can. No more than they can stop God. But are you going to be afraid about your body and your stuff? About things that aren't yours? About things that don't concern you at all?

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: and what else have you been studying from the beginning than to distinguish between your own and not your own, the things which are in your power and not in your power, the things subject to hindrance and not subject? and why have you come to the philosophers? was it that you may nevertheless be unfortunate and unhappy? You will then in this way, as I have supposed you to have done, be without fear and disturbance. And what is grief to you? for fear comes from what you expect, but grief from that which is present. But what further will you desire? For of the things which are within the power of the will, as being good and present, you have a proper and regulated desire; but of the things which are not in the power of the will you do not desire any one, and so you do not allow any place to that which is irrational, and impatient, and above measure hasty.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: What else have you been studying from day one? How to tell what's yours from what isn't. What you control from what you don't. What can be stopped from what can't. Why did you come to philosophers in the first place? So you could stay miserable? If you've done what I think you have, you'll be fearless and calm. What's grief to you now? Fear comes from what you expect to happen. Grief comes from what's happening right now. But what more could you want? You have proper, controlled desires for the good things that are up to you. You don't want anything that's not up to you. So there's no room left for anything irrational, impatient, or wildly rushed.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: Then after receiving everything from another and even yourself, are you angry and do you blame the giver if he takes anything from you? Who are you, and for what purpose did you come into the world? Did not he (God) introduce you here, did he not show you the light, did he not give you fellow-workers, and perceptions and reason? and as whom did he introduce you here? did he not introduce you as subject to death, and as one to live on the earth with a little flesh, and to observe his administration, and to join with him in the spectacle and the festival for a short time?
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: You've received everything from someone else — even your own self. So why do you get angry and blame the giver when he takes something back from you? Who are you anyway? Why are you here? Didn't God bring you into this world? Didn't he show you the light, give you other people to work with, and give you the ability to see and think? And what did he make you? He made you mortal. He put you on earth in a fragile body to watch how he runs things and to join the show and celebration for a little while.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: Will you not then, as long as you have been permitted, after seeing the spectacle and the solemnity, when he leads you out, go with adoration of him and thanks for what you have heard and seen? No; but I would still enjoy the feast. The initiated too would wish to be longer in the initiation; and perhaps also those at Olympia to see other athletes. But the solemnity is ended; go away like a grateful and modest man; make room for others; others also must be born, as you were, and, being born, they must have a place, and houses, and necessary things. And if the first do not retire, what remains? Why are you insatiable? Why are you not content? why do you contract the world? Yes, but I would have my little children with me and my wife.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: So you've been allowed to watch the show and take part in the ceremony. When it's time to leave, won't you go with gratitude and thanks for what you've experienced? "No," you say, "I want to keep enjoying the feast." The people at religious ceremonies want to stay longer too. So do the spectators at the Olympic games — they want to see more athletes compete. But the ceremony is over. Leave like a grateful and humble person. Make room for others. Other people need to be born, just like you were. And once they're born, they need space and homes and the basics of life. If the first people never leave, what's left for anyone else? Why can't you ever have enough? Why aren't you satisfied? Why do you try to squeeze the whole world for yourself? "But I want my young children and my wife with me."

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: What, are they yours? do they not belong to the giver, and to him who made you? then will you not give up what belongs to others? will you not give way to him who is superior? Why then did he introduce me into the world on these conditions? And if the conditions do not suit you, depart. He has no need of a spectator who is not satisfied. He wants those who join in the festival, those who take part in the chorus, that they may rather applaud, admire, and celebrate with hymns the solemnity.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: What, do you own these things? Don't they belong to the one who gave them to you — the one who made you? Then why won't you give back what belongs to someone else? Why won't you step aside for someone who's in charge? "But why did he bring me into the world under these conditions?" If you don't like the conditions, leave. He doesn't need spectators who complain. He wants people who join the celebration — people who take part in the dance, who cheer and marvel and sing praise songs for the festival.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: But those who can bear no trouble, and the cowardly, he will not unwillingly see absent from the great assembly ([Greek: panaeguris]) for they did not when they were present behave as they ought to do at a festival nor fill up their place properly, but they lamented, found fault with the deity, fortune, their companions; not seeing both what they had, and their own powers, which they received for contrary purposes, the powers of magnanimity, of a generous mind, manly spirit, and what we are now inquiring about, freedom. For what purpose then have I received these things? To use them. How long? So long as he who has lent them chooses. What if they are necessary to me? Do not attach yourself to them and they will not be necessary; do not say to yourself that they are necessary, and then they are not necessary.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: But those who can't handle any trouble, and cowards — he won't mind seeing them absent from the great gathering. When they were present, they didn't act as they should at a festival. They didn't fill their proper place. Instead, they complained, blamed God, blamed fortune, blamed their companions. They couldn't see what they had or their own powers, which were given to them for the opposite purpose — powers of courage, generosity, manliness, and what we're talking about now: freedom. So why did I receive these things? To use them. For how long? As long as the one who lent them to me decides. What if they're necessary to me? Don't attach yourself to them and they won't be necessary. Don't tell yourself they're necessary, and then they're not necessary.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: You then, a man may say, are you free? I wish, by the gods, and pray to be free; but I am not yet able to face my masters, I still value my poor body, I value greatly the preservation of it entire, though I do not possess it entire. But I can point out to you a free man, that you may no longer seek an example. Diogenes was free. How was he free? Not because he was born of free parents, but because he was himself free, because he had cast off all the handles of slavery, and it was not possible for any man to approach him, nor had any man the means of laying hold of him to enslave him.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: Someone might ask you: "So are you free?" I wish I were! By the gods, I pray to be free. But I'm not there yet. I still can't face my masters. I still value my pathetic body. I care too much about keeping it safe and whole, even though it's not really mine. But I can show you a truly free man, so you don't have to keep looking for an example. Diogenes was free. How was he free? Not because his parents were free citizens. He was free because he made himself free. He threw away all the handles that slavery uses to grab you. No one could get close enough to him to put chains on him. No one had any way to get a grip on him and make him a slave.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: Therefore see what Diogenes himself says and writes: "For this reason," he says, "Diogenes, it is in your power to speak both with the King of the Persians and with Archidamus the King of the Lacedaemonians, as you please." Was it because he was born of free parents? I suppose all the Athenians and all the Lacedaemonians, because they were born of slaves, could not talk with them (these kings) as they wished, but feared and paid court to them. Why then does he say that it is in his power? Because I do not consider the poor body to be my own, because I want nothing, because law is everything to me, and nothing else is. These were the things which permitted him to be free.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: So look at what Diogenes himself says and writes: "For this reason," he says, "Diogenes, it is in your power to speak both with the King of Persia and with Archidamus the King of Sparta, however you want." Was it because he was born to free parents? I guess all the Athenians and all the Spartans, because they were born to slaves, couldn't talk with these kings as they wished. Instead they were afraid and sucked up to them. So why does he say it's in his power? Because I don't consider this weak body to be mine. Because I want nothing. Because law is everything to me, and nothing else matters. These things are what let him be free.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: Think of these things, these opinions, these words; look to these examples, if you would be free, if you desire the thing according to its worth. And what is the wonder if you buy so great a thing at the price of things so many and so great? For the sake of this which is called liberty, some hang themselves, others throw themselves down precipices, and sometimes even whole cities have perished; and will you not for the sake of the true and unassailable and secure liberty give back to God when he demands them the things which he has given? Will you not, as Plato says, study not to die only, but also to endure torture, and exile, and scourging, and, in a word, to give up all which is not your own? If you will not, you will be a slave among slaves, even if you be ten thousand times a consul; and if you make your way up to the palace (Cæsar's residence), you will no less be a slave; and you will feel that perhaps philosophers utter words which are contrary to common opinion (paradoxes), as Cleanthes also said, but not words contrary to reason.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: Think about these ideas, these beliefs, these words. Look at these examples if you want to be free — if you want freedom for what it's really worth. And why be surprised if you have to pay a high price for something so valuable? For the sake of what people call liberty, some kill themselves. Others throw themselves off cliffs. Sometimes entire cities have been destroyed. So won't you give back to God what he gave you when he asks for it — for the sake of true, unshakeable, secure freedom? Won't you do what Plato says and learn not just to die, but to endure torture, exile, beatings — in short, to give up everything that isn't really yours? If you won't, you'll be a slave among slaves. Even if you become consul ten thousand times. Even if you make it to Caesar's palace. You'll still be a slave. And you'll discover that maybe philosophers say things that sound crazy to most people — as Cleanthes said — but they don't say things that go against reason.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: For you will know by experience that the words are true, and that there is no profit from the things which are valued and eagerly sought to those who have obtained them; and to those who have not yet obtained them there is an imagination ([Greek: phantasia]), that when these things are come, all that is good will come with them; then, when they are come, the feverish feeling is the same, the tossing to and fro is the same, the satiety, the desire of things, which are not present; for freedom is acquired not by the full possession of the things which are desired, but by removing the desire.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: You'll learn from experience that these words are true. The things people value and chase after don't actually benefit those who get them. And for those who don't have them yet, there's this fantasy that once they get these things, everything good will come with them. But when they finally get them, the restless feeling is the same. The tossing and turning is the same. The dissatisfaction is the same. The wanting of things they still don't have is the same. You don't get freedom by getting everything you want. You get it by stopping the wanting.

discourses_about-freedom.originalText: And that you may know that this is true, as you have labored for those things, so transfer your labor to these: be vigilant for the purpose of acquiring an opinion which will make you free; pay court to a philosopher instead of to a rich old man; be seen about a philosopher's doors; you will not disgrace yourself by being seen; you will not go away empty nor without profit, if you go to the philosopher as you ought, and if not (if you do not succeed), try at least; the trial (attempt) is not disgraceful.
discourses_about-freedom.plainEnglish: You want proof this is true? Then work as hard for wisdom as you worked for other things. Stay alert to develop thoughts that will set you free. Hang around a philosopher instead of sucking up to some rich old man. Be seen at a philosopher's door. You won't embarrass yourself by being there. You won't leave empty-handed or without gaining something — if you approach the philosopher the right way. And if you don't succeed? At least try. There's no shame in trying.

discourses_on-familiar-intimacy.originalText:
To this matter before all you must attend, that
you be never so closely connected with any of your former intimates or
friends as to come down to the same acts as he does. If you do not
observe this rule, you will ruin yourself. But if the thought arises in
your mind, “I shall seem disobliging to him and he will not have the
same feeling towards me,” remember that nothing is done without cost,
nor is it possible for a man if he does not do the same things to be
the same man that he was. Choose then which of the two you will have,
to be equally loved by those by whom you were formerly loved, being the
same with your former self; or, being superior, not to obtain from your
friends the same that you did before.
discourses_on-familiar-intimacy.plainEnglish: Pay attention to this above all else: never get so close to your old friends that you start doing the same things they do. If you don't follow this rule, you'll destroy yourself. You might think, "He'll be offended and won't like me as much." Remember that nothing comes without a price. You can't do different things and still be the same person you were. So choose: do you want to be loved the same way by the same people, staying exactly who you were before? Or do you want to become better, knowing your friends might not treat you the same way they used to?

discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.originalText: Keep this thought in readiness, when you lose anything external, what you acquire in place of it; and if it be worth more, never say, I have had a loss; neither if you have got a horse in place of an ass, or an ox in place of a sheep, nor a good action in place of a bit of money, nor in place of idle talk such tranquillity as befits a man, nor in place of lewd talk if you have acquired modesty. If you remember this, you will always maintain your character such as it ought to be.
discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.plainEnglish: Keep this idea ready: when you lose something external, ask what you gained instead. If what you gained is worth more, never say you suffered a loss. Don't call it a loss if you got a horse instead of a donkey, or an ox instead of a sheep. Don't call it a loss if you did something good instead of making money, or found peace instead of empty chatter, or gained modesty instead of crude talk. Remember this, and you'll always keep your character where it should be.

discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.originalText: But if you do not, consider that the times of opportunity are perishing, and that whatever pains you take about yourself, you are going to waste them all and overturn them. And it needs only a few things for the loss and overturning of all—namely, a small deviation from reason. For the steerer of a ship to upset it, he has no need of the same means as he has need of for saving it; but if he turns it a little to the wind, it is lost; and if he does not do this purposely, but has been neglecting his duty a little, the ship is lost. Something of the kind happens in this case also; if you only fall a nodding a little, all that you have up to this time collected is gone.
discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.plainEnglish: But if you don't, realize that your chances are slipping away. Whatever effort you put into improving yourself will be wasted and destroyed. It takes only small things to lose and destroy everything — just a tiny mistake in thinking. A ship's captain doesn't need much to wreck his vessel. He needs skill and attention to save it, but if he turns it just slightly into the wind, it's lost. Even if he doesn't mean to do this — if he just gets careless for a moment — the ship is lost. The same thing happens here. If you just let your guard down a little, everything you've built up until now is gone.

discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.originalText: Attend therefore to the appearances of things, and watch over them; for that which you have to preserve is no small matter, but it is modesty and fidelity and constancy, freedom from the affects, a state of mind undisturbed, freedom from fear, tranquillity, in a word liberty. For what will you sell these things? See what is the value of the things which you will obtain in exchange for these.—But shall I not obtain any such thing for it?—See, and if you do in return get that, see what you receive in place of it. I possess decency, he possesses a tribuneship: he possesses a prætorship, I possess modesty. But I do not make acclamations where it is not becoming: I will not stand up where I ought not; for I am free, and a friend of God. and so I obey him willingly.
discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.plainEnglish: So pay attention to how things appear to you. Watch over your thoughts carefully. What you're trying to protect isn't small stuff. It's your dignity, your honesty, your steady character. It's freedom from wild emotions, a calm mind, freedom from fear, and inner peace. In short — your liberty. What would you sell these things for? Look at what you'd get in exchange. But won't I get something good for it? Look closely. If you do get something back, see what you're really trading for. I have decency — he has a government position. He has high office — I have my dignity. But I don't cheer for things that are wrong. I won't stand when I shouldn't. I'm free, and I'm God's friend. So I obey him willingly.

discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.originalText: But I must not claim (seek) anything else, neither body nor possession, nor magistracy, nor good report, nor in fact anything. For he (God) does not allow me to claim (seek) them, for if he had chosen, he would have made them good for me; but he has not done so, and for this reason I cannot transgress his commands. Preserve that which is your own good in everything; and as to every other thing, as it is permitted, and so far as to behave consistently with reason in respect to them, content with this only. If you do not, you will be unfortunate, you will fail in all things, you will be hindered, you will be impeded. These are the laws which have been sent from thence (from God); these are the orders. Of these laws a man ought to be an expositor, to these he ought to submit, not to those of Masurius and Cassius.
discourses_what-things-we-should-exchang.plainEnglish: I must not chase after anything else — not physical health, not possessions, not positions of power, not a good reputation, not anything external. God doesn't want me chasing these things. If he did, he would have made them truly good for me. But he didn't. So I can't go against his commands. Keep what is truly your own good in everything you do. As for everything else, deal with them as circumstances allow, but only as far as reason permits. Be content with this approach alone. If you don't follow this, you'll be miserable. You'll fail at everything. You'll be blocked and frustrated at every turn. These are the laws sent down from above. These are your orders. You should interpret and follow these divine laws — not the legal codes of Masurius and Cassius.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: Remember that not only the desire of power and of riches makes us mean and subject to others, but even the desire of tranquillity, and of leisure, and of travelling abroad, and of learning. For, to speak plainly, whatever the external thing may be, the value which we set upon it places us in subjection to others. What then is the difference between desiring to be a senator or not desiring to be one; what is the difference between desiring power or being content with a private station; what is the difference between saying, I am unhappy, I have nothing to do, but I am bound to my books as a corpse; or saying, I am unhappy, I have no leisure for reading?
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: Remember: it's not just wanting power and wealth that makes you dependent on others. Even wanting peace, free time, travel, or education can do the same thing. Here's the truth: whatever outside thing you value highly will put you under someone else's control. So what's the difference between wanting to be a senator and not wanting to be one? What's the difference between craving power and being happy with ordinary life? What's the difference between saying "I'm miserable because I have nothing to do except sit with my books like a corpse" and saying "I'm miserable because I have no time to read"?

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: For as salutations and power are things external and independent of the will, so is a book. For what purpose do you choose to read? Tell me. For if you only direct your purpose to being amused or learning something, you are a silly fellow and incapable of enduring labor. But if you refer reading to the proper end, what else is this than a tranquil and happy life ([Greek: eusoia])? But if reading does not secure for you a happy and tranquil life, what is the use of it?
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: Greetings and power are external things that aren't up to you. So is a book. Why do you choose to read? Tell me. If you're just reading to be entertained or to learn some facts, you're foolish and can't handle real work. But if you're reading for the right reason, what else could that be except a calm and happy life? If reading doesn't give you a calm and happy life, what's the point?

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: But it does secure this, the man replies, and for this reason I am vexed that I am deprived of it.—And what is this tranquil and happy life, which any man can impede, I do not say Cæsar or Cæsar's friend, but a crow, a piper, a fever, and thirty thousand other things? But a tranquil and happy life contains nothing so sure as continuity and freedom from obstacle. Now I am called to do something: I will go then with the purpose of observing the measures (rules) which I must keep, of acting with modesty, steadiness, without desire and aversion to things external; and then that I may attend to men, what they say, how they are moved; and this not with any bad disposition, or that I may have something to blame or to ridicule; but I turn to myself, and ask if I also commit the same faults. How then shall I cease to commit them? Formerly I also acted wrong, but now I do not: thanks to God.
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: But it does give me security, the man says, and that's why I'm upset that I'm losing it. What kind of peaceful, happy life is this that anyone can mess up? Not just Caesar or his friends, but a crow, a flute player, a fever, or any of thirty thousand other things? A truly peaceful and happy life has nothing more reliable than staying steady and being free from obstacles. Now I'm called to do something. I'll go with the goal of following the right rules. I'll act with humility and steadiness. I won't desperately want or hate external things. Then I can pay attention to people — what they say and how they act. But not with bad intentions, and not so I can find fault or make fun of them. Instead, I turn to myself and ask: Do I make the same mistakes? How can I stop making them? I used to act badly too, but now I don't. Thank God.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: What then is the reason of this? The reason is that we have never read for this purpose, we have never written for this purpose, so that we may in our actions use in a way conformable to nature the appearances presented to us; but we terminate in this, in learning what is said, and in being able to expound it to another, in resolving a syllogism, and in handling the hypothetical syllogism. For this reason where our study (purpose) is, there alone is the impediment. Would you have by all means the things which are not in your power? Be prevented then, be hindered, fail in your purpose.
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: So why does this happen? Because we never read or write with the right goal in mind. We don't study so we can handle life's situations naturally and wisely. Instead, we just want to learn what the books say. We want to explain ideas to others. We want to solve logical puzzles and work through arguments. That's where we put our effort, so that's where we hit roadblocks. Do you insist on wanting things outside your control? Then expect to be blocked, frustrated, and disappointed.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: But if we read what is written about action (efforts, [Greek: hormae]), not that we may see what is said about action, but that we may act well; if we read what is said about desire and aversion (avoiding things), in order that we may neither fail in our desires, nor fall into that which we try to avoid; if we read what is said about duty (officium), in order that remembering the relations (of things to one another) we may do nothing irrationally nor contrary to these relations; we should not be vexed, in being hindered as to our readings, but we should be satisfied with doing the acts which are conformable (to the
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: But what if we read about action not just to see what's written about action, but to actually act well? What if we read about desire and avoiding things so we can get what we want and avoid what we don't want? What if we read about duty so we remember how things relate to each other and never act irrationally or against those relationships? Then we wouldn't get upset when something interrupts our reading. We'd be satisfied with doing the right actions that match what we've learned.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: relations), and we should be reckoning not what so far we have been accustomed to reckon: To-day I have read so many verses, I have written so many; but (we should say), To-day I have employed my action as it is taught by the philosophers; I have not employed my desire; I have used avoidance ([Greek: echchlisei]) only with respect to things which are within the power of my will; I have not been afraid of such a person, I have not been prevailed upon by the entreaties of another; I have exercised my patience, my abstinence, my co-operation with others; and so we should thank God for what we ought to thank him.
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: We shouldn't keep track of what we usually count: 'Today I read this many lines, I wrote this much.' Instead we should say: 'Today I acted the way philosophers teach. I didn't desire things I can't control. I only avoided things that are actually up to me. I wasn't afraid of that person. I didn't give in when someone begged me to do something wrong. I practiced patience, self-control, and cooperation with others.' That's what we should thank God for.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: There is only one way to happiness, and let this rule be ready both in the morning and during the day and by night: the rule is not to look towards things which are out of the power of our will, to think that nothing is our own, to give up all things to the Divinity, to Fortune; to make them the superintendents of these things, whom Zeus also has made so; for a man to observe that only which is his own, that which cannot be hindered; and when we read, to refer our reading to this only, and our writing and our listening. For this reason I cannot call the man industrious, if I hear this only, that he reads and writes; and even if a man adds that he reads all night, I cannot say so, if he knows not to what he should refer his reading.
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: There's only one path to happiness. Keep this rule ready morning, noon, and night: don't focus on things outside your control. Think that nothing truly belongs to you. Give everything up to God, to Fortune — let them manage what Zeus has put them in charge of. You should only pay attention to what's actually yours, what can't be taken from you. When you read, connect it back to this principle. Same with your writing and listening. This is why I can't call someone hardworking just because they read and write. Even if someone reads all night, I won't call them diligent if they don't know how their reading connects to what really matters.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: For neither do you say that a man is industrious if he keeps awake for a girl, nor do I. But if he does it (reads and writes) for reputation, I say that he is a lover of reputation. And if he does it for money, I say that he is a lover of money, not a lover of labor; and if he does it through love of learning, I say that he is a lover of learning. But if he refers his labor to his own ruling power that he may keep it in a state conformable to nature and pass his life in that state, then only do I say that he is industrious.
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: You wouldn't call a man hardworking just because he stays up all night for a girl. Neither would I. But if he reads and writes for fame, I call him fame-seeking. If he does it for money, I call him money-loving, not hardworking. If he does it because he loves learning, I call him a learner. But if he works to keep his mind in its natural state and live according to that — only then do I call him truly hardworking.

discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.originalText: For never commend a man on account of these things which are common to all, but on account of his opinions (principles); for these are the things which belong to each man, which make his actions bad or good. Remembering these rules, rejoice in that which is present, and be content with the things which come in season. If you see anything which you have learned and inquired about occurring to you in your course of life (or opportunely applied by you to the acts of life), be delighted at it.
discourses_to-those-who-are-desirous-of-.plainEnglish: Don't praise someone for things that everyone has in common.
